papers.title: From Decoding Leakage to Full Key Recovery: A Single-Trace Attack on FALCON
papers.abstract: FALCON is one of the post-quantum signature schemes selected by NIST. Its compact keys make it attractive for embedded devices, which are exposed to side-channel attacks. Such attacks on FALCON have so far targeted its Gaussian sampler, its floating-point arithmetic, and its number-theoretic transform. We instead attack a step that runs before any of these and has gone unexamined: the routine that decodes the secret key at the start of every signing. We show that this decoding leaks each secret coefficient through two intermediate values it forms. One arises in the decoding itself, the other in the modular conversion that follows. A profiled template attack on these two points recovers each coefficient of the secret polynomials from a single power trace with $98.32\%$ accuracy. Each prediction also carries a confidence score. A single trace does not recover every coefficient, so we add a key-recovery step. It ranks the predictions by confidence and solves the public key relation $g = h\cdot f$ for the rest, using only linear algebra and no lattice reduction. We evaluate the attack on an off-the-shelf ARM Cortex-M4 running FALCON-1024 at its nominal clock. The attack recovers the complete secret key for all 1000 tested keys, requiring 11.04 seconds on average. The decoding routine is shared across FALCON implementations, and the countermeasures proposed for the sampler and the arithmetic do not cover it. It must therefore be protected before FALCON is deployed.
papers.authors: Merve Karabulut, Panasayya Yalla, Reza Azarderakhsh, Mehran Mozaffari Kermani

papers.title: Quorus 2.0: Practical and Scalable Threshold Signature Scheme for NIST-Standardized ML-DSA
papers.abstract: ML-DSA is a widely adopted post-quantum signature algorithm, standardized by NIST as FIPS 204. A threshold signature scheme for ML-DSA lets a group of signers, none of whom holds the key, produce signatures that verify under the unmodified, standardized verification. Existing approaches are limited in different ways: they are bound to at most 6 parties, require threshold fully homomorphic encryption, or scale to many parties but spend tens of online rounds and a heavy preprocessing phase involving mixed arithmetic--Boolean computation. Moreover, to avoid evaluating a cryptographic hash function inside multi-party computation (MPC), they reveal the transcripts of rejected signing attempts. To make these transcripts simulatable, they either modify the underlying ML-DSA signing algorithm by adding noise, or rely on a computational assumption beyond those underlying ML-DSA. We first prove that rejected ML-DSA transcripts can be simulated statistically, with no added noise and no additional assumption, so that output signatures follow exactly the standardized distribution. Building on this result, we construct an efficient threshold protocol using only arithmetic modulo ML-DSA's native modulus $q$ that, for the first time, simultaneously (i) scales to any number of parties $n$ with $t<n/2$ malicious corruptions, (ii) has only 4 online signing rounds and $3.3\times$ less online communication than the round-optimized instantiation of the closest previous protocol, Quorus (USENIX Security~'26), which takes 16 rounds, (iii) has a far lighter preprocessing phase, with fewer than 20 rounds against 81 to 108 for Quorus, and over an order of magnitude less communication as the number of parties grows, and (iv) avoids any extra primitive or assumption beyond those underlying ML-DSA. In a wide-area deployment with tens of parties spread over different continents worldwide, the online phase of our protocol completes in under a second.
papers.authors: Alexander Bienstock, Leo de Castro, Antigoni Polychroniadou, Akash Shah, Akira Takahashi

papers.title: End-to-End Framework for Maliciously Secure Threshold Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: We study $t$-out-of-$n$ threshold homomorphic encryption (ThHE) and its instantiation as a maliciously secure multiparty computation (MPC) protocol. We observe that recent ThHE constructions often focus on individual phases, such as distributed key generation or distributed decryption, rather than providing an end-to-end protocol with a comprehensive security analysis. Furthermore, most existing constructions either consider only passive security or address malicious security at a theoretical level, without providing concrete instantiations or evaluating the associated overhead. Consequently, there remains a lack of practical ThHE constructions that can serve as a drop-in replacement for an MPC functionality while achieving malicious security without relying on additional ideal functionalities for key generation or secure decryption, such as a trusted dealer or an external MPC functionality. In this work, we address these limitations by constructing a ThHE scheme and its associated secure computation protocol in an end-to-end manner, covering all phases from distributed key generation to distributed decryption. We provide a comprehensive security analysis of the resulting protocol against malicious adversaries within the universal composability framework. Furthermore, we quantify the concrete overhead of achieving malicious security by instantiating and benchmarking all the required zero-knowledge arguments of knowledge for verifying the well-formedness of cryptographic materials generated throughout the protocol execution. Our benchmarks demonstrate the practicality of our proof system instantiations, with proving times typically around 5 seconds per phase for a small parameter setting with ring degree $2^{13}$ and a 200-bit ciphertext modulus, and around one minute per phase even for a large parameter setting with ring degree $2^{15}$ and an 800-bit ciphertext modulus, using only a single thread. Furthermore, the resulting proof sizes remain practical, reaching at most 10 MiB per phase, while the public key materials can be as large as 90 MiB.
papers.authors: Intak Hwang, Jinyeong Seo

papers.title: De-Folklorizing Paillier-Based VOLE: UC Security and Reusable Keys
papers.abstract: Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation (VOLE) is a fundamental building block underlying secure computation protocols. Protocols for threshold ECDSA and related applications commonly employ "folkloric" or implicit OLE-like constructions based on Paillier encryption. Although these embedded techniques are used to secure substantial value in the blockchain ecosystem, they lack standalone, context-independent security proofs, preventing their principled use as general-purpose composable building blocks. The practical risk of relying on such components without standalone analyses is illustrated by key-extraction vulnerabilities discovered in more than ten deployed wallets and libraries. In this work, we "de-folklorize" this common approach. We present a two-message Paillier-based VOLE protocol that achieves two central goals: -- We prove its security within the UC framework based on standard cryptographic assumptions. Although the core of Paillier-based OLE follows readily from additive homomorphism, obtaining a standalone UC-secure realization requires resolving nontrivial challenges arising from maliciously generated long-lived keys, the mismatch between Paillier plaintext arithmetic and VOLE's field arithmetic, and the concurrent reuse of shared setup state. -- We address a critical deployment challenge by introducing explicit support for key reusability. We separate the protocol and its ideal functionality into an initialization phase and a subsequent repeatable execution phase. A single Paillier key can then be securely reused across any polynomial number of concurrent executions and across multiple clients, each of which receives and verifies a one-message, client-specific setup. Consequently, a server supporting $M$ clients maintains just one persistent Paillier secret-key state. Finally, we validate our protocol through an experimental evaluation. Although our protocol has lower computational throughput than the state-of-the-art OT-based approach, it remains bandwidth-competitive and offers a significant deployment advantage: whereas the OT-based approach requires pairwise initialization and management of $M$ independent dynamic states for $M$ clients, our protocol requires only one persistent server key state, substantially simplifying state management in modern client-server architectures.
papers.authors: Yehuda Lindell, Gil Segev

papers.title: Anamorphism Beyond One-To-One Messaging: PKE with Public-Key Anamorphic Broadcast Encryption
papers.abstract: To date, Anamorphic Cryptography [EC22] has been developed to support the addition of an anamorphic plaintext message to a ciphertext carrying a regular message. The anamorphic message remains hidden even in the presence of a strong adversary that possesses the receiver’s key and/or determined the sent regular message. In this paper, we expand one-to-one encrypted anamorphic communication to one-to-many anamorphism, naturally assuming communication over a broadcast channel. What we show is that using a previously designed public-key encryption scheme, two things can happen: First, the receiver of an added hidden message may be a party different from the actual receiver (i.e., a shadow party) who has initially collaborated with the sender. Secondly, and perhaps more surprisingly, the receiving party need not be a singleton, and can be a number of different shadow (i.e., anonymous) groups, each receiving a different anamorphic message, where all these messages are extracted from one single-receiver ciphertext. The idea of having multiple hidden channels to different shadow groups is highly handy if, for example, the anamorphic messages are warnings with operational instructions, sent to the groups, and will be received by (at least one member of) a group even if the adversary is able to temporarily cut off all but one member of a channel. More specifically, • First, we motivate and formalize the notion of Public-Key Encryption with an Anamorphic Broadcast Mode, starting with the secret-key setting, where the sender and the shadow receivers share secret key material. • We then present, as an initial result of an independent interest, the first lattice-based construction of Anonymous Multi-Channel Broadcast Encryption. It is important to note here that all Multi-Channel Broadcast schemes to date are in the pairing-based setting (and are, thus, insecure against quantum adversaries). • We then show how to transform a strong form of anonymity (where the ciphertext also hides the number of channels) into a system with anamorphism in the multi-channel broadcast setting for the well-known Dual Regev Public-Key Encryption scheme. The resulting anamorphic ciphertext carries the sender’s chosen message and stays indistinguishable from a regular Dual Regev encryption of it even to an adversary holding the receiver’s secret key. • Finally, we remove the shared secret key and obtain a public-key anamorphic broadcast mode, in which the shadow receivers are addressed by their identities. To this end we build an identity-based anonymous multi-channel broadcast scheme whose public parameters are derived from the regular Dual Regev public key, and prove, in the random oracle model under the k-LWE assumption, that it endows Dual Regev with a public-key anamorphic broadcast mode: anamorphic ciphertexts are indistinguishable from regular Dual Regev ciphertexts, and, even when the dictator coerces some shadow receivers into surrendering their keys, it learns only the anamorphic bits addressed to those very receivers, and nothing about the remaining (uncoerced) receivers, neither their identities nor the messages delivered to them.
papers.authors: Xuan Thanh Do, Gaspard Meunier, Giuseppe Persiano, Duong Hieu Phan, Moti Yung

papers.title: (Significantly) Faster Post-Quantum Public-Key PCFs for OT
papers.abstract: Public-Key Pseudorandom Correlation Functions (PK-PCFs) enable N users to locally generate and publish their public keys on a bulletin board, from which any pair of users can non-interactively compute an unbounded number of correlated strings. These outputs can then be used to significantly speed up secure computation protocols. A line of work has focused on building efficient PK-PCFs for Oblivious Transfer (OT) in the post-quantum regime. To this end, the recent work of Agrawal, Bhushan, Couteau and Riahinia (CRYPTO 2026), henceforth ABCR, introduces a family of lattice-based PK-PCFs that can generate 500-1K OTs per second. However, a significant gap remains compared to quantum-insecure counterparts: the state-of-the-art classical (group-based) PK-PCFs for (standard) OTs reach a throughput of roughly 30K OTs per second making them nearly two orders of magnitude faster. In this work, we significantly improve the state-of-the-art of post-quantum PK-PCFs for OTs. We provide a new construction whose security is based on roughly the same lattice-based assumptions as used by ABCR. In contrast, we achieve a much higher throughput; we implement our construction and measure a rate of 208k OTs/sec for the sender, and 189k OTs/sec for the receiver on a single thread, and 746k/709k on six threads. Our key sizes, remain in the megabytes, similar to ABCR. Concretely, sender and receiver respectively store keys of size 188MB and 66MB. Our speedup is obtained via a new blueprint for constructing PK-PCFs from public-key algebraic homomorphic MACs (PK-aHMACs), that we introduce and instantiate. We are optimistic that our ideas will find independent applications.
papers.authors: Shweta Agrawal, Kaartik Bhushan, Geoffroy Couteau, Mahshid Riahinia

papers.title: Stable Private Intersection with Consistency
papers.abstract: Private set intersection (PSI) enables two mutually distrusting parties to learn only the intersection of their private sets. Malicious security for PSI, however, constrains how a party computes and not which inputs it computes on. A party running multiple PSI sessions can use different inputs each time or change its inputs across sessions to bias the output or infer more information from the intersection. Recent work binds parties to committed sets [Goel et al., USENIX Security 2026; Sun et al., CCS 2024, 2025] but gives the sender only weak input consistency. That is, the sender cannot inject elements but it can omit any elements from the intersection. Omitting elements causes (1) false negatives (i.e., an element in both sets is silently dropped from the intersection) and (2) biased outputs (i.e., the sender picks which intersection elements each receiver gets). We introduce Stable Private Intersection with Consistency (SPICy), a framework that binds both parties to their exact committed input sets across an unbounded number of intersections. We define two notions of input consistency: (1) strong input consistency (SIC) wherein each party uses its full committed set, though the receiver's output may still differ from the intersection of the committed sets; (2) complete input consistency (CIC) wherein the receiver's output is the exact intersection of the committed sets. SPICy builds on MiniPSI [Rosulek and Trieu, CCS 2021], the fastest known small-set PSI protocol, through a new primitive, the Mutual Oblivious PRF (MOPRF). In an MOPRF, both parties evaluate a PRF under their own keys, and the receiver learns the sender's output only on elements held by both parties. SPICy achieves CIC for both the sender and receiver and requires a single round of online communication. We implement SPICy in Rust and evaluate it end-to-end on deployed PSI applications. For sets of sizes between 2⁷ and 2¹⁰, SPICy has 1.7–1.9× online runtime overhead and around 4.5× communication overhead compared to MiniPSI.
papers.authors: Manya Garg, Debayan Gupta, Arup Mondal, Aryan Nath

papers.title: Computational Bernoulli Smoothing and Worst-Case Errors in LPN Reductions
papers.abstract: Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) is a central problem in modern post-quantum cryptography. Recently, Aggarwal et al. (TCC 2026) proposed a new approach toward establishing worst-case foundations for the hardness of LPN in the low-noise regime. Their reduction turns an average-case LPN solver into two algorithms such that, for every (worst-case) linear code, either one decodes noisy codewords of that code or the other distinguishes noisy codewords of its dual from uniform. Their main technique, computational code smoothing, relaxes a requirement of earlier reductions: noisy dual codewords need only be computationally pseudorandom, rather than statistically close to uniform. However, their result requires random Bernoulli errors for the decoding alternative (so only the code is worst case) and fixed-weight noise for the dual distinguishing alternative (rather than the more common Bernoulli noise). We remove both of these restrictions using a new analytical technique. As our main technical tool, we establish a computational Bernoulli perturbation bound for finite groups, which may be of independent interest. We show that if multiplying a random group element from some distribution $D$ by a fixed element with probability $\beta<1/2$ produces an $\varepsilon$-pseudorandom distribution, then $D$ itself is $\varepsilon/(1-2\beta)$-pseudorandom. This bound is tight. As a result, for Bernoulli-weighted sums in abelian groups, we show that revealing any $k$ coefficients increases the distinguishing advantage by at most a factor of $(1-2\beta)^{-k}$. This can be viewed as the computational generalization of the Bernoulli smoothing technique of Yu and Zhang (CRYPTO 2021).
papers.authors: Nathan Geier, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan

papers.title: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
papers.abstract: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.
papers.authors: Kelsey A. Jackson, Carl A. Miller

papers.title: Improving Lindell's Two-Party ECDSA: Faster Key Generation and UC Security Without Global Abort
papers.abstract: The two-party ECDSA signing protocol constructed by Lindell (CRYPTO '17) has a substantial implementation footprint across the blockchain industry. Despite its advantage of completely static state management, the protocol admits two main limitations: (1) its key generation phase is computationally intensive due to the usage of somewhat inefficient zero-knowledge proofs, and (2) its security relies on a "global abort" mechanism (requiring that if a certain error is detected then all current and future executions must halt), which poses significant operational challenges in high-throughput environments. In this work we demonstrate that these limitations are not inherent, presenting "drop-in" improvements that preserve the protocol's structure while delivering substantial gains in both efficiency and security: -- Faster key generation. We overcome the main bottleneck in the protocol's key generation by constructing a drastically improved zero-knowledge proof for the Paillier-EC discrete logarithm (PDL) relation. Utilizing aggregated inner-product arguments (Bulletproofs), we address the algebraic mismatch between Paillier encryption and elliptic curves by constructing a "commitment bridge" that links a Paillier ciphertext to a set of Pedersen commitments over an elliptic curve. This allows us to minimize Paillier operations by shifting the computational cost to significantly faster elliptic-curve operations. -- UC security without global abort. We augment the protocol with a highly efficient non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (integrated into the protocol's second message). We prove that this addition eliminates the need for a global abort mechanism, upgrading the protocol's security from its original game-based definition to UC security against malicious adversaries (under the Paillier and Strong RSA assumptions in the random oracle model). We provide rigorous security proofs and report on the performance of a production-grade implementation, demonstrating that our approach reduces the estimated key-generation time by a factor of approximately four and achieves UC security without global abort with minimal signing overhead: less than $22$ms of additional computation per party and only $3.5$KB of additional communication.
papers.authors: Yehuda Lindell, Gil Segev

papers.title: Faulting the Proof: Key Recovery Attacks on MQOM, SDitH and FAEST
papers.abstract: MQOM, SDitH and FAEST are three candidates in the third round of NIST’s additional call for post-quantum signature schemes. The signature in all of them is a proof of knowledge of the secret key. We study their resistance to faults during the computation of this proof and present practical key-recovery attacks on all three schemes. Our attacks exploit a common feature among them: a value that is omitted from the signature to reduce its size is still bound through a hash. We show how an attacker can use this hash to test guesses about secret key material from faulty signatures. This yields new attacks on all three schemes and corrects an earlier analysis of fault attacks on MQOM, which assumed that the omitted value is available to the attacker. We demonstrate the attacks with clock glitches on an STM32F405 microcontroller running code from the round-3 reference implementations. The validated attacks recover the full secret key of all three schemes. These results show that the proof evaluation is a practical fault target in signature schemes based on the MPC-in-the-head and VOLE-in-the-head paradigms.
papers.authors: Mohamed Abdelmonem, Håvard Raddum

papers.title: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality: Fuzzy PSI without $O((\log \delta)^d)$ Overhead
papers.abstract: Private Set Intersection (PSI) enables two parties—a sender holding set $Q$ and a receiver holding set $W$—to securely compute their intersection $Q \cap W$. Fuzzy PSI (FPSI) extends this functionality by allowing the receiver to learn the items $\mathbf{q}\in Q$ for which there exists $\mathbf{w}\in W$ such that $\mathbf{dist}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{w}) \leq \delta$ with respect to some distance metric. This work focuses on FPSI for $L_\infty$ distance, a metric with important practical uses including industrial tolerance verification and cryptographic key matching. Existing FPSI is commonly constructed using fuzzy matching combined with spatial hashing technique. However, these works mainly suffer from one or more of the following limitations: 1. Reliance on strong \textit{separate} assumptions about input distributions; 2. Dependence on computationally expensive public-key operations; 3. Suboptimal asymptotic complexity in fuzzy matching that scales either linearly ($O(d\delta)$) or logarithmically ($O(d\log\delta)$) but with an additional $O((\log\delta)^d)$ factor. This work presents a novel FPSI protocol for $L_\infty$ distance that simultaneously achieves three key improvements. First, our protocol requires only weak \textit{apart} assumptions about input distributions. Second, it only uses OT and symmetric-key operations. Third, it achieves optimal $O(d\log\delta)$ fuzzy matching complexity without introducing $O((\log\delta)^d)$ factor. At the core of our construction lies a newly introduced protocol called secret-shared private intersection test (ssPIT), which may be of independent interest. We give two constructions of ssPIT and use ssPIT to construct a secret-shared version of the fuzzy matching protocol. By combining fuzzy matching and hashing techniques, we obtained our final FPSI protocol. We also extend our protocol to FPSI variants including FPSI-cardinality (FPSI-CA), FPSI with sender privacy (FPSI-SP), and labeled FPSI (LFPSI). We implement our FPSI protocols and compare them with the state-of-the-art FPSI protocols. Experiments show that our protocols perform better than state-of-the-art under all the parameters we tested. Specifically, our protocols achieve a $1.2-174 \times $ speedup in running time and $1.5-97.4 \times$ shrinking in communication cost, depending on set sizes, dimension and distance threshold.
papers.authors: Cong Zhang, Yang Cao, Yujie Bai, Shuaishuai Li, Juntong Lin, Yu Chen, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang

papers.title: One-Bit-per-Gate Distributed Garbling and Constant-Round Malicious MPC
papers.abstract: Distributed garbling, introduced by Beaver, Micali, and Rogaway (BMR), lets N mutually distrustful parties jointly run the garbling algorithm: as long as one of them is honest, the resulting garbled circuit, together with its input, decoding, and authentication keys, satisfies the privacy and authenticity guarantees of the base garbling scheme, as if produced by a single trusted garbler. A long line of work has improved upon BMR, achieving malicious security against all-but-one corruptions and impressive concrete efficiency. However, these protocols all inherit the Ω(𝜆|C|) garbling size of Yao-style schemes, resulting in every garbler incurring Ω(𝜆) bits of communication per circuit gate. We present a distributed garbling protocol in which every garbler communicates an amortized one bit per gate, assuming Ring-LWE and constant-locality PRGs. It enjoys constant round complexity and is secure against a malicious adversary corrupting all but one garbler. Moreover, for sufficiently large circuits C (relative to their depth, input / output length and the security parameter), our garbling scheme and distributed protocols have the following efficiency features: • One bit per gate. The garbled circuit is |C|(1+o (1)) bits, as is each garbler’s total communication for generating and revealing it. • Distributing the garbler is almost free. Each garbler’s communication and computation exceed those of a single trusted garbler by only an additive o(|C|) term. • An efficient base scheme. Our one-bit-per-gate garbling scheme is itself lightweight: garbling is dominated by O(1) operations in the Ring-LWE ring per gate, plus a global computation dependent only on the depth, input, and output lengths of the circuit. Our protocol immediately gives constant-round maliciously secure MPC for any number of parties with per-party communication of one bit per gate, and removes the single point of failure in other applications of garbling, such as enabling distributed generation of ciphertexts in one-key functional encryption or distributed preprocessing in outsourced computation. Previously, for more than two parties, distributed succinct garbling was known only as a feasibility result via running generic MPC on succinct-time RAM garbling schemes, which rely on iO or similarly heavyweight tools and are prohibitively expensive computationally. Since other (more efficient) succinct garbling schemes are only succinct in size rather than time, running said schemes under generic MPC yields communication |C|poly(𝜆) as overhead from the latter.
papers.authors: Hanjun Li, Huijia Lin, George Lu

papers.title: Beskar: Efficient Threshold ML-DSA via Preprocessed Rejection Sampling
papers.abstract: Efficient threshold variants of ML-DSA are important for the transition to post-quantum cryptography, as they allow parties to jointly produce standard ML-DSA signatures without reconstructing the signing key. The main obstacle is rejection sampling: before releasing a candidate signature, the parties must jointly evaluate several norm checks on secret-shared values and restart the computation if any check fails. In existing MPC-based protocols, these checks account for much of the cost of the online phase. We present Beskar, a threshold ML-DSA protocol secure against malicious adversaries in the honest-majority setting. Building on Quorus (Bienstock et al., USENIX 2026), we reduce online signing from sixteen rounds to three and reduce online communication by a factor of 10. Our main technical contribution is a method for moving most of the computation required by rejection sampling into preprocessing and combining the remaining checks with signature release. In contrast to Mithril (Celi et al., USENIX 2026), Beskar relies only on standard secret sharing, rather than short secret sharing, and its expected number of signing attempts does not grow with the number of parties. Our implementation demonstrates practicality with a 5 party threshold signing attempt running in under 700ms in a high latency setting.
papers.authors: Sebastian Kolby, Claudio Orlandi, Stanislas Pawlak

papers.title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed–Solomon Codes
papers.abstract: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.
papers.authors: Valentina Astore, Martino Borello, Alain Couvreur

papers.title: Dovetail: Group-Action Adaptor Signatures via a Heterogeneous Two-Block Construction
papers.abstract: Adaptor signatures bind the adaptation of a pre-signature into a valid signature to the disclosure of a witness, enabling atomic swaps, payment channels, and scriptless scripts. However, existing group-action constructions face key limitations: O-IAS requires commutative actions with costly zero-knowledge proofs, Fast ORCAS incurs prohibitive communication on large group elements, and GATOR couples soundness amplification with pre-signing search cost. We present Dovetail, a group-action adaptor signature scheme built from a heterogeneous two-block construction over multiple public keys. By pairing a large non-cheating block with a small cheating block, Dovetail decouples soundness amplification from pre-signing search cost: the pre-signer fixes both commitments, searches over nonces until the challenge hits a target support, and uses its secret key to adjust the selected responses to the challenged public keys while preserving the ordinary signature format. Following Gerhart et al.\ (EUROCRYPT 2024), we prove Dovetail secure in the classical random oracle model under the Multiple Group Action Inverse Problem ($\mathsf{mGAIP}$). Benchmarks across CSI-FiSh, LESS, MEDS, and ALTEQ at the $128$-bit security level confirm these gains. On actions with large group elements, Dovetail outperforms both GATOR and Fast ORCAS in pre-signature size and pre-signing time, generating $15.39$ kB pre-signatures in $16.25$ ms on LESS ($s=32$, $4.6\times$ faster than Fast ORCAS) and $14.29$ kB pre-signatures in $15.20$ ms on ALTEQ ($s=64$, $121.7\times$ faster than GATOR). On compact-element actions such as CSI-FiSh ($s=4$), it produces $1.32$ kB pre-signatures in $2.49$ s, outperforming both GATOR and O-IAS.
papers.authors: Kexiang Xiong, Gang Tang, Jie Chen, Debiao He

papers.title: EpochPIR: Low Amortized Communication PIR at Near-Optimal Throughput
papers.abstract: Existing single-server private information retrieval (PIR) schemes face a sharp trade-off between server throughput and communication. Schemes built on SimplePIR scan the database at nearly memory bandwidth using native integer arithmetic, but require either a large client-side hint or hundreds of kilobytes of communication per query. Conversely, schemes based on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), such as Spiral, require only a few to tens of kilobytes per query, but process the database several times more slowly. We present EpochPIR, a single-server PIR scheme that achieves amortized communication comparable to Spiral’s while maintaining server throughput close to SimplePIR’s. Our starting point is the observation that SimplePIR queries do not require independent secrets: under a fixed public matrix, the d negacyclic rotations of a single ring-LWE (RLWE) secret can safely serve as the secrets for d consecutive queries under the standard RLWE assumption. Uploading a single encrypted secret once every d queries allows the server to precompute the homomorphic hint-products for the entire batch of d queries, eliminating the per-query homomorphic hint evaluation of prior hintless schemes. Because the rotated secrets form a negacyclic Toeplitz matrix, the server can evaluate all d encrypted hint-products simultaneously in quasilinear time using two-dimensional number-theoretic transforms, producing the results directly in packed RLWE ciphertexts. This yields a modular two-stage framework: a SimplePIR-based column selector reduces PIR over the entire database to homomorphic selection over a single encrypted column, and any FHE row selector using long-lived client evaluation keys can then compress that column into a compact response with minimal impact on overall throughput. Instantiated with a Spiral-style CMUX row selector, EpochPIR retrieves a 256-byte entry from an 8 GB database with 74 KB of communication per query at a sustained single-core throughput of 10.7 GB/s, 77% of SimplePIR’s, without a clientside hint. A communication-optimized variant communicates only 26 KB per query, 41× less than the hintless ReinsPIRe at 97% of its throughput and 25% less than Spiral at 14× its throughput.
papers.authors: Rasoul Akhavan Mahdavi, Sarvar Patel, Joon Young Seo, Kevin Yeo

papers.title: On the Hardness of Decomposed Learning with Errors Problems
papers.abstract: This work strengthens the known hardness reduction for the decision variant of Decomposed Learning With Errors (LWE) problem and additionally presents a reduction of its search variant. The Decomposed LWE is $t$-parametrized variant of LWE, where $t$ denotes the number of decomposed blocks. In both the cases, we reduce $t$-succinct LWE problem to the Decomposed LWE. The exiting hardness reduction for decision variant relies on Gaussian noise flooding paradigm, as a result the modulus-to-noise ratio is super-polynomial of security parameter. In this work, both the reductions hold in polynomial regime for polynomial number of decompositions.
papers.authors: Biswajit Mandal, Shashank Singh

papers.title: Classical Key Agreement with Near-Quadratic Quantum Security
papers.abstract: In 1974, Merkle proposed a key exchange protocol where the honest parties make $N$ queries to a random oracle to compute a secret key, while the best attacker needs to make $\Omega(N^2)$ queries to recover the key with constant probability. This protocol was later proved to be optimal by Barak and Mahmoody (Crypto'09). In the quantum setting, Belovs et al. (TQC'17) proved that for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a classical protocol with $O(N)$ expected honest queries, for which any quantum eavesdropper making $O(N^{1.5-\varepsilon})$ queries has vanishing key recovery probability. In this paper, we give two families of classical key-establishment protocols in the random oracle query model. The first is a two-message protocol and the second is a three-message protocol with perfect agreement. In both cases the honest parties make $\widetilde O(N)$ classical oracle queries, whereas every constant-success quantum eavesdropper needs $\widetilde\Omega(N^2)$ quantum queries to recover the key. Our result is tight up to logarithmic factors, as the quadratic classical attack of Barak and Mahmoody applies in this setting. The construction combines two levels of hidden sum relations. In the two-message protocol, Alice samples random labels and encodes their bits using masked oracle blocks. A zero is encoded by a uniformly random block, while a one is encoded by a block containing a planted sum relation. Bob decodes a random subset of the labels and publishes their sum. Alice uses her original labels to identify this subset, which becomes their shared key. We also give an efficient implementation with $O(N\log N)$ honest oracle queries and $O(N(\log N)^2)$ combined honest running time, for which recovering the key with constant probability requires $\Omega(N^{4/3})$ quantum queries.
papers.authors: Samuel Bouaziz--Ermann

papers.title: Security Analysis of Homogeneous MQ-Based Post-Quantum Signature Schemes
papers.abstract: The security of multivariate cryptography relies on the hardness of solving the public multivariate quadratic (MQ) systems over finite fields. For a homogeneous MQ map $P$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and a nonzero target $t$, Ostuzzi recently introduced the target quotient that removes one equation from $P(x)=t$, and then each solution $x$ of the resulting system has $P(x)=bt$ for some $b\in \mathbb{F}_q$. This implies that a preimage of $t$ can be recovered exactly when $b$ is a nonzero square. In this paper, we first compare reoptimized direct and quotient costs using scheme-specific Wiedemann XL (WXL) gate-count estimates. The comparison covers Hashimoto's method on all 19 recommended UOV, SNOVA, and QR-UOV parameter sets, and Thomae-Wolf (TW) and Furue-Nakamura-Takagi (FNT) on the 13 characteristic-two sets. With the ideal retry multiplier $1/p_0(q)$, where $p_0(q)$ is the acceptance probability for uniform $b$, nominal Hashimoto-WXL savings are 2.04-4.61, 1.81-3.20, and 0.05-2.44 bits, respectively. Over $\mathbb{F}_{256}$, Hashimoto's quotient procedure recovered preimages in 640 of 1,000 reduced-parameter random UOV trials (64.0% overall), corresponding to 640 of 642 non-oil returns (99.69%), close to $255/256$ (99.61%). Second, we establish an exact recovery law in the random UOV model with independent coefficients. Solvers may select solutions with arbitrary bias using only quotient equations and randomness independent of key generation. Averaged over keys and solver randomness, single-trial recovery probability equals $p_0(q)$ times the valid non-oil return probability. With positive return probability, the residual conditional on return is uniform exactly when oil-space returns have probability zero; otherwise zero has excess mass and nonzero values remain equiprobable. We also derive finite recovery bounds under stated geometric candidate conditions and exhaustive residual-blind search; the FNT argument uses collinear-quadruple counting.
papers.authors: Kosuke Sakata, Tsuyoshi Takagi

papers.title: MechCrypto: Agent-Assisted Cryptanalysis of the First-Round NGCC Candidates
papers.abstract: Evaluating large batches of cryptographic submissions demands sustained scrutiny across mathematical design, security proofs, concrete parameters, and implementation code. Although large language model (LLM) agents have begun uncovering genuine flaws in public competitions, general-purpose coding agents remain brittle in cryptanalysis: they routinely miss implicit security notions and community conventions, drift outside the intended parameter or threat-model scope, and lose consistency across coupled proofs, complexity estimates, code, and prior literature. We present MechCrypto, a cryptanalytic research agent built on a persistent graph-structured framework. MechCrypto combines explicit task contracts, typed cross-artifact provenance, adaptively loaded cryptographic knowledge packs, and an independent verification gate that checks both evidential soundness and contract coverage before releasing reproducible artifacts. We evaluate MechCrypto blind on all 119 first-round candidates of the Next-generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms (NGCC) program (34 digital signatures, 41 key encapsulation mechanisms, 9 key exchange protocols, and 35 hash functions) without access to existing NGCC attack reports. The campaign with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 produces 115 comparable principal results, including 23 Critical findings. Against the 24 November 2026 public-results snapshot, MechCrypto achieves higher candidate-level severity on five submissions and identifies 57 principal findings whose underlying mechanisms have no matching public entry. Notably, for MEGASCON, MechCrypto derives an explicit, zero-search collision in the AVX-512 S-box compiled from Listing~3 of the specification, raising the candidate from the public tracker's High rating to Critical. Reports, proofs, code, and campaign data are available at https://github.com/MechMath/NGCC-results.
papers.authors: Zhengyang Wang, Yichuan Cao, Kunyu Wu, Hongbo Li, Xiao-Shan Gao

papers.title: Resource-Aware Deployment of NIST Additional PQC Signatures on Automotive ECUs
papers.abstract: The transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is vital for securing next-generation automotive architectures. However, deploying candidate algorithms from the NIST Round 3 Additional PQC Signature track onto automotive ECUs, such as those based on the Infineon AURIX TC4 (TriCore v1.8 architecture), is severely obstructed by stringent hardware constraints. Standard reference implementations incur excessive stack and heap memory demands that exceed the limited capacity of the core's Data Scratchpad RAM (DSPR), triggering memory overflows and fundamentally jeopardizing real-time predictability and system dependability. To resolve this challenge, this paper presents a systematic software-level memory optimization approach framed as a resource-aware design-space exploration across the NIST Round 3 additional signature candidates. We strategically tailor memory layouts and buffer lifetimes to strictly satisfy the hard DSPR boundaries of the AURIX TC4 core, targeting a core RAM budget of at most 171.4\,kB (with up to 139.4\,kB stack and 32\,kB heap) while offloading non-sensitive artifacts to global RAM, while preserving execution efficiency and worst-case timing behavior for time-critical automotive tasks. We evaluate our optimized implementations of MQOM, SDitH, MAYO, and QR-UOV on real automotive hardware, providing comprehensive empirical benchmarks of execution cycle counts and memory footprints against baseline implementations of ML-DSA and SLH-DSA. Our results identify MAYO-3 with our memory optimizations (MAYO-3-memopt) as the best-performing candidate overall, achieving keygen, sign, and verify times of 10.4\,ms, 24.9\,ms, and 11.5\,ms, respectively, while candidates such as SLH-DSA and SDitH remain unsuitable for on-device signing due to prohibitive execution latency, despite fitting comfortably within the memory budget. Our findings show that not all NIST Round 3 additional signature candidates are equally suited to such constrained environments, but that with targeted memory optimization, at least some can be predictably integrated into memory-constrained automotive controllers without compromising real-time guarantees or system reliability.
papers.authors: Dominik Marchsreiter, Georg Carle

papers.title: ClearWater: A Zero-Knowledge Local-Context Hardware IP Watermarking Framework
papers.abstract: ClearWater embeds hardware IP watermarks during standard-cell placement in LLM-assisted flows and verifies detection without revealing the owner's key. Bounded fan-in contexts identify carrier pairs, and keyed Poseidon2 determines their relative placement order. A Groth16 proof verifies agreement over an externally audited carrier table. In our testbench, routed AES, SHA-256, and ChaCha layouts retained every registered mark with no measured cell-area growth. Copied fragments retained matching bits even when too few survived to support a detection claim. For AES, verification took 16 milliseconds. The public carrier table dominated communication, while timing impact varied across designs.
papers.authors: Sakib Anwar Rieyan, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos

papers.title: Automated Verification of Glitch- and Transition-Robust Composable Masked Circuits via Logic Simulations
papers.abstract: Power analysis attacks can extract sensitive information processed by electronic circuits. To mitigate information leakage, the most common approach is to transform the circuit using the masking countermeasure. Specifically, such a transformation replaces each circuit gate with a masked counterpart, known as a gadget. This process represents a key step in security-aware EDA flows and yields a provably secure circuit, provided that an efficient and provably composable secure gadget library exists. This work contributes to the automated verification of such gadgets, thereby enabling the systematic development of gadget libraries for secure hardware designs. Although several automated solutions exist for verifying the security of gadgets, particularly against glitch-induced leakages under the PINI security notion, an automated method for verifying the absence of joint leakages arising from both glitches and signal transitions, captured by the O-PINI security notion, remains lacking. To address this gap, this work introduces an automated procedure for checking whether a gadget satisfies O-PINI, and provides an analysis report covering the gadgets existing in the literature.
papers.authors: Nicolai Müller, Amir Moradi

papers.title: Exploring Redundant PMNS Arithmetic for Side-Channel Leakage Reduction in ML-DSA
papers.abstract: Polynomial Modular Number Systems (PMNS) have been proposed as an efficient alternative to classical modular arithmetic, with applications to elliptic curve cryptography. While existing work has focused on large-prime arithmetic, lattice-based cryptography operates over small moduli, a regime in which PMNS has not yet been studied. In this work, we explore this setting and propose a tailored PMNS instantiation for the modulus of ML-DSA, whose structure enables particularly efficient modular reductions. We further leverage the intrinsic redundancy of PMNS to construct a randomized arithmetic layer that decorrelates intermediate values from secret data, thereby reducing side-channel leakage without resorting to classical masking schemes. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed countermeasure through a comprehensive side-channel analysis, combining leakage detection with machine-learning-based profiling attacks targeting the Number Theoretic Transform. Our results demonstrate that PMNS-based randomization significantly reduces first-order leakage and provides strong resistance to practical side-channel attacks. We further assess the performance overhead of the proposed approach through cycle-accurate profiling on a RISC-V CVA6 core using Verilator. The observed slowdown is comparable to standard side-channel countermeasures reported in the literature. We identify the main computational bottlenecks and discuss how existing hardware acceleration strategies could substantially reduce this overhead, making PMNS a practical candidate for side-channel-resistant embedded implementations of lattice-based cryptography.
papers.authors: Tom Voitzwinkler, Alexandre Berzati, Andersson Calle Viera, Fangan-Yssouf Dosso, Nadia El Mrabet

papers.title: Remote Fault Attacks on PIOP-based Post-Quantum Digital Signatures using Statistical Ineffective Fault Analysis
papers.abstract: The threat posed by quantum computing has necessitated the replacement of existing public-key cryptographic algorithms. NIST is currently running the third round of a competition to identify additional post-quantum digital signature schemes beyond the ML-DSA and SLH-DSA standards. Among the competition's remaining candidates are MQOM, FAEST, and SDitH, based on Polynomial Interactive Oracle Proof (PIOP) protocols. They are favoured for standardisation due to their conservative security assumptions. In this paper, we present a remote fault attack that recovers the secret key of these schemes by targeting the polynomials underlying the PIOP protocol. The attack employs Statistical Ineffective Fault Analysis (SIFA), a powerful method introduced in 2018 in the context of AES. We demonstrate the attack end-to-end using Rowhammer. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first remote attack on a post-quantum cryptographic signature scheme capable of bypassing fault detection countermeasures. Previous attacks relied on fault models impractical for remote exploitation. In addition, we present a novel approach to bypass Address Space Layout Randomisation (ASLR) that reliably determines the ASLR-induced intra-page offset from a single set of stack accesses during libc initialisation. Furthermore, we refine existing approaches for acquiring physically contiguous memory and propose countermeasures against the presented attack.
papers.authors: Sönke Jendral, Mona Sobhani, Elena Dubrova

papers.title: Principally Polarized Superspecial Surfaces over Prime Fields: Counts and Isogeny Graphs
papers.abstract: Isogeny graphs are central to isogeny-based cryptography, and their connectivity can change when one restricts to isogenies defined over the base field. We study rational $(\ell,\ell)$-isogeny graphs of principally polarized abelian surfaces over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with Weil polynomial $(T^2+p)^2$ for a prime $p\ge7$. We retain polarized $\mathbb{F}_p$-isomorphism classes as vertices and count $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational maximal-isotropic subgroups as edges. Using the correspondence with positive-definite self-dual Hermitian lattices, we express the total vertex count as an unweighted rank-two Hermitian class number. We give exact counts for split elliptic products and Weil restrictions, and estimate the number of genus-two Jacobians. For each prime $\ell\ne p$, we determine the rational kernel counts and relate reverse edge multiplicities to rational automorphism groups. The graph is disconnected whenever $\ell$ is odd. For $\ell=2$, the graph is disconnected when $p\not\equiv7\pmod8$. When $p\equiv7\pmod8$, its connected components are indexed by the ideal class group of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$ modulo the subgroup generated by the class of a prime ideal above two. In this case, the graph is connected precisely when that ideal class generates the class group. We also carry out computations for small examples, which provide additional checks of our results.
papers.authors: Bin Wang, Wei Yu, Tingyu Xing, Song Tian, Kunpeng Wang

papers.title: Exact Post-Quantum Security Analysis of Ascon Authenticated Encryption under Nonce Misuse
papers.abstract: Ascon AEAD is a lightweight authenticated encryption algorithm recently standardized by NIST as SP 800-232, and is expected to be deployed in a wide range of resource-constrained applications. In this paper, we study its post-quantum security under nonce reuse in the quantum random permutation model. We assume that the adversary makes classical queries to the keyed construction and quantum queries to the public permutation and its inverse. We prove the security up to $\min\{2^{\kappa/2},2^{c/3}\}$ quantum and classical query complexities for nonce-misuse resilience confidentiality and authenticity under release of unverified plaintext, where $\kappa$ is the key length and $c$ is the capacity size. This improves the dependence on the key length in the previous security bound proved by Hosoyamada (ASIACRYPT 2025) from $2^{\kappa/3}$ to $2^{\kappa/2}$. To obtain this bound, we introduce a new representation that decomposes Ascon AEAD into an initialization function and a tweakable block cipher, and establish the joint post-quantum security of these components. The representation allows the analysis to exploit $c$ bits of randomness, whereas Hosoyamada's alternative representation of Ascon AEAD used in the previous proof allows $\kappa$ ($\le c$) bits of randomness. Combining the joint post-quantum security with the classical security of Ascon AEAD, we prove the post-quantum security of Ascon AEAD. We also construct quantum attacks based on the classical nonce-misuse attacks of Lefevre and Mennink (ToSC 2025(1)), using quantum search with quantum random access memory (qRAM) following the approach of Brassard, Høyer, and Tapp. We first recover an internal state and then use it to construct forgery and key-recovery attacks that break the two security notions considered. Under the stated parameter conditions, these attacks use $O(2^{c/3})$ primitive queries and processed message blocks. Together with Grover's exhaustive key search, our attacks show that our security bounds are tight in the exponent.
papers.authors: Rentaro Shiba, Tetsu Iwata

papers.title: Parity Leakage and Sparse-Mask Sampling in Distorted-McEliece Pseudorandom Codes
papers.abstract: Dyseryn, Francati and Venturi (DFV) recently proposed binary public-key pseudorandom codes that combine robustness to a constant fraction of substitutions with conjectured subexponential security. Their public key is a generator matrix of a binary expansion of a Reed--Solomon subcode, called a Raw Reed--Solomon code, multiplied by the inverse of a uniformly random invertible matrix in which every row has the same weight $\gamma\ge3$. That this key is indistinguishable from a uniform matrix is their Distorted McEliece Public Key assumption (DistMcEPKP), from which the hardness of the ciphertext-level assumption is derived. We observe that over $\F_2$ such a matrix necessarily has odd row weight and therefore fixes the all-ones vector, so that the distortion preserves the parity of the weight of every codeword. Raw Reed--Solomon codes whose support is all of $\F_{2^m}^*$, the support for which these codes were originally defined and one that the definition used by DFV does not exclude, contain only even-weight words. For this support DistMcEPKP is false: the $K\times N$ public key is distinguished from a uniform matrix with advantage $1-2^{-K}$ by computing $K$ parities, for every distortion weight. For arbitrary supports the leak occurs if and only if certain power sums of the support vanish. For the two code families of Silbak, Kopparty and Shaltiel, whose odd exponents are $1,3,\dots,2\tau-1$, this means that the support is a codeword of the primitive BCH code of designed distance $2\tau+1$. The leak therefore never occurs when between $1$ and $2\tau$ points are removed from the full support, and it occurs for a uniformly random support with probability at most $\binom{\lceil M/2\rceil+\tau}{\tau}^{-1}$ unconditionally and $(1+o(1))2^{-m\tau}$ in the Weil range, where $M=2^m-1$. We then study the action of sparse distortions on dual codewords: we give the exact mean weight of the image of a fixed word, a binomial domination of its moment generating function derived from the log-concavity of matroid basis polynomials (hence Chernoff concentration without independence of the rows), the images of the words of the shortened BCH codes that the dual of every Raw Reed--Solomon code contains, and a worst-case contraction to weight one. Finally we analyse how the mask can be sampled: rejection of independent rows succeeds with probability $e^{-\Theta(N)}$, row-by-row rejection runs in polynomial time but is not uniform, diagonal anchoring is biased by the permanent, and the basis-exchange walk produces an $\varepsilon$-uniform mask with $O(N\log(N/\varepsilon))$ rank-one updates, that is, $O(N^3\log(N/\varepsilon))$ bit operations. All statements are accompanied by exact enumerations and reproducible experiments. The results refute DistMcEPKP for the full support and determine how the support must be restricted. They give neither a key recovery nor a distinguisher for ciphertexts at constant noise rate, so the ciphertext-level assumption is not refuted.
papers.authors: Yongge Wang

papers.title: One Algebra to Multiply Them All: Fast Homomorphic Linear Algebra in Every Encoding
papers.abstract: Linear algebra is a core primitive of many applications of fully homomorphic encryption, including privacy-preserving machine learning, statistical analysis, and encrypted search. Efficient homomorphic matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplications are therefore an essential tool, and have been intensely studied over the last fifteen years. Recent work, notably by Bae et al. and Park reduces homomorphic matrix multiplication in large dimension to the multiplication of plaintext matrices, plus a number of key switchings only linear in the dimension, enabling the use of highly efficient linear algebra primitives, such as those of the BLAS library, while limiting the homomorphic cost. These results have been extended by Cheon et al. to batches of matrix multiplications in smaller dimension. In CKKS, the corresponding algorithms rely on dedicated encodings (coefficient, SinC). Using these encodings constrains integration of these algorithms into a larger computation; in practice, one has either to perform an expensive conversion or to schedule the linear algebra within bootstrapping. Alternatively, Gentry and Lee obtain reductions in the slot encoding through a different ciphertext ring. We obtain reductions to plaintext matrix multiplication directly in the slot encoding, over the standard power-of-two CKKS ring, showing that the change of ring of Gentry and Lee is not required for this functionality. Our approach uses the cyclic algebra of the field extension $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2N})/\mathbb Q(\mathrm{i})$ to describe endomorphisms independently of the choice of coordinates. We show that choosing a basis (which identifies endomorphisms with matrices) is exactly choosing an encoding. Algorithms written once in this language cover the functionalities of the classical encodings, for single matrices and, over subfields, for batches of smaller ones. This language also makes explicit the commutation of the secret key with the matrix, which is the key step in the product of two encrypted matrices. The resulting algorithms admit elementary descriptions, corresponding to a precise scheduling of the key switchings, which allows them to be grouped, while the algebraic framework explains their common structure across various packings. Our framework extends to products of an encrypted $d \times d$ matrix by an encrypted $d \times c$ matrix, where it allows a baby-step giant-step strategy even though both factors are encrypted. For ring degree $N$, with $c \mid d \mid N/2$, we evaluate a batch of $N/(2d)$ such products with $O(\sqrt{dc})$ key switchings in total, without any preprocessing of the encrypted inputs. In particular, an encrypted matrix-vector product requires only $O(\sqrt{d})$ key switchings.
papers.authors: Jonghoo Lee, Guillaume Hanrot, Seongsu Jeon

papers.title: Constant-Size Identity-Based Linkable Ring Signatures from Standard Assumptions
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose an identity-based linkable ring signature (IB-LRS) scheme that achieves constant-size signatures and is provably secure in the standard model under standard assumptions. All previous IB-LRS schemes are only proven secure in the random oracle model (ROM), and those achieving constant-size signatures additionally rely on non-standard assumptions. In contrast, our scheme removes both limitations simultaneously. To do this, we build our IB-LRS scheme from a constant-size hierarchical identity-based encryption (HIBE) scheme. First, we adapt this HIBE to a matrix-based dual-system framework to replace its non-standard assumptions with standard assumptions. Then, we use the ``all-but-one'' technique to aggregate all ring identities and get constant-size ring signatures. Finally, to support linkability, we add a separate matrix to bind each user's tracking key to the ring signature. Moreover, our scheme provides unconditional anonymity, and we prove its unforgeability, linkability, and non-slanderability under the Matrix Decisional Diffie-Hellman (MDDH) assumption.
papers.authors: Zhi Zhang, Jie Chen, Debiao He

papers.title: (Almost) Tight Bounds for Pairing-Based SNARGs
papers.abstract: We construct a publicly verifiable succinct non-interactive argument (SNARG) for NP in the asymmetric bilinear generic group and random oracle models. At $\lambda$ bits of security, a proof consists of one $\mathbb{G}_1$ element and $\lambda+o(\lambda)$ additional bits. Assuming exponentially secure pseudorandom generators, we show that the additional bit string cannot have length $o(\lambda)$ under natural restrictions on setup and verification. The lower bound applies to schemes with exponentially small completeness and soundness errors, where soundness holds against subexponential adversaries. Our construction uses a variant of the KZG polynomial commitment scheme that may be of independent interest. The commitment is the hash of a target group element, and an opening proof still consists of one $\mathbb{G}_1$ element. Given the opening proof and the claimed evaluation, the verifier reconstructs the target group element with one pairing and checks its hash against the commitment, saving one pairing over standard KZG verification.
papers.authors: Gal Arnon, Eylon Yogev

papers.title: HCENC: How to Design an Efficient Committing Beyond-Birthday-Bound Accordion from a Block Cipher with n-Bit Blocks and Keys
papers.abstract: Many accordions, that is, tweakable encryption modes for inputs of variable length, offer security beyond the birthday bound, but they differ in cost and in how they obtain key commitment (CMT-1) or full commitment (CMT-4). Practical deployment needs inexpensive schemes that follow well-established design criteria and proof methods, use standardized primitives, and have small overheads for each master key and message. We introduce HCENC, a generalization of HCTR built from a block cipher with n-bit blocks and keys, an n-bit AXU hash function, and the keystream generator of CENC, that is, a simply masked counter mode. We prove that in the ideal-cipher model it is a strong tweakable pseudorandom permutation up to about $2^n/w$ blocks, where w is the frame width of the keystream, for every key derivation that satisfies three weak conditions. We show that with the block cipher alone, CMT-1 stays at the birthday bound for every key derivation that computes unrelated derived keys from different master keys. To achieve beyond the birthday bound we admit a second block cipher with longer keys. In concrete instantiations, with HCENC on AES-128 and the transform UCX with a Feistel concealer on AES-256, we obtain CMT-1 and CMT-4 of 116 bits, at a cost of two AES-256 calls for each message, and of one hash evaluation and one AES-256 key expansion more for CMT-4. Among the accordions with a complete proof of security beyond the birthday bound using a single 2n-bit master key, HCENC has among the smallest overheads for each master key and each message. NOTE: The formal proofs are embedded in the PDF file. They can be downloaded from the PDF by clicking on "attached to this PDF" in the paragraph "Machine-checked proofs." This works with many PDF viewers and browsers, but, curiously, not Preview under macOS. Under macOS, use PDFcraft, Adobe Acrobat (Reader), Firefox or Chrome.
papers.authors: Roberto Avanzi

papers.title: Beyond Stepwise Transformation: MILP Model for Low-Area Implementations of Linear Layers
papers.abstract: Low-area linear layers play an important role in lightweight symmetric-key cryptography. Across gate libraries, multi-input XOR gates are effective in reducing the area of linear layers, but finding lower-area implementations using XOR gates of different input sizes remains challenging. At ToSC 2022, Liu et al. proposed a heuristic stepwise framework that constructs lower-area implementations with \(n+1\)-input XOR gates from given implementations with \(n\)-input XOR gates. However, we observe that such a stepwise strategy may restrict the search space and fail to find lower-area implementations. To address this limitation, we propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP)-based model that starts from a given XOR2 circuit and searches for lower-area implementations with two-, three-, and four-input XOR gates within a prescribed candidate space. It jointly selects candidate coefficient vectors and admissible XOR implementations to form a valid acyclic circuit that preserves the required outputs and minimizes the area under the given gate costs. Using the proposed MILP-based model, we first re-evaluate the implementations reported by Liu et al. and obtain lower-area implementations for most of the representative linear layers. For AES MixColumns, we obtain an implementation requiring 236.99 gate equivalents (GE) in the STM 130 nm library, improving upon the previous result of 243 GE. We then evaluate the MILP model on a set of more than 5000 \(32 \times 32\) maximum distance separable (MDS) matrices proposed by Li et al. at ToSC 2019 and reduce their average area by up to about 28% over the initial XOR2 circuits and 8% over previous stepwise multi-input XOR implementations. These results indicate that jointly optimizing two-, three-, and four-input XOR gates within the prescribed search space can be more effective than stepwise transformation in obtaining lower-area implementations of linear layers.
papers.authors: Pengju Zhao, Qun Liu, Jingwen Chen, Qingyuan Yu, Chenhao Jia, Meiqin Wang

papers.title: On the NP-Completeness of Worst-Case (2,1)-Quasi-Cyclic Syndrome Decoding
papers.abstract: We study the worst-case $(2,1)$-Quasi-Cyclic Syndrome Decoding problem ($\mathsf{QCSD}_{n,w}$) over $R_n = \mathbb{F}_2[X]/(X^n - 1)$. Given explicit polynomials $h, s \in R_n$ and an integer $w \ge 0$, the problem asks whether there exist $x, y \in R_n$ satisfying $x + hy = s$ with equal block weights $|x| = |y| = w$. We prove that worst-case $\mathsf{QCSD}_{n,w}$ is NP-complete in the low-weight regime $w < \sqrt{n}$ by giving a polynomial-time reduction from 3-Dimensional Matching (3DM). We also show that the same reduction establishes the NP-completeness of the relaxed variant requiring only $|x|, |y| \le w$. Additionally, our result extends to prime block lengths and to general fixed $(a, b)$-QCSD instances.
papers.authors: Tianrui Wang, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang

papers.title: BIFOLD: Memory-Efficient Homomorphic CNN Inference over Bivariate Rings
papers.abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables private convolutional neural network (CNN) inference, but large evaluation keys hinder practical deployment. We introduce an exponential bootstrapping method exploiting an exact trigonometric identity to achieve latency comparable to standard bootstrapping, alongside low-depth and efficient functional bootstrapping for densely packed inputs. GL's bivariate ring enables compact plaintexts and convolution fused into bootstrapping. At ring degree $N=2^{15}$, ResNet-20 inference on an RTX 5090 takes 127.8 ms, $2.19\times$ faster than RBOOT, the fastest state-of-the-art baseline implemented on the same GPU backend, with $6.1\times$ smaller evaluation keys. Seeding mask polynomials reduces keys to 0.84 GB at 140.1 ms latency, advancing practical privacy-preserving machine learning.
papers.authors: Rostin Shokri, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos

papers.title: DEEP Revisited: Proximity Gaps up to List-Decoding Radius via Out-of-Domain Samples
papers.abstract: We revisit the use of out-of-domain samples in proximity gaps, introduced in DEEP-FRI [BGKS20]. With multiple samples, we obtain proximity gaps up to the list decoding radius of any linear code. We highlight two regimes that our results make possible, that were previously not possible. First, for general linear codes, our approach extends the standard proximity-gap guarantee from the one-and-a-half Johnson bound to the full Johnson bound, at the expense of a constant number of out-of-domain samples. Moreover, with a constant fraction of agreement loss, we can achieve error $O(1/q)$ when the field size $q$ is at least the blocklength $n$, adding $20-30$ bits of security in typical hash-based SNARK constructions using general linear codes Second, for Reed--Solomon codes, our bounds apply beyond the Johnson radius even when the list size, $L$ is very large, e.g. $L \gg 2^\lambda$. While standard proximity gaps would typically achieve trivial error probability in this setting, our approach shows that one can still obtain $2^{-\lambda}$ error probability using $O(\log L/\lambda)$ out-of-domain samples.
papers.authors: Alexander Frolov, Justin Thaler, Eylon Yogev, Kai Zhe Zheng

papers.title: Anamorphic Broadcast Encryption, Revisited
papers.abstract: Anamorphic encryption lets ordinary ciphertexts carry an additional message whose presence remains hidden even when the ordinary decryption key is exposed. We revisit this goal in the broadcast setting studied by Do et al. (EUROCRYPT 2025) and give a distinguishing attack against their Dual-Regev construction. Given one encryption query and the ordinary secret key, an adversary distinguishes ordinary and anamorphic ciphertexts with non-negligible advantage by testing the decryption residual before rounding. We construct an anamorphic broadcast channel for the Dual-Regev public key encryption scheme that delivers a common $L$-bit message to a fixed group in one ordinary ciphertext. Using only public information from the ordinary setup, the sender samples encryption randomness correlated with the recipients' anamorphic public keys, leaving ordinary decryption and its residual distribution unchanged. We prove anamorphic security and anamorphic-message privacy with the ordinary secret key exposed, and joint message privacy for both messages when that key is not exposed. These guarantees follow from LWE in the standard model. We instantiate the channel in the batched laconic encryption core of registration-based encryption (Klooß et al., S&P 2026) and in the encryption layer of Epoque (Boyen et al., EuroS&P 2021). These instantiations illustrate the broader applicability of our embedding technique to schemes built on Dual-Regev encryption. We implement the basic construction and both applications in Rust and demonstrate ordinary and anamorphic message recovery from the same ciphertext using the corresponding decryption keys. With the same parameters for the ordinary layer, both modes have comparable encryption times after a one-time preprocessing of the group members' anamorphic public keys.
papers.authors: Dennis Faut, Chuanwei Lin, Tapas Pal, Andy Rupp

papers.title: When Verification Leaks: Breaking and Repairing Verifiable PIR with Small Client Storage
papers.abstract: Verifiable private information retrieval (vPIR) lets a client retrieve a database entry privately and check the server's answer. Efficient designs such as VeriSimplePIR require clients to retain a large hint: preprocessed database information needed to recover answers. Rathee, Lee, and Popa (IEEE S&P 2026) reduce this storage by using homomorphic encryption to delegate the computations involving the hint to the server. They argue that the client's acceptance or rejection of a respon se reveals no query information. We refute this claim with two selective-failure attacks. A malicious server can modify an encrypted result so that, after decryption, the client's correctness check tests a guess about the query. Our attacks make acceptance more likely when the query matches a chosen position or falls within a chosen set. For a single-position test under the original parameters, the client accepts with probability about 6% when the guess is correct and negligible probability otherwise. Our repair requires the server to prove that the returned ciphertext is the output of the prescribed computation. The client verifies this proof before decryption, so it rejects manipulated ciphertexts without testing their decrypted contents. We exploit the linear structure of the delegated computation to construct a compact proof checked against a short commitment to the hint. The resulting vPIR scheme provides query privacy and answer correctness against a malicious server without requiring the client to retain the large hint.
papers.authors: Ruida Wang, Xinxuan Zhang, Zirui Wang, Yijian Liu, Zhihao Li, Yi Deng, Xianhui Lu

papers.title: Beyond the Input-Length Barrier: AND and OT Complexity of Two-Party Computation
papers.abstract: A natural quantitative question in secure two-party computation is how many calls to a complete primitive (AND, Oblivious Transfer) are necessary to securely compute a given function. Beimel and Malkin (2004) initiated a systematic study of this question for one-sided AND in perfect information-theoretically secure model against semi-honest adversaries. They gave lower bounds of $n$, the per party input length, for functions satisfying explicit combinatorial characterizations. The secure zero-communication reduction framework of Narayanan, Prabhakaran, and Prabhakaran (2020) recovered this input-length frontier by a different route. Nevertheless, unconditional lower bounds for both AND, OT beyond the per party input length for deterministic Boolean functions have remained elusive, even existentially. Our first result gives explicit AND lower bounds beyond the input length. For Inner Product, equality and Hamming proximity of $n$ bit strings, we prove lower bounds of \(1.29n+\Omega(\log n)\) AND calls. We then consider OT and show almost every Boolean function on two \(n\)-bit inputs requires \(1.26n-O(\log n)\) OT calls. For Inner Product we also improve the classical \(2n\) AND upper bound, giving a perfectly secure randomized protocol using \(1.71n+o(n)\) AND calls. The combinatorial constructions underlying this protocol may be of independent interest. Finally, we revisit the role of private randomness. We prove a general derandomization theorem showing that, near the natural counting limit, randomized protocols can be derandomized in a fully parallel way without increasing the number of AND calls. This settles the 2 and 3 AND call derandomization cases left open by Beimel and Malkin and, together with their 4 call separation, identifies 4 as the first level at which randomness helps.
papers.authors: Divesh Aggarwal, Rishav Gupta, Ananta Mukherjee, Hai H. Nguyen, Maciej Obremski

papers.title: Minimizing Toffoli Gate Counts in In-Place S-Box Implementations
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study ancilla-free in-place quantum implementations of the Ascon S-box and the 5-bit Keccak $\chi_5$ mapping. We develop a complete synthesis method that treats NOT and CNOT gates as affine operations and uses canonical state representation together with a proven lower bound to prune the search space. Using this method, we settle the previously unresolved minimum Toffoli count for the Ascon S-box at exactly seven, extend the same minimum to Keccak $\chi_5$ via affine equivalence, and establish a minimum Toffoli depth of seven for both functions. We further optimize Clifford+$T$ realizations of these minimum-Toffoli circuits by resynthesizing the decomposed circuits across Toffoli-decomposition boundaries. For both targets, the resulting implementations achieve either 33 $T$ gates with $T$-depth 8 or 29 $T$ gates with $T$-depth 10. To the best of our knowledge, these achieve the lowest reported $T$-depth and $T$-count, respectively, among existing 5-qubit ancilla-free in-place implementations.
papers.authors: Seungjun Baek, Wonwoo Song, Namil Kim, Anubhab Baksi, Jongsung Kim

papers.title: Efficient and Verifiable One-Shot Secure Aggregation with Dynamic Client Participation
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving federated learning (PPFL) often relies on multi-round secure aggregation, which increases communication overhead and the risk of client dropout. Recent one-shot secure aggregation protocols, including Willow (CRYPTO 2025), OPA (CRYPTO 2025), and TACITA (CCS 2026), successfully eliminate multi-round client interactions. However, they still incur substantial computation and communication overhead due to heavy cryptographic primitives. More critically, none of them provides public verifiability against a malicious server, meaning the server can forge or omit inputs without detection. We present OSA, a committee-assisted one-shot secure aggregation protocol that supports dynamic client participation. OSA securely realizes the summation functionality against a malicious server with abort under the ring learning with errors (RLWE) assumption. We further present VOSA, a verifiable extension of OSA that enables an independent verifier to check the correctness of the server’s reported aggregate. We evaluate OSA against state-of-the-art one-shot protocols (Willow, OPA, and TACITA), and VOSA against the state-of-the-art aggregate signature scheme, mPVAS (USENIX Security 2026). Under the default experimental setting, OSA achieves speedups of approximately $11.41\times$--$761.96\times$ for client-side computation, $2.43\times$--$106.21\times$ for server-side computation, and $1.28\times$--$11.35\times$ for committee-member computation, while reducing communication overhead by approximately $76.83\%$--$94.01\%$ for clients, $64.47\%$--$89.40\%$ for the server, and $0.30\%$--$78.78\%$ for committee members. Compared with mPVAS, VOSA achieves speedups of approximately $2.78\times$, $11.10\times$, and $54.78\times$ for client-side, server-side, and verifier-side computation, respectively, while reducing the server communication overhead by approximately $92\%$. These results establish a new efficiency and verifiability baseline for one-shot secure aggregation in dynamic FL deployments.
papers.authors: Fucai Luo

papers.title: Near-n-Bit Preimage and Second-Preimage Security of the JH Mode
papers.abstract: Existing direct bounds on preimage and second-preimage resistance for the JH mode remain at the birthday scale. We revisit this mode in the ideal-permutation model, with a \(2n\)-bit state and permutation, \(n\)-bit message blocks, and an \(n\)-bit digest. Each permutation query supplies one edge into every column of the state graph. We use Menger's theorem to bound which endpoints those edges can connect through the residual graph, and a potential to bound the growth of the states on either side. For messages of at most \(2^{64}\) bits and padding with \(\ell(M)\leq\lceil |M|/n\rceil+1\) blocks, the resulting bounds give negligible advantage up to \(2^{n-2\sqrt{2n}-O(\log n)}\) queries. For the widths of JH-512, the unweighted certificates bound success probability below \(1/2\) up to \(2^{431}\) queries for preimages and \(2^{416}\) for second preimages.
