Both budgets include candidate evaluation. Our Lean 4 development covers the fixed-target preimage proof and the second-preimage bound with a common occupancy threshold.
papers.authors: Changlun Li, Hongli Li, Yijun Yuan, Fengmei Liu, Shanwen Wang, Honggang Hu

papers.title: Stateful LLM Guardrails without Surveillance via Anonymous Risk Token
papers.abstract: Safety guardrails for large language models (LLMs) judge each message on its own, yet multi-turn jailbreaks spread a harmful request over messages that each look benign. To catch them, a guardrail must remember the user's earlier messages. If the provider, who hosts and runs the model, keeps this memory, it holds a permanent record of every user, almost all of whom are innocent, along with how suspicious the guardrail judged each of their private queries. One data breach, court order, or change of policy could expose this record. If the user keeps the memory instead, a malicious user can roll it back or reset it. We therefore ask whether a guardrail can remember what it needs for safety without profiling its users. We first show that a guardrail needs far less memory than a full transcript: two numbers per user suffice. Using the classifier Llama Guard 3 on about 10,000 public conversations from automated multi-turn attacks, human red-teaming, and real users, we keep a fast and a slow running average of each user's scores; when the fast one rises above the slow one, the user's messages are becoming more harmful. At a 5% false-alarm rate, the two averages detect 34% of escalating attacks, against 25% for judging each message on its own. Kept across conversations, they cannot be evaded by splitting an attack over several conversations, unlike memory that restarts with each one. Against red-team attacks, which are often harmful from the first message, memory adds little. To keep these averages without a profile, we introduce and design a new cryptographic primitive, anonymous risk tokens (ART), in which the user holds its own averages. For each message, the provider learns only a coarse risk level (e.g., low or high) and cannot link it to the user's earlier conversations; the user cannot lower, roll back, or copy its averages, or reset them without forfeiting a prepaid balance. We formalize the security of ART and give a provably secure construction from Pointcheval-Sanders (PS) blind signatures and zero-knowledge arguments. The price is some loss of detection within a single conversation, because the averages must start from a public value. We implement a prototype of ART in Rust and evaluate it: each message takes each party about 0.4s on one laptop core, and the user uploads 90KB, regardless of the history length.
papers.authors: Anirban Chakrabarti, Stefan Dziembowski, Arup Mondal

papers.title: TB-IOPP: Repair-Group-Local IOPs of Proximity for Tamo–Barg Codes
papers.abstract: Reed-Solomon IOPPs underpin transparent succinct arguments but inherently lack small-locality symbol repair: by the MDS barrier, reconstructing missing queries requires global recovery, creating a fundamental structural mismatch in distributed, authenticated, and data-availability settings. We introduce TB-IOPP, the first repair-group-local IOP of proximity for locally recoverable Tamo-Barg codes. TB-IOPP delegates global proximity testing to an arbitrary Reed-Solomon backend via full-rank matrix folding while strictly confining every query to the committed original oracle within a fiber, an individual local repair group. The central technical challenge is cross-fiber stitching, where locally valid repair groups fail to combine into a globally consistent codeword. We resolve this by proving a robust anti-stitching theorem that bounds distance to the code in the fiber metric, showing that our original-oracle query complexity is optimal up to a constant factor in the ideal-IOPP model. Furthermore, we establish round-by-round knowledge soundness assuming only round-by-round soundness and efficient witness decoding of the backend, and compile the protocol under BCS into a non-interactive argument whose extraction guarantee binds directly to the published commitment. Finally, we establish a correlated-agreement theorem directly in the fiber metric to enable batched verification, and construct a splicing-resistant repairable proximity certificate tailored for authenticated distributed storage.
papers.authors: Seunghyun Cho, Saehoon Jung, Young-Sik Kim

papers.title: Unmasking Glitches: Why Secure Hardware Gadgets Still Leak
papers.abstract: Probing-based security notions underpin the design and verification of masked hardware. Glitch-aware extensions, such as the robust probing model, provide strong guarantees within their abstraction and enable systematic gadget constructions and automated verification. Yet these guarantees do not preclude physically observable leakage: prior work shows that temperature or voltage manipulations can still induce leakage, often blamed on transient glitches without a clear root cause. To clarify, we perform a gate-level evaluation of three representative masked AND gadgets, namely HPC2, HPC3, and COMAR, under timing perturbations induced by input transitions, clock skew, and temperature variation. Our results show that these seemingly different factors share a common mechanism: they create timing differences in signal arrivals, which in turn alter glitch onset, duration, and propagation. We introduce three metrics to determine whether a glitch can reveal sensitive value-dependent behavior: (1) change of glitch behavior across sensitive equivalence classes, (2) variation of glitch timing with the sensitive value, and (3) recurrence of glitches on the same internal node for one sensitive value but not another. Using these metrics, we show that timing perturbations can induce reproducible, sensitive-value-dependent glitches that indicate potential vulnerabilities. We support these observations with HSPICE supply-current NICV and correlation analyses, as well as post-route glitch-only NICV. We further complement the simulation study with the first-of-its-kind post-silicon optical probing measurements that support the same timing-difference mechanism in secure gadgets. Overall, our results show that even gadgets with formal probing security and composability guarantees can exhibit observable, data-dependent glitch patterns, motivating timing-aware refinement layers for secure hardware evaluation.
papers.authors: Dev M. Mehta, Mehmet A. Cetin, Domenic Forte, Shahin Tajik, Fatemeh Ganji

papers.title: Adams Bridge is Falling Down: A New Chosen Ciphertext Side-Channel Attack on the PQC Accelerator
papers.abstract: With ML-KEM and ML-DSA now standardized by NIST, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is moving from research into real world. Adams Bridge is an industry-oriented hardware accelerator that implements both ML-KEM and ML-DSA in a unified architecture. It is used as the post-quantum engine of Caliptra 2.1, a silicon root of trust designed to be integrated into data center chips from multiple vendors. This broad integration makes its security particularly important, as vulnerabilities could affect a wide range of deployed systems. In this paper, we reveal new vulnerabilities in the centered binomial sampling and ciphertext compression and comparison operations. We demonstrate the first practical key recovery attack on the released Adams Bridge v2.0.3 hardware implementation of ML-KEM with all countermeasures enabled. We further propose a new non-profiled chosen ciphertext attack method, achieving full secret key recovery for ML-KEM-1024 using 18 580 traces in 49.5 minutes. Compared to our profiled attack, the new method reduces the number of traces by at least 29.2%. More broadly, our findings highlight a gap between the countermeasures recommended by the research community and those adopted in industrial PQC hardware designs. As the transition to PQC accelerates, bridging this gap is crucial to ensuring the security of real-world deployments.
papers.authors: Ruize Wang, Aikata, Péter Horváth, Thomas Szymkowiak, Markku-Juhani Saarinen, Lejla Batina

papers.title: Lightning-fast Two-Party Secure Sampling Protocol for Arbitrary Public Discrete Distributions
papers.abstract: Secure sampling enables randomized mechanisms to be executed within secure computation without revealing the generated randomness. Existing approaches, however, are often specialized to particular distributions or incur substantial costs when supporting general discrete distributions. We present a two-party protocol for securely sampling from arbitrary public discrete distributions. Our approach compiles a target distribution into a representation based on table-representable mixtures and deterministic transformations. The protocol then generates arithmetic shares of a sample from the represented approximation; all approximation error arises during representation construction. We prove security against a static semi-honest adversary who corrupts one party. We evaluate our approach on five families of discrete distributions used in randomized algorithms and differential privacy (DP). For most evaluated distributions, our method achieves high approximation accuracy with low sampling cost. For the three general-purpose distributions, the total variation distance (TVD) between each target distribution and its represented approximation is at most $2^{-60}$, and the per-sample runtime is below $0.16$ ms in the localhost setting. For discrete Laplace noise yielding $(1.0,10^{-10})$-DP at sensitivity $\Delta=1$, our protocol takes $0.0616$ ms per sample in the LAN setting and requires $2.690$ KiB of communication, making it approximately $706\times$ faster than the fastest baseline and reducing communication by a factor of approximately $128$ compared with the baseline with the lowest communication.
papers.authors: Masanobu Kii

papers.title: Aggregation techniques for the SPoCK scheme
papers.abstract: In preceding work, we formalized a novel cryptographic primitive called Specialized Proof of Confidential Knowledge (SPoCK). The SPoCK scheme allows any two independent parties to convince a third party that they possess a common secret without revealing it. The proof is non-interactive, bound to the specific party that generated it, and cannot be forged without knowledge of the secret. A SPoCK scheme can be used in systems where members must independently attest to knowledge of a shared secret. One such application is addressing the Verifier’s Dilemma in distributed systems. While the original scheme works with two provers and a single secret, this work introduces new proving and verification schemes with multiple provers and multiple secrets. These schemes improve scalability in distributed systems with numerous participants by reducing proof size and verification time. We define the new Multi-SPoCK scheme, which allows two sets of provers to convince a verifier that they generated proofs from the same secret. Additionally, we propose the Aggregate Multi-SPoCK scheme, which further aggregates proofs from multiple secrets into a single proof. We first formalize the multi-proving schemes and their security model. We then give new pairingbased constructions of both schemes from BLS multisignatures. We provide proofs for the proposed schemes under suitable computational assumptions.
papers.authors: Tarak Ben Youssef

papers.title: A One-Residual Procedure for Deriving Inverse Expressions of Shift-Invariant Transformations
papers.abstract: We present a one-residual procedure for deriving factorized inverse expressions of a class of shift-invariant (SI) transformations. The procedure uses iterative substitution to isolate a single residual input variable and propagates the resulting recurrence along cyclic orbits. For SI transformations with a single nonlinear product term (SNPT-SI) satisfying explicit cancellation conditions, we prove a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for bijectivity. The criterion determines the bijective state sizes and directly yields the corresponding inverse expressions. We apply these results to construct degree-$t$ SNPT-SI permutations attaining the known inverse-degree bound $D_t(n)=n-\lceil(n-1)/t\rceil$ for every $t\ge2$ and $n>t$, except when $t=2$ and $n$ is even. Fixed-parameter families also attain this bound at infinitely many state sizes. The criterion covers the four main and all 14 additional transformations studied by Liu et al. (Journal of Cryptology, 2026). For $\chi_{n,t}$, we recover known inverse expressions and characterize multiple-preimage fibers. A bounded search certifies bijective families for 69 of 378 anchored parameter sets.
papers.authors: Jianhua Wang, Siwei Sun, Shahram Rasoolzadeh, Ruixi Lv

papers.title: Elligator Prime: Injective Encodings to Elliptic Curves Without Torsion Assumptions
papers.abstract:
extit{Encoding functions} map finite-field elements to rational points on elliptic curves and are used in many cryptographic protocols. Injective encodings with efficient inversion are of particular interest, since they allow elliptic curve points to be transmitted as strings indistinguishable from uniformly random ones, as in 	extit{Elligator}. However, existing injective encodings rely on rational points of small order, which excludes important families of curves, notably those of prime order. Constructing efficient injective encodings to curves of prime order has thus remained a challenging open problem for more than a decade. Classical deterministic encodings based on Ska{\l}ba's equality apply to all curves, but this equality only guarantees that some candidate abscissa is valid and does not control the fibres of the encoding. In this paper, we introduce \emph{Elligator Prime}, which takes a new direction in the design of encoding functions by replacing Ska{\l}ba's equality with an odd-parity identity on four injective M"obius branches, arranged as two pairs exchanged by a fixed-point-free involution. Exactly one pair then contains exactly one valid abscissa, and the sign of the resulting point identifies that pair. This yields uniform $2{:}1$ encodings whose fibres are the orbits of the involution; choosing one representative per orbit gives an injective encoding with efficient inversion, without any rational torsion point of a prescribed order. In characteristic $p>3$, it covers every curve with $j(E)
otin\{0,1728\}$, in particular every curve of prime order with $j(E)
eq0$, and the curves with $j(E)\in\{0,1728\}$ that have a nonzero rational $2$-torsion point. It also covers all ordinary elliptic curves in characteristic~$3$ and all ordinary binary elliptic curves $y^2+xy=x^3+ax^2+b$ with $b
eq1$, closing a gap left by earlier constructions.
papers.authors: Mojtaba Fadavi, David Jao

papers.title: Which Pairs Belong Together? An Optimization Approach to Pair Selection in $F_4$
papers.abstract: The security of multivariate public key cryptosystems (MPKC) relies in part on the hardness of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem, which consists in finding a solution to a system of quadratic equations over a finite field. One of the main approaches to solving such systems is to compute a Gröbner basis, which is often done with Faugère's $F_4$ algorithm. In each iteration, $F_4$ selects a set of critical pairs to reduce, and the selection strategy strongly affects its performance. The standard approach, the normal strategy, selects pairs by degree alone. In this work, we introduce two features of critical pairs, novelty and column growth, and use them to formulate pair selection as a weighted quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem. By studying different weightings, we find that penalizing novel pairs and strongly weighting column growth reduces the computation time of $F_4$, excluding the cost of selection, by a median factor of about 1.5, at the cost of a far more expensive selection step. Based on these findings, we design the coverage strategy that keeps the two features but replaces the optimization by a sequential rule with a budget derived from the expected number of new head terms. Experiments on weakly overdetermined MQ instances over $\mathbb{F}_{31}$ with 11 to 16 equations show that the coverage strategy reduces the total computation time, including selection, by 35% to 67% compared to the normal strategy, without additional memory, and that this improvement grows with the size of the system.
papers.authors: Noah Peroš, Alessandro Amadori, Jins de Jong, Pınar Kılıçer

papers.title: LUTune: Automated Lookup Table Optimization for Efficient TFHE-Based ML Inference
papers.abstract: TFHE evaluates quantized activation functions by programmable bootstrapping (PBS) using lookup tables (LUTs). The input precision of a LUT and the noise tolerance of its consumers affect PBS latency and evaluation-key size. LUTune rewrites activation LUTs using the outputs permitted by Concrete ML's approximate rounding rule. It folds LUTs to reduce their input precision and decomposes plaintext weights into signed digits to reduce the output-noise variance predicted for dense layers. LUTune checks the circuit failure bound under Concrete's noise model at the selected parameters. On VGG6 it achieves a $5.2\times$ speedup and a $17.2\times$ reduction in evaluation-key size relative to the lowest-latency Concrete ML configuration, using the same frozen weights and quantizers.
papers.authors: Rostin Shokri, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos

papers.title: FLoRA: LoRA Fine-Tuning for Language Models under Fully Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: Deploying and fine-tuning Language Models (LMs) on cloud infrastructure introduces privacy risks when handling sensitive prompts and proprietary datasets. While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces fine-tuning overhead, it requires processing data in plaintext, exposing sensitive data to curious cloud providers. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce FLoRA, a privacy-preserving framework for encrypted LM fine-tuning and inference via Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). FLoRA allows training low-rank adapters and performing inference entirely on encrypted data, guaranteeing data confidentiality against untrusted environments. We evaluate FLoRA by fine-tuning the SmolLM2-360M model on the SST-2 dataset, demonstrating stable performance and efficiency for privacy-preserving LM adaptation.
papers.authors: Omar Ahmed, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos

papers.title: DC-NPSCA: Data-Constrained Non-profiled Side-Channel Analysis using Metric Learning
papers.abstract: Reliable key-byte recovery with limited power traces remains challenging in non-profiled side-channel analysis (NPSCA). This letter presents data-constrained NPSCA (DC-NPSCA), a metric learning framework for key-byte recovery without a profiling device or secret-dependent training labels. Known-plaintext relationships define positive and negative trace pairs for training a Siamese feature extractor. Candidate keys are then ranked by the separability of the embedding partitions induced by their hypothetical leakage labels, reusing one trained extractor for all candidates. Experiments on four ASCAD-derived datasets reuse the same collected traces for training and attack. With 5,120 original traces on each synchronized dataset and 7,680 and 15,360 traces on ASCAD\_50 and ASCAD\_100, respectively, all ten independently trained models recover the target key byte in all ten attack trials per model. Compared with the non-profiled variant of weakly profiling side-channel analysis (WPSCA), DC-NPSCA achieves higher key-byte recovery reliability under the evaluated limited-trace budgets, while WPSCA requires fewer ranking traces at the largest evaluated budget.
papers.authors: Yinhao Han, Meiling Zhang, Dong Zheng

papers.title: Extending the Security of Arithmetic Masking to All Finite Cyclic Groups via Fourier Analysis
papers.abstract: Let $N\geq 2$ and let $G=\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. A secret $s\in G$ is shared by choosing a tuple $(X_1,\ldots,X_k)$ uniformly subject to $X_1+\cdots+X_k=s$ in $G$. Represent each share by the unique integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ in its residue class. Let $D_s$ denote the joint distribution of the Hamming weights of the $k$ shares, and let $D_U$ denote the corresponding distribution when the secret is uniform on $G$. The problem is to bound the total variation distance between these distributions uniformly in $s$. Biswas et al. established an upper bound for this distance when the modulus is close to a power of two. In this paper we prove that for every integer $N\geq 2$ and every fixed $k\geq 3$, putting $n=\lceil\log_2 N\rceil$, we have $$\max_{s\in G}\operatorname{TV}(D_s,D_U)=O_k\bigl(n^{-k/2+5/4}\bigr).$$ We obtain this bound using Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube and a decomposition of $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ into intervals whose lengths are powers of two. This removes the restriction on the modulus without weakening the exponent in the general bound of Biswas et al.
papers.authors: Ishan Kumthekar

papers.title: A Generalization of A Randomized AKS-Class Primality Proving Algorithm via Twisted Polynomials
papers.abstract: We study extensions of Bernstein's combinatorial primality certificates obtained by varying the linear factors and the coefficient degree in a Kummer-type quotient ring. We then separate the coefficient period from the extension degree and replace an auxiliary factor by direct period tests. The results strengthen certificate criteria under stated hypotheses; they do not establish a smaller general complexity exponent than Bernstein's essentially quartic algorithm.
papers.authors: Haining Fan

papers.title: On Perfect Additive Randomized Encodings
papers.abstract: An Additive Randomized Encoding (ARE) for $f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ reduces the task of securely computing $f$ to computing the sum of locally encoded inputs. Concretely, an ARE for $f$ over an Abelian group $\mathbb G$ randomly encodes each input $x_i$ into $\tilde x_i\in\mathbb G$, such that from $\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde x_i$ one can decode $f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ (correctness) but cannot learn anything else about the inputs (security). Previous works constructed AREs for simple functions such as $\sf{OR}$ with perfect security and imperfect correctness (namely, the decoder's output is incorrect with a small probability), and AREs for general functions with imperfect correctness and security, where imperfect security was shown to be inherent. This leaves open the existence of ARE for nontrivial functions with perfect correctness. We make progress on this question, obtaining the following negative results. $\bullet$ Ruling out a perfect ARE for ${\sf OR}$: We rule out the existence of a perfect ARE, namely ARE satisfying both perfect security and perfect correctness, for ${\sf OR}(x_1,x_2)=x_1\vee x_2$ over any finite Abelian group. We also rule out any perfect ARE for ${\sf XOR}(x_1,x_2)=x_1\oplus x_2$ over $\mathbb Z_p$, for any prime $p>2$, assuming that the encoding probabilities are rational. $\bullet$ Towards ruling out perfectly correct AREs: We partially rule out AREs for ${\sf OR}$ that have perfect correctness and imperfect security, under some natural restrictions on the ARE that are met by existing constructions. Concretely, assuming that the input 0 is always encoded as 0, we rule out perfectly correct AREs whose security error is negligible in the bit-length of group elements. If the encodings of 1 are also uniform over their supports, we rule out security error at most $10^{-5}$. Finally, we rule out perfectly secure AREs with nontrivial correctness error for ${\sf OR}$ and ${\sf XOR}$ over histograms, i.e., elements $h\in\mathbb N^\mathbb N$ whose support is finite. This also rules out perfectly secure protocols with the same correctness guarantee for ${\sf OR}$ and ${\sf XOR}$ in the (non-interactive) shuffle model, a popular model in the differential privacy literature, where parties can broadcast anonymous messages from which the output is computed.
papers.authors: Yuval Ishai, Eyal Kushilevitz, Sahar Alon Yerushalmi

papers.title: Faster Provable Algorithm For Random Modular Subset Sum
papers.abstract: We study random modular subset sum with $n$ coefficients sampled independently and uniformly modulo $Q$. The target is $t=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf x\pmod Q$, where the hidden binary vector $\mathbf x$ is fixed independently of the coefficients. We focus on the balanced density-one setting, a standard hard case with $Q=2^n$ and $\mathbf x$ of Hamming weight $n/2$. In this balanced density-one setting, Bonnetain, Bricout, Schrottenloher, and Shen (ASIACRYPT 2020) reported the best previously known classical time bound of $\widetilde O(2^{0.283n})$ bit operations, using $\widetilde O(2^{0.283n})$ bits of space, under heuristic assumptions. We present a classical randomized algorithm for the same setting that finds a solution with overwhelming probability using at most $2^{0.2614n}$ bit operations and $2^{0.2373n}$ bits of space for sufficiently large $n$, without heuristic assumptions.
papers.authors: Hyeonhak Kim, Jiseung Kim, Changmin Lee

papers.title: Forging Encrypted Linear Checksums in Verifiable FHE: A Cryptanalysis of DataSeal
papers.abstract: DataSeal (IEEE S&P 2025) gives an FHE evaluator encrypted secret linear checksums. We study whether it can use them to make an incorrect output pass verification. Each of DataSeal's two published matrix checks separately admits substitution of a different public function without ciphertext multiplication. Even when both checks are enforced, two independent authenticated input columns yield a nonzero checksum-preserving error with probability $1-q^{-2}$ over a uniform key, provided the forged circuit decrypts correctly. This attack has multiplication depth one when the input columns are encrypted; public basis columns permit depth-zero attacks. We then analyze a natural repair: adding independent checksum rows. For $t\ge2$ rows, we bound the success probability of fixed-coefficient affine attacks and give nearly matching public-vector constructions of order $q^{-(t-1)}$. Extra rows reduce success in this class, but exposing encrypted tags costs approximately one row of protection relative to blind rank-one errors. With $t+1$ independent authenticated vectors, a cofactor attack succeeds with probability at least $1-1/(q(q-1))$ if its circuit decrypts. Its depth is $\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil$ for encrypted vectors. For public vectors, depth $\lceil\log_2t\rceil$ is necessary and sufficient for universal polynomial cancellation in our fixed-coefficient model and field range; partial cofactors characterize intermediate attacks. Independent SEAL/BGV runs execute the DataSeal forgeries and selected multi-row circuits, including a depth-two three-row cofactor. A parameter study finds settings where honest workloads decrypt but an added depth-one forgery fails, while depth-zero public-basis forgeries still execute. Independent MNIST models show forgeries that pass verification and change predictions. These experiments measure feasibility for our layouts and modulus chains; the authors' unpublished implementation and settings remain untested.
papers.authors: Jiseok Bang, Seungkwang Lee

papers.title: Internal Differential Collision Attacks against Round-Reduced SHA-3
papers.abstract: The \sc{Keccak} hash function was selected by NIST as the winner of the \texttt{SHA-3} competition in 2012 and was adopted as the \texttt{SHA-3} hash standard of NIST in 2015. This paper focuses on internal differential collision attacks on round-reduced \texttt{SHA-3} and various \sc{Keccak} variants. Inspired by the work of Dinur, Dunkelman and Shamir in 2013, we propose an improved variant of internal differential cryptanalysis as well as a new target internal difference algorithm by probabilistic linearization. More exactly, we improve the internal differential cryptanalysis by abstracting new concepts such as \emph{differential transition conditions} and \emph{differential transition system}, and propose conditional internal differentials to reduce the complexity of the first two rounds. In terms of Sbox linearization, we proposed \emph{full Sbox linearization} and \emph{probabilistic Sbox linearization} techniques for internal differentials. We also exploit new strategies for optimizing the internal differential characteristic. Furthermore, we determine the expected size of collision subsets in internal differentials, by analyzing the collision probability of the digests rather than the intermediate states input to the last nonlinear layer. These techniques enhance the analysis of internal differentials, leading to the best theoretical collision attacks on nine \sc{Keccak} instances, including six round-reduced instances of \texttt{SHA-3} and three instances of \sc{Keccak} contest. Specifically, the number of attacked rounds is extended to 5 from 4 for \texttt{SHA3-384}, and the attacks on 4-, 5- and 6-round \texttt{SHAKE256} are the first collision attacks on reduced \texttt{SHAKE256}. We also present the best collision attacks for 4-round \texttt{SHA3-512} and 6-round \texttt{SHAKE128}. For the \sc{Keccak} contest, we propose theoretical collision attacks on up to 6 rounds, and successfully reduce the complexity of one previously unbroken instance to $2^{53}$.
papers.authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Chengan Hou, Meicheng Liu

papers.title: CRAFTing an Attack on the Full-Round CRAFT
papers.abstract: CRAFT is a 64-bit block, 128-bit key tweakable block cipher presented in 2019 by Beierle et al. can be efficiently protected against differential fault attacks. Since its introduction, numerous attacks were presented, where the best one (in number of attacked rounds) can break up to 26 rounds out of the cipher's 32. In this paper, we present the first full-round attack on CRAFT in the single-key model. The attack uses the recently presented (FSE 2026) observation that CRAFT can be decomposed into two parts, with minimal inter-part mixing. We use this property to construct a dissection attack that breaks the full 32-round CRAFT in $2^{121}$ time and $2^{120}$ memory, using 3 known plaintexts; an information-theoretic argument suggests that two already suffice. The same attack extends to 36 rounds of CRAFT in $2^{126}$ time and $2^{124}$ memory with 3 known plaintexts, and so remains faster than exhaustive search well beyond the specified number of rounds.
papers.authors: Orr Dunkelman, Eran Lambooij

papers.title: A Deterministic Subexponential-time Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem
papers.abstract: Classical deterministic algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem (DLP) in prime fields $\mathbb{F}_p^*$ and on elliptic curves $E(\mathbb{F}_p)$ require $p^{1/2+o(1)}$ bit operations in the worst case when no unproven number-theoretic hypotheses are assumed. Following the October 2026 refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), Akshima et al. (2026) and Kaarelson (2026) obtained Las Vegas subexponential algorithms for the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem over prime fields, while leaving deterministic $p^{o(1)}$ discrete logarithm algorithms open even in $\mathbb{F}_p^*$. In this paper, we show that assuming the Cauchy--Hermite Boolean tensor contraction construction of OpenAI (October 2026), there is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that solves both the discrete logarithm problem on prime-order elliptic curves over $\mathbb{F}_p$ ($p > 3$) and the discrete logarithm problem in $\mathbb{F}_p^*$ in worst-case time \[ 2^{O(b/\sqrt{\log\log b})} = p^{o(1)} \] and space $2^{O(b/(\log b)^{1/4})}$, where $b = \lceil \log_2 p \rceil$. The algorithm uses zero random bits and relies on neither the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis nor smoothness heuristics. Our proof combines two technical ingredients: (i) a deterministic conditional-expectation construction of small affine-interval factor bases whose $2m$-fold sumsets cover the entire group, and (ii) a terminal-preserving partial contraction procedure that bypasses the degree barrier of candidate-label table lookups by compressing the low-degree arithmetic core onto $\Theta(b)$ boundary wires prior to exact digitwise contraction. All the theorems/lemmas have passed the Lean verification on https://prove2.me/missions/A_Deterministic_Subexponential-time_Algorithm_for_the_Discrete_Logarithm_Problem .
papers.authors: Shuchang Liu, Bingsheng Zhang, Kui Ren

papers.title: Rotten CHERIs - A Comprehensive Study of Faults in CHERI RISC-V
papers.abstract: The relentless stream of exploits based on memory vulnerabilities has prompted hardware developers to engineer new solutions that prevent these vulnerabilities at a deep hardware level. One such solution is CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions), which has attracted significant interest from academia and industry. While CHERI has proven effective at mitigating memory-safety vulnerabilities under its architectural threat model, real-world environments often expose devices to advanced attack strategies. In particular, physical attackers can launch fault attacks that greatly exceed the fault model assumed during CHERI's development. Although memory and fault attacks are vastly different, the question arises whether CHERI's memory-protection guarantees hold under a fault attack model. To address this issue, we conduct the first fault analysis of CHERI on RISC-V systems. We analyze the impact of faults on capabilities and capability management instructions. Our threat analysis reveals opportunities and limitations for attackers, showing that CHERI raises the bar for meaningful fault attacks, but does not prevent them entirely. In order to evaluate fault attacks on generic CHERI-RISC-V systems, we have developed a functional, Spike-based fault simulator. We demonstrate successful fault attacks that can still violate CHERI's memory-safety guarantees and evaluate and discuss potential countermeasures.
papers.authors: Jan Philipp Thoma, Maja Malenko, Yan Yan, Carl Shaw

papers.title: CHARTS: Compute-efficient Homomorphic Anonymous Routing with Tag Sums
papers.abstract: Anonymous routing is a fundamental tool to protect communication privacy by hiding who communicates with whom. Existing constructions based on a single untrusted router, including NIAR (EUROCRYPT'21) and the recent sPAR (CCS'26), typically rely on oblivious permutation or placement of encrypted messages, which incurs substantial computational overhead at the router. In this paper, we present CHARTS, a compute-efficient anonymous routing protocol that eliminates the need for oblivious placement or permutation. Instead, CHARTS uses random tags and homomorphic aggregation to recover encrypted messages as an unordered multiset. Each sender encrypts its message under the intended receiver's public key and associates the resulting ciphertext with a fresh random tag. Using multiparty homomorphic encryption, the router computes power sums of the tags and tag-weighted ciphertext aggregates, from which it recovers a multiset of the encrypted messages. We prove simulation-based security against static semi-honest adversaries under decisional RLWE and an IND-CPA-secure, key-private, weakly robust public-key encryption scheme. We implement CHARTS in Go using Lattigo. Our direct construction requires only homomorphic additions and evaluates a batch of 128 messages in approximately 260 ms of router computation, achieving a speedup of over 35,000 times compared with sPAR using its published parameters, on the same hardware and with the same thread count. We also introduce a factorized variant that reduces sender communication at the cost of additional router computation.
papers.authors: Anthony Flath, Ke Wu

papers.title: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
papers.abstract: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.
papers.authors: Kelsey A. Jackson, Carl A. Miller

papers.title: Northstar: Efficient Verifiable Negacyclic Polynomial Arithmetic with Applications to Encrypted Lattice-based Multi-Asset ERC-20 and Verifiable FHE
papers.abstract: Lattice-based cryptography can be used to construct a variety of post-quantum cryptographic schemes, ranging from standard cryptographic primitives such as digital signatures and encryption, to fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). However, the verification of correct lattice computations remains relatively expensive, particularly for computationally intensive FHE operations and for resource-constrained environments such as on-chain verification via smart contracts. We propose Northstar, an efficient technique for proving negacyclic arithmetic natively. When integrated with existing STARK proving frameworks, Northstar achieves the best overall performance across prover time, verifier time, and proof size compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches for verifiable FHE constructions. Furthermore, Northstar is used to construct the first verifiable encrypted multi-asset (~ 1000 assets) variant of ERC-20 that is efficiently verifiable by a smart contract, and is practically deployable in the current blockchain ecosystem.
papers.authors: Yeoh Wei Zhu, Shaltiel Eloul, Yash Satsangi, Rob Otter

papers.title: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth
papers.abstract: Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 $μ$s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.
papers.authors: Anthony Mikhaiel, Essam Ghadafi

papers.title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes
papers.abstract: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.
papers.authors: Valentina Astore, Martino Borello, Alain Couvreur

papers.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM
papers.abstract: Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ into a commitment whose size is independent of $n$, such that a verifier can open any bit $x_i$ using $\log n$ hash evaluations. The security of the scheme (intractability of finding two distinct openings for a given bit using the same commitment) follows from the collision resistance of the hash function. The verifier's runtime complexity is a bottleneck in many key applications of vector commitments, including SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries. As such, a longstanding open question has been whether it is possible to construct hash-based vector commitments where the verifier makes a sublogarithmic number of hash evaluations. We prove that sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible to achieve through black-box use of a hash function; we not only rule out constructions from collision resistant hash functions, but in fact show that commitment schemes with sublogarithmic verifier complexity are unachievable in the random oracle model. In particular, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers has verifier query complexity $Ω_θ(\log n)$, where $θ$ is the input length of the random oracle. This bound is matched up to constant factors by high-arity Merkle trees. The key technical lemma in our proof is a disjoint product lemma, which can be viewed as a computational analog of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer (BKR) inequality. We believe this lemma is of independent interest, and in particular may be useful for showing other lower bounds and separations in the random oracle model.
papers.authors: Miranda Christ, Oliver Korten, Tal Malkin, Noam Mazor, Shyamal Patel

papers.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM
papers.abstract: Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ into a commitment whose size is independent of $n$, such that a verifier can open any bit $x_i$ using $\log n$ hash evaluations. papers.authors: Miranda Christ, Oliver Korten, Tal Malkin, Noam Mazor, Shyamal Patel

papers.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
papers.abstract: Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving. FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$). Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.
papers.authors: Liang Song

papers.title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
papers.abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.
papers.authors: Jon Carmona, Jon Irureta, Jon Imaz, Aizea Lojo, Juan Martínez-Romo, Lourdes Araujo

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
papers.abstract: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). Across 56 reproducible experiments spanning a multi-layer enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (SOREL-20M, BODMAS, LANL, and DARPA Transparent Computing), we test twelve architectural claims governing modern fleet-scale defense. First, we show that fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget even at negligible compute cost (<$0.0003 per million events), and that rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms GraphSAGE without neural training. Second, evaluating frontier reasoning models (Gemini) and fine-tuned open-weight models (Qwen3-4B) for alert triage reveals that unconstrained LLM auto-closure eliminates 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases. Third, post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) causes severe reward hacking on unseen attack classes, suppressing up to 86% of novel attacks compared to two-epoch supervised fine-tuning. Finally, against an adaptive adversary generating plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields, LLM triage evasion rises sharply unless gated by a deterministic policy harness prior to model invocation.
papers.authors: Jeremy Canale

papers.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.
papers.authors: Alessandro Cantelli-Forti, Isabella Marasco, Hosam Alamleh, Giada Boschi, Michele Colajanni

papers.title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
papers.abstract: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.
papers.authors: Yaser Kord, Moritz Hess

papers.title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs
papers.abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.
papers.authors: Yan Lin, Zhongliang Guo, Jingyu Lin, Daizong Liu

papers.title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys
papers.abstract: Modern cryptographic protocols such as WPA2-PSK, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Bluetooth Classic (BC) tolerate low-entropy keys for user-friendliness, backward compatibility, or resource-constrained deployment, yet existing symbolic protocol verifiers rely on the perfect-encryption assumption and therefore cannot reason about brute-force attackers. Prior work addresses this gap only through protocol-specific, manually encoded reveal rules, which neither generalize across protocols nor systematically explore compound-key decomposition. We introduce the first protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic methodology for low-entropy keys, built on three abstractions: the message-derivation fact MDerive, which captures brute-force prerequisites independently of concrete function symbols; a three-tier breaking-oracle design (value-breaking, relationship-breaking, message-derivation) that composes with the standard Dolev-Yao attacker; and a graded bit-level attacker model that bounds the key length an attacker is allowed to exhaust. We realize the methodology as EntropyVerif, a syntax-sugar extension of Tamarin that requires no kernel modification. Using EntropyVerif we automatically rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks, and uncover a new attack on BC which we call the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack: by repeatedly downgrading one side of a BC session and recombining the recovered key fragments, an attacker reduces session-key recovery against devices using the maximum 128-bit key from $2^{128}$ to $n \cdot 2^{128/n}$, bottoming out at $2^{12}$ for $n=16$---a factor of $2^{116}$ reduction that has been responsibly disclosed to the Bluetooth SIG. Across three real-world protocols and six BC device configurations, our results show that entropy-aware symbolic analysis is both feasible and necessary.
papers.authors: Yongkang Xiao, Jing Chen, Min Shi, Kun He, Mei Wang, Ruiying Du

papers.title: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework for Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification with Quantitative RTL Analysis
papers.abstract: The growing complexity of modern hardware designs is making security assurance increasingly difficult. One of the foundational steps in pre-silicon security verification is identifying security assets. While primary assets are often evident from design functionality, the internal signals that can facilitate their compromise are much less apparent. Complex data- and control-flow dependencies create many such internal security-critical locations, whose exploitation depends on the threat-specific attack mechanism---these are the secondary assets. To precisely identify these, we propose SecID, a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis with bounded dynamic evaluation and LLM reasoning to identify threat-specific secondary assets. Each asset decision is supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms. We demonstrate SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P. The experimental results are corroborated through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, and further evaluated through pipeline- and final-stage ablation, threshold-sensitivity studies, and final-stage repeatability analysis. Together, these evaluations show that SecID can identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets with respect to a given primary asset, providing a scalable path toward hardware-security verification.
papers.authors: Md Ajoad Hasan, Dipayan Saha, Upoma Das, Sujan Kumar Saha, Mark Tehranipoor, Farimah Farahmandi

papers.title: From Models to Services: Systematizing Security Assurance for Model-as-a-Service
papers.abstract: Large language models are mainly delivered as cloud services, in which the assets of different principals are coupled within a single service pipeline, while the related security research is scattered across several fields with differing threat models. This paper systematizes this research from a service perspective. We decompose Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack and five trust boundaries, define six adversary classes and six security goals, use them to code 120 studies, and evaluate 50 defenses under a unified set of criteria. The results show that 44.2% of the studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%. Defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware mechanisms that protect against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers. Finally, we propose a research agenda by comparison with current standards and regulations.
papers.authors: Jianming Zhou, Yang Luo, Guangpu Chen, Zhaoyu Chen, Yifeng Gao, Qingni Shen, Zhonghai Wu

papers.title: From Conversations to Commitments: A Design Study of Shared Records for Agent-to-Business Coordination
papers.abstract: Business commitments require accepted terms to be linked to delegated authority, reserved resources and durable evidence. We examine how a shared, attributable interaction record can support these links across independently operated organisations. Talea combines signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution. We use its coordination sandbox and a proposed commercial extension in a design study of an airline booking disrupted passengers into three competing hotels. Four observations follow. First, AT Protocol provides mechanisms supporting five of six coordination requirements, while record-level access and release controls require additional enforcement. Second, the case's confidentiality constraints restrict each hotel's authorised view to its bilateral exchange; only the airline can correlate all three deals. Third, this leaves a possible benefit for late-joining participants inside the airline's trust boundary, but does not establish an advantage over an equally instrumented point-to-point design. Fourth, a deterministic release interface constrains fixed, approved payloads but cannot bound disclosure when negotiated values depend on private state. Finite-model explorations and deterministic interface checks reproduce the specified behaviours and counterexamples when selected controls are removed. They do not measure comparative benefit or validate a deployed commercial system. The remaining hypothesis is that, within one trust boundary, shared records improve decision reconstruction and recovery under changing participation relative to point-to-point exchange with equivalent authority, reservation, retention and correlation evidence. We specify an experiment to test it.
papers.authors: Carlos Eberhardt, Mansura Habiba

papers.title: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning for TEE-based Edge AI Protection
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further shows that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.
papers.authors: Daniela M. Vela Hernandez, Samuel Hildebrand, Sean Oesch, Brian Weber, Shayan Monadjemi

papers.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
papers.abstract: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.
papers.authors: S M Zia Ur Rashid, Sazidul Islam Hira, Suman Rath

papers.title: Non-Complete Set Coverings as Combinatorial Designs
papers.abstract: Non-complete set coverings provide a combinatorial framework for constructing threshold implementations, a masking countermeasure against side-channel attacks. For a function of algebraic degree $t$, a family of subsets of the input shares yields a $d$-th order threshold implementation if every $t$ shares lie in a common subset and no $d$ subsets cover all the shares. In this work we study non-complete set coverings as combinatorial designs. We introduce incomplete coverings, a family of designs that contains non-complete set coverings and is closed under the dual complement operation. We show that coverage and incompleteness are dual properties under this operation, and we define reduced incomplete coverings, which do not contain redundant blocks nor redundant elements, two notions that are dual to each other. In addition, we prove analogues for incomplete coverings of classical properties of uniform coverings. Namely, we prove the existence of derived sub-coverings, a recursion rule for covering numbers and Schönheim's bound. We use these results to improve several lower bounds on the minimal number of blocks of non-complete set coverings. Moreover, we also find new coverings and upper bounds on the covering numbers based on enhanced algorithms, in particular for degree four and order three.
papers.authors: Oriol Farràs, Óscar Fidalgo, Carlos Andres Lara-Nino

papers.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.
papers.authors: Joy Bose, Srinivas Adyapak

papers.title: Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Technical Validation of Re-identification Tests under the EDPB Anonymisation Guidelines
papers.abstract: The Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), published for consultation in July 2026, assess anonymity relative to the entities that may access data. They bring AI models into scope and call for testing, but do not say how a re-identification test should be designed or validated, or how far its result counts as evidence. Building on our reply to the consultation, we describe a framework based on a secure processing environment whose outputs are reviewed before release (an airlock), and distinguish forms of release and three types of evidence: formal, empirical and indirect. We raise seven open questions, each with a scenario, and examine their technical side in three settings: the release of model weights (the trained parameters of a machine learning model), review at an airlock, and regulatory sandboxes, in which an authority supervises development and testing. In each setting the assessment depends on how far a test result can be relied on, since a failed re-identification attempt may mean only that the test was too weak. Drawing on measurement practice in other regulated fields, we call for re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods, with stated detection limit, bias and uncertainty.
papers.authors: Rickard Brännvall, Henrik Forsgren, Erik Ylipää, Aslak Felin, Michael Popoff, Susanne Stenberg

papers.title: Distance from the Truth: Why Fragmented Merchant Underwriting Misses Risk, and What Source-Attributable Evidence Changes
papers.abstract: Merchant underwriting becomes vulnerable when evidence is evaluated without enough visibility into its source, freshness, relationship to the applicant, or meaning for the proposed activity. Individually favorable checks do not necessarily establish that the same business is operating the merchant account, that its representative may bind it, or that its settlement instructions are authorized. We describe three failure modes of fragmented underwriting: distance from the source, the gap between a decision and the evidence needed to justify it; the correlation gap, in which material relationships among the person, legal entity, owners or controllers, representative, business activity, and settlement destination are not evaluated when each signal is considered alone; and point-in-time controls, in which a historical verification is treated as present eligibility. We map these failure modes to identity-proofing, customer-due-diligence, sanctions, third-party-risk, card-network, and Nacha requirements, and propose a merchant-underwriting application of the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture built on provenance, correlation, and persistence. The application keeps a logically unified evidence record that identifies what was checked, the subject and relationship involved, the relevant times, the applicable policy, the decision, and any exceptions, and it keeps evidence validation, applicant verification, organizational authority, and the institution's risk judgment separate. We also set out a proposed evidence and decision receipt, a defined 90-day shadow enrollment pilot with adjudicated outcome measures and deliberate control-failure tests, and a ten-question self-assessment. Proposed controls, illustrative scenarios, and pilot measures are identified as such and are not represented as observed production results.
papers.authors: Russell Lessard, Jeremy Blackburn, Tim Hines, Matthew Koepp, Jason Patrick

papers.title: Fuel as Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links after Total Key Compromise
papers.abstract: Optical inter-satellite links form the backbone of entire constellations in low Earth orbit, yet their security rests on keys alone. When an attacker obtains every key of a satellite, no secret is left to authenticate it again. Existing fixes fail, since ground rekeying encrypts new keys under the leaked ones, and post-compromise protocols assume an authenticated start. As a remedy, the satellite's orbit can take over as the trust anchor. The attacker then needs an impostor satellite that blocks and retransmits the beam, a chord beneath the curved orbit. Hence, the blocking point lies off free fall and costs the impostor continuous thrust. We formalize this position-gated adversary and prove, for satellites on a shared circular orbit, a tight lower bound on the propellant cost in delta-v of a point-mass craft that keeps blocking, however it moves. We present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol that combines this position gate with ML-KEM. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how combining links forces an impostor onto every link. Once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant, every key back to the first is authenticated retroactively. A satellite thus needs no crosslink key before launch, so none can leak in the supply chain. The same mechanism heals the link after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness. A passive attacker is shut out at the next round, whereas an active one splits the chains and is exposed once its propellant runs out. The chain can then heal after an operator reset. As a result, every Starlink satellite has a partner on whose link a CubeSat-class impostor runs out of propellant in about two days. This holds against one rigid craft per link running the best attack we know, if each terminal enforces a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol only uses under 0.02% of the link.
papers.authors: Leon Birkel, Mohammad Hamad, Sebastian Steinhorst

papers.title: Poisoning Attacks to Local Differential Privacy Protocols for Dynamic Graphs
papers.abstract: With the increasing adoption of privacy-preserving techniques in dynamic graph analysis, local differential privacy (LDP) has become a fundamental paradigm for protecting user data in decentralized environments. However, despite its strong privacy guarantees, LDP-based dynamic graph protocols remain vulnerable to data poisoning attacks through malicious data injection. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of data poisoning attacks against privacy-preserving dynamic graphs under the LDP framework. Considering the temporal evolution of dynamic graphs, we identify key challenges in attack design and evaluation, including how to schedule attack resources across time and how to measure cumulative attack impact. To address these challenges, we introduce an absolute gain metric to quantify the overall deviation of graph statistical metrics before and after attacks across time. Based on this metric, we further propose a unified poisoning attack framework for dynamic graphs, which consists of target node selection, dynamic fake node scale scheduling, and fake edge injection. Within this framework, we design a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy that dynamically schedules attack resources to maximize attack effectiveness, along with two baseline strategies, equal-scale attack (ESA) and random-scale attack (RSA), for comparison. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed attacks can significantly degrade the accuracy of graph metric estimation for target nodes.
papers.authors: Shang Liu, Yuhan Bao, Hongbin Zhao, Yanmei Zhang, Guan Yuan, Yang Cao

papers.title: FlipVLA: Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action(VLA) Models Only Through Bit Flips
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions in real-world environments, making malicious model tampering a potential threat to physical safety. We study whether object-triggered backdoors can be implanted through a small, fixed set of parameter bit flips without retraining. The central challenge is to make persistent weight modifications disrupt trigger-present behavior while preserving performance on non-trigger inputs. We propose FlipVLA, a two-stage selector-amplifier method that exploits existing visual features within an FC-GELU-FC structure. The selector constructs a trigger-dependent response in a selected channel, using GELU to attenuate background activity. The amplifier modifies a connected downstream weight to convert this response into an action-relevant perturbation. Channel screening and discrete bit search construct both components under a limited modification budget. Experiments on OpenVLA-OFT and GR00T N1.7 across four LIBERO suites achieve attack success rates of 90.22% to 100%, with task success decreasing by at most 1.5 percentage points on clean scenes.
papers.authors: Zexi Zhao, Zizhen Liu, Jing Justin Ye, Huawei Li

papers.title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
papers.abstract: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.
papers.authors: Ishaq Aden-Ali, Adam Sealfon, Adam Smith, Thomas Steinke, Jonathan Ullman

papers.title: WADJET: Whole-Job Authorization and Dispatch for Job Execution Trust on FPGA System-on-Chip Accelerators
papers.abstract: On an FPGA system-on-chip, the software that submits work to an accelerator also decides what the accelerator does. It writes the registers one by one, and the hardware runs whatever it finds, so faulty or compromised software can change one address or resend a job. Existing protections decide who may reach an accelerator or keep its data safe. Deciding whether one job was approved and is still unused takes three things in one place: the only way to the accelerator, the whole job held back until checked, and a record of used approvals. WADJET puts the three in one gate in FPGA logic. A separate authority encrypts and authenticates each approved job, with a sequence number, using Ascon-AEAD128. The gate verifies the whole job before releasing any part, accepts only a newer sequence number, uses it up, and writes the registers of an unmodified accelerator itself. The gate replaces only the processor's direct line to the registers and works beside the existing protections. In a software model, a check on each write ran jobs mixed from two approved ones; the whole-job rule released none. Its release path is proven on the Verilog for all inputs. On a Zynq-7020 running a language model, it released all 21,000 approved jobs and none of 14,700 altered or repeated ones. It needs a third of the lookup tables of ShEF's register protection, which protects more, and adds about ten microseconds to starting a job. It assumes trusted control of its key, reset, and configuration.
papers.authors: Mohamed El-Hadedy

papers.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
papers.abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%).
