A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.
papers.authors: Abdullah Kaya, Cevheri Bozoglan, Yusuf Gundogdu

papers.title: Bounded Autonomy: A Trust-Anchored Defense Against Resource-Exhaustion Attacks on Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to resource-exhaustion attacks that amplify model-token consumption through persistent context amplification, large tool output amplification, and error-induced agentic loops. Despite growing attention to agent security and resource-abuse risks, a systematic defense framework specifically targeting these attacks remains lacking. Meanwhile, existing general-purpose agent defense frameworks, which address a broader range of security threats, often rely on prompt-level safeguards or coarse-grained resource limits and lack deterministic runtime mechanisms for controlling token consumption. They also provide limited support for balancing fault recovery against the risk of repeated resource-consuming execution. To address these limitations, we propose a trust-anchored closed-loop defense framework consisting of four phases: certificate-guided orchestration with deterministic handoffs, calibrated one-time node budgeting, Gateway-based runtime enforcement, and bounded recovery through a shared, non-resettable recovery pool. By accounting for both input and output tokens across all model invocations, our experiments demonstrate that the framework bounds cumulative token consumption, mitigates resource-amplification attacks, and preserves benign task utility under trusted execution assumptions.
papers.authors: Ziyuan Chen, Yueming Lyu, Songze Li, Huafeng Chen, Caifeng Shan

papers.title: PseuDRAGON: Knowledge-Guided Local LLMs for Financial-Data Pseudonymization in Closed Networks
papers.abstract: Staff pseudonymizing financial data in closed networks must interpret abbreviated column names, identify personal information, and choose processing methods. Local language models can assist, but may give different labels for the same input. PseuDRAGON keeps confirmed judgments and corrections outside a fixed model and reuses them through exact-name lookup and learned rules. For expert review, the workflow searches institutional policy, national privacy law, then international sources. Across 92 columns from one institution, rules increase reuse under the same approval checks from 75 to 83 labels without reuse errors when all training judgments are available. With 25% of the training judgments, withholding non-PII rules for unseen names eliminated the extra PII misses in replay at the cost of lower reuse. Revising or withdrawing approvals rebuilds derived rules, and tests on synthetic records verify that selected methods produce the specified outputs. In three paired runs, the history-first baseline cut automated identification time by 83.0% on average versus no reuse.
papers.authors: Gwangui Hong, Seonho An, Seonkyu Lim, KyungTae Lim, Min-Soo Kim

papers.title: CHIP: Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection. Can OpenAI CLIP Reconstruct Images from the CPU Computational Footprint?
papers.abstract: Image inference on a shared CPU leaves input-dependent traces in software-visible performance counters and execution time. CHIP (Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection) trains a lightweight residual projector on public images to map these measurements into the 768-dimensional visual embedding space of a frozen OpenAI CLIP model. A frozen Stable unCLIP generator uses the projected embeddings to reconstruct recognizable color scenes for held-out inputs. The attack requires no physical probe, candidate image gallery, domain-specific generator, or shared cache, and elapsed time alone retains the signal. We evaluate full-counter, single-counter, and timing-only measurements on Intel Haswell and Sapphire Rapids. The projected embeddings achieve 0.85 ROC AUC for held-out image identification, compared with a 0.50 baseline. Exact-image top-five retrieval reaches 24% on CIFAR-100 and 56% on Unsafe-Diffusion. Across both processors, reconstructions average $1.4\times$ the baseline RGB color-palette overlap and $2.5\times$ the baseline structural similarity.
papers.authors: Debayan Sengupta, Darsh Asher, Kaushal Mhapsekar, Bita Aslrousta, Amna Hassan, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz

papers.title: Attributing Security Outcomes in LLM-Agent Evaluations: The Role of Content-Free State
papers.abstract: Security benchmarks for LLM agents record whether each attack succeeded and compare agents, attacks, and defenses by attack success rate (ASR). Such comparisons are valid only if the agent, the attack, and the defense cause each verdict. We show that verdicts also depend on content-free state: details of a run that carry no information about the system under test, such as the Python hash seed, the order of tools or evidence, and the scoring of failed runs. We require that this state influence no verdict (decision noninterference) and treat it as untrusted input, because evaluators and requesters of LLM-based gates can choose it. Our framework, TARE (Testing Attribution of Reported Effects), attributes a reported effect to the agent, attack, or defense only if it exceeds the measured influence of content-free state. On Agent Security Bench (ASB), runs with a fixed hash seed are identical for seven agents from four model families, yet changing the seed changes up to 17% of an agent's verdicts while the ASR moves by at most 5 points. The seed acts through the tool order: sorting the tool list instead of reverse-sorting it raises the ASR by up to 19 points, because ASB's naming convention places attacker tools first. When the same evidence is reordered, six of seven LLM judges change their decision on 17-91% of 98 proposed actions. Across eighteen agent-defense combinations, TARE's worst-case test attributes effects to two of three defenses, one of them in opposite directions on two agents, and a test fixed in advance confirms a 4.8-point decrease from the third; in the attributed decreases, 35-69% of the stopped attacks end without any tool call, which ASB counts as a failed attack. Reproducible verdicts are thus not necessarily attributable, and security evaluations of LLM agents should report the influence of content-free state. We release TARE, the ASB patch, and all verdict tables.
papers.authors: Abdelmonaim Bounite, Zangir Iklassov

papers.title: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling
papers.abstract: We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $α$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors. The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.
papers.authors: Raoof Zare Moayedi, Mohammad Hossein Yassaee, Javad B. Ebrahimi

papers.title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current
papers.abstract: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.
papers.authors: Tom Kimpson

papers.title: LODESTONE: Linking System Events to Threat Intelligence for Evidence-Grounded Cyber Attack Investigation
papers.abstract: System provenance graphs help reconstruct attacks through causal dependencies, but these connections alone do not explain how events accomplish an adversary's goal. Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) provides the necessary security knowledge, yet linking it to execution evidence requires bridging differences in meaning and granularity between events and attack relations amid scarce labels and sparse relevant evidence. We present LODESTONE, a cross-graph alignment system that links observed system events to CTI attack relations to support evidence-grounded attack reports. LODESTONE uses a novel CTI-driven training-data engine and an expert-verified benchmark of edge-level correspondences and reference attack reports. The engine pairs real CTI knowledge graphs with provenance graphs from isolated executions. A large language model (LLM) agent recursively improves correspondences by checking execution evidence and repairing retrieval, parsing, and reproduction failures; experts independently verify benchmark correspondences. LODESTONE combines text cross-encoder and directed-graph relevance scores to extract compact alert-centered subgraphs, retrieves article-level knowledge graphs through node- and edge-level dual-softmax assignment, and uses a fine-tuned 4B-parameter LLM to align event combinations with CTI attack steps. We evaluate LODESTONE on 27 expert-verified attack cases amid continuous benign activity from real applications, using 713 CTI articles. LLM judgments aligned with multiple human experts yield an attack-step description score of 82%, and attack identification reaches 91%, versus 73% and 32% using the same generator with provenance alone. Baseline pipelines and coding agents achieve description scores of at most 57%. Human-verified correspondences further demonstrate advantages in balancing attack-edge coverage with subgraph size, CTI retrieval, and cross-graph alignment.
papers.authors: Liangyi Huang, Zichen Liu, Fei Shao, Xusheng Xiao

papers.title: Unshardable Codes
papers.abstract: We propose a new coding-theoretic problem motivated by censorship resistance. Is it possible to intertwine many pieces of data by encoding them jointly in a way that makes it impossible to remove any single piece without destroying many others as well? In particular, we want to encode $k$ data components $(m_1,\ldots, m_k)$ into a codeword $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with the following properties: 1. Local recovery: every data component can be recovered (in the absence of erasures or errors) by reading at most $\ell$ correct codeword symbols. 2. Unshardability: if an adversary erases some arbitrary subset of the codeword symbols, the remaining codeword symbols either uniquely determine all $k$ data components, or there are at least $s$ data components that cannot be determined. We call such codes $(\ell, s)$-unshardable. Intuitively, such codes prevent an adversary from selectively censoring individual pieces of data by erasing codeword symbols, without destroying large amounts of other data as collateral damage. We show that codes whose generator matrix has certain superregularity properties are unshardable. Using this connection, we construct linear codes that are $(\ell, s)$-unshardable with $s = (1-\varepsilon)k$ and locality $\ell = O_\varepsilon(1)$. We also show that linear unshardable codes are subject to the lower bound $s \leq k - k/\ell + 1$. Finally, we consider a strengthening of local recovery to also require local decodability from some constant fraction of erasures or even errors. With the help of AI tools, we achieve the above notion by showing that any Locally Decodable Code (LDC) can be converted into one that is unshardable while preserving locality via a certain careful change of basis over an appropriate extension field.
papers.authors: Prashanth Amireddy, Yevgeniy Dodis, Rohan Goyal, Ethan Mook, Madhu Sudan, Daniel Wichs

papers.title: MobileGrail: Learning Compact Guardrails for On-Device deployable Mobile GUI Agent Safety
papers.abstract: Runtime guardrails protect mobile GUI agents by assessing each proposed action before execution, but existing guardrails rely on cloud hosted large multimodal models, exposing every screen to a remote server, including private information such as payments, messages, and medical records. We propose MobileGrail, an on-device deployable model that addresses both. It maintains a recurrent task state that retains only the evidence subsequent safety decisions depend on, so that authorization and execution progress persist beyond the short context. To intervene early while keeping the safety boundary precise, it learns two labels, unsafe and block: unsafe marks the action that commits a violation, whereas block may be issued at any step of an intervention window, which spans from the first action that the user's authorization no longer explains to the committing action itself. To support training, we build an environment of 32 applications whose backends verify the effect of every action, supplying verified labels for supervision and rewards for reinforcement learning to calibrate intervention timing. We also build MobileVeto, an offline benchmark of unsafe trajectories largely on held-out applications, each paired with a benign counterpart. On MobileVeto, MobileGrail built on Qwen3.5-2B intercepts 76.2% of violations, up from 64.5% for its prompted backbone, while reducing premature intervention from 58.6% to 5.2%, outperforming the cloud-based OS-Sentinel on both. We further conduct online evaluation on GhostEIBench, where MobileGrail guarding a Qwen3.8-27B agent reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while raising task completion from 48 to 58. Quantized to 4 bits, MobileGrail runs on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at a median latency of 4.7 s, comparable to the 5.1s of cloud-hosted Gemini 3.8 Flash.
papers.authors: Zhiyu Zhang, Yuankai Li, Muhao Chen

papers.title: FORGETMENOT: Auditing Memory Driven Privacy Risks in Commercial AI Agents
papers.abstract: Commercial AI agents increasingly incorporate long-term memory (both persistent and chat-history) to enable more accurate and personalized responses, raises significant privacy and policy concerns. Yet little is known about user privacy risks associated with memory behavior, in particular, about memory storage, disclosure, transparency and deletion control. To bridge this gap, we propose FORGETMENOT, an auditing framework for analyzing the privacy risks of long term memory in commercial AI agents. Using our framework, we collect around 3800 multi-turn sessions comprising around 6M tokens across five popular AI agents. Our results show that agents store a wide range of personal attributes, including demographics, health, and sensitive details. Furthermore, user visible memory reveals substantially less (around 20% on average) attributes than the agents store in practice, exposing a significant transparency gap. Our stealth memory injection (SMI) technique further increases the amount of personal and sensitive attribute stored in memory, raising it by 25% and 15% for Copilot and Claude, respectively. We further observed memory deletion control is unreliable, as all five agents exhibit non-zero post deletion leakage, including health and self-harm related attributes. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of memory disclosure to a 3rd-party email recipient as a proof-of-concept, as Gemini shows 31.9% leakage rate. Together, our findings reveal notable privacy risks in commercial agents memory. Finally, we discuss both design implications and regulatory recommendations to protect users memory privacy in commercial agents.
papers.authors: Ismat Jarin, Tu Le, Athina Markopoulou

papers.title: Relativising Integrity and Robustness: Prompt Injection and Partitioned Enclaves
papers.abstract: Relative security (RS) judges a system against a reference system, but has only been applied to confidentiality. We introduce relative integrity (RI), which states that every behaviour a system exhibits under an attacker's influence must be one the reference can exhibit for the same trusted inputs. RS and RI each choose their own reference runs, so together they accept attacks whose leak and effects the reference reproduces only in different runs. We therefore develop a further property, relative robustness (RR), which asks the same runs to reproduce both and is strictly stronger than RS and RI together. We give proof methods for RI and RR and a disproof method for RI, and apply them in two domains: (1) LLM agents under prompt injection, where the reference runs the same plan with a model that never obeys untrusted content, and (2) C programs partitioned across an SGX or TrustZone enclave boundary, where the reference keeps every function inside. We evaluate the properties on models of five published attacks, a support desk, an OP-TEE HOTP token and common agent defences. Two cases pass RS and RI but fail RR: an injection that makes the support desk's model accept any customer, as one input did in the Tensor Trust game, and the simulation step of the attack on Secret Network, in which an SGX enclave reveals a transfer's outcome without committing it. Our work is fully mechanised in Isabelle/HOL, with the enclave programs verified in C using AutoCorres2.
papers.authors: Brijesh Dongol

papers.title: NRSnooper: Enabling Real-Time Bidirectional Traffic Decoding in Commercial 5G NR Networks
papers.abstract: Decoding both uplink and downlink cellular traffic reveals lower-layer protocol behavior, unprotected signaling, and encrypted higher-layer packets beyond what scheduling metadata exposes. In commercial 5G NR networks, however, passive decoding must overcome UE-dedicated configurations hidden in encrypted signaling, unknown identifiers of ongoing connections, and the computational demands of wideband traffic. We present NRSnooper, a passive sniffer that decodes downlink control and bidirectional data traffic in real time, including traffic from already-connected UEs and traffic after encrypted configuration updates. NRSnooper learns reusable physical-layer configurations through an instrumented open-source UE that reproduces commercial UE capabilities. It recovers connection-specific identifiers from ongoing transmissions and selects matching configurations through CRC-validated data decoding. A hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline sustains continuous wideband processing. Evaluations on a controlled testbed and two commercial networks show that, compared with using only configurations from unencrypted signaling, NRSnooper decodes 1.3x and 6.3x as many control messages and 9.0x and 17.7x as many downlink data blocks, respectively. NRSnooper also decodes traffic from an already-connected UE during an ongoing phone call and achieves real-time bidirectional decoding on 100 MHz commercial NR channels.
papers.authors: Tuan Dinh Hoang, Quang Huy Pham, Taekkyung Oh, Hazem Issa, Marco Mezzavilla, Yongdae Kim

papers.title: HiPerfCC-StateReuse: Ciphertext Reuse for Fast Confidential GPU Data Movement
papers.abstract: Confidential GPUs offer near-native on-device compute performance, but transfers between CPU and GPU TEEs through untrusted host memory require bulk CPU encryption and decryption, even for unchanged data. Existing software techniques overlap or parallelize these operations but retain their per-byte CPU cost. Reusing exported ciphertext could avoid this work, but GPU TEE firmware enforces direction-specific encryption keys and fresh per-transfer initialization vectors (IVs), preventing direct reuse. We introduce ciphertext rebinding, a purely software primitive enabling repeated and cross-GPU ciphertext reuse on existing GPU TEEs without hardware changes, while preserving confidentiality, integrity, and freshness. Specifically, ciphertext rebinding exploits the separation between ciphertext-dependent and IV-dependent components in GPU TEE's AES-GCM authentication: a GPU-precomputed summary under the destination key can enable the CPU to update authentication tags without processing the payload. With this modification, GPU's subsequent read on the retained ciphertext can still proceed through the GPU's hardware-fixed copy-engine interfaces, which cannot be modified by software. An additional GPU correction step can then compensate for differences in the keys and IVs to recover the original plaintext. By retaining GPU-exported ciphertext in untrusted host memory, ciphertext rebinding avoids bulk CPU decryption and re-encryption, improving effective bandwidth for GPU-state restoration and sharing. We implement this primitive in HiPerfCC-StateReuse through only driver and library changes, combining batched submissions with pipelined GPU processing and copy-engine transfers. We evaluate transfer efficiency and CPU overhead through microbenchmarks, and application performance through three case studies: model switching, key-value cache offloading, and cross-instance cache sharing.
papers.authors: Haoxuan Xu, Shaoyu Wang, Minghao Lin, Beijie Liu, Potung Yu, Yongqin Wang, Vincent Quentin Ulitzsch, Seo Jin Park, Murali Annavaram, Mengyuan Li

papers.title: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority
papers.abstract: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.
papers.authors: Guijia Zhang, Huihao Jing, Bing Li, Shing-Chi Cheung, Harry Yang, Ziqi Zhang

papers.title: Ads for Agents: Measuring Ad-Serving MCP Servers
papers.abstract: AI agents call external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Some MCP servers return paid advertisements (ads) into the model's context. The model then decides whether these ads and their disclosures reach the user. We trace these ads from their sources to the agent's tool results across public MCP servers and packages. We find the servers through their public traces in ad networks, package registries, certificate logs, hostnames, MCP directories, and GitHub configurations. We then query the ad-serving servers with read-only requests and inspect their ad links. Ads appear on only 0.57% of 101,363 open MCP endpoints and 0.04% of 122,656 local MCP packages. Although 173 ad networks target agents, operators insert the ads themselves on about half of the 226 ad-returning servers. Nearly all ad-serving packages likewise carry the operator's own affiliate identifier. While ads adapt to the topic and intent of the query, their disclosure stays fixed within each tool. Only 9.3% of the ads carry an explicit sponsored label. Most ad links also hide their destinations. Since operators insert most ads themselves and label them inconsistently, we propose a per-item ad annotation in MCP results. Clients can show this annotation to the user independently of the model's answer.
papers.authors: Shahrooz Pouryousef, Sohini Chakraborty, Ali Montazer, Muoi Tran

papers.title: When Being Wrong Is Right: Reverse-Capability Audio CAPTCHAs through Psychoacoustic Design
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have recently been shown to bypass audio CAPTCHAs designed around limitations of automatic speech recognition. To address this threat, we introduce reverse-capability verification, a general CAPTCHA framework that reverses the conventional human-easy, machine-hard relationship with respect to the physical ground truth. It selects challenges in which stable human perceptual limitations cause the human-reference answer to differ from the physical ground truth, while machine analysis tends toward that truth. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation. We instantiate the framework through psychoacoustics and design two audio CAPTCHAs: HIPI, a classification task, and YINGCHEN, a counting task, together with their conjunctive composition. Across seven LALMs and eight attack strategies, the maximum observed machine acceptance rates are 19%, 17%, and 3% for HIPI, YINGCHEN, and their composition, respectively, compared with 45-100% for nine prior schemes. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.
papers.authors: Mingjie Bao, Yu Dai, Guangke Chen, Guozhu Meng

papers.title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. CRELT separates retrieval, conversation history, and attack strategy through a full-factorial design, uses a retrieval corpus verified to contain none of the target PII, and counts an item as leaked only when it is absent from the model input at the turn it is produced. In our main experiment, this criterion excludes 29-53% of raw matches that were already present in the input. Across GPT-J-6B, Pythia-6.9B, and Pythia-12B, targeting real Enron contact details, retrieval reduces disclosure under both full and cleared history, consistent with prior single-turn results. A length-matched control with random passages reproduces 91-99.5% of this reduction under cleared history and 47-78% under full history, so much of it comes from the added context rather than from what is retrieved. With retrieval enabled, however, retaining full conversation history increases disclosure by a factor of 3.6-4.9, while retaining only one previous turn already restores disclosure to approximately the full-history level. With retrieval, clearing the history reduces disclosure by 72-79%, but does not eliminate it. These results show that single-turn privacy audits can substantially underestimate training-data leakage in conversational RAG systems and that conversation-history policy is a critical dimension of privacy evaluation.
papers.authors: Syed Khaderi, Karima Makhlouf, Sami Zhioua

papers.title: HiPerfCC-KVCache: Accelerating Confidential LLM Serving with Hierarchical KV Caching
papers.abstract: Hierarchical key-value (KV) caching reduces repeated prefill computation in large language model serving by retaining reusable state beyond GPU memory. Under GPU confidential computing (CC), however, protected transfers can erase this benefit. We show that bulk KV copies hold driver locks during prolonged CPU-side processing, stalling independent serving operations despite separate threads and streams. Our characterization on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs shows how lock scope, copy granularity, and allocation ownership affect foreground progress and transfer parallelism. Guided by these findings, we present HiPerfCC-KVCache, which manages resource lifetimes, prioritizes ready token readback between bounded backup submissions, and parallelizes KV restores through auxiliary contexts with shared GPU staging. Implemented in SGLang, HiPerfCC-KVCache uses existing protected transfer interfaces without hardware or driver changes. Across three models and three workloads on H200, HiPerfCC-KVCache achieves a geometric-mean output-token throughput speedup of $1.74\times$ (up to $2.72\times$) over the staged KV-transfer HiCache-Workers baseline at the highest tested loads. Mean time to first token decreases by 36% on average and up to 59%. The benefits generalize to RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, with a geometric-mean throughput speedup of $1.28\times$ (up to $2.20\times$) over the same baseline. A capacity analysis further models and explains variation in gains and remaining gaps to CC-off serving.
papers.authors: Haoxuan Xu, Shaoyu Wang, Minghao Lin, Beijie Liu, Potung Yu, Yongqin Wang, Vincent Quentin Ulitzsch, Seo Jin Park, Murali Annavaram, Mengyuan Li

papers.title: Anti OS Fingerprinting, Revisited: A Loadable Kernel Module for FreeBSD and What Twenty-Five Years Changed
papers.abstract: In 2001 we published a paper on an Anti OS Detection (AoD) system: a modified FreeBSD 4.3 kernel that makes a host answer the probes of an OS fingerprinting tool as if it ran another operating system. This report revisits that work on FreeBSD 15.1. We do not claim a new method. We report three things. First, the same goal is now reachable from a loadable module of about 800 lines that uses the packet filter hook interface and sets one kernel variable, without changing the kernel source. Second, the module covers both active and passive fingerprinting: Nmap 7.98 reports an exact match for Linux and for Windows 10/11, and p0f 3 reports the same systems from the connections the host opens. Third, an exact match in Nmap was not enough: a passive tool, plain FIN scans and a comparison with real hosts each exposed a mismatch that the previous step could not see. A real Windows 11 host and the final Windows personality get the same verdict from Nmap and the same signatures from p0f and JA4T; a real Linux 7.0 host is not an exact match in Nmap at all, while the personality built from Nmap's database is. We describe those mismatches, how we removed them, what the module costs, and what it still cannot hide.
papers.authors: Daisuke Miyamoto

papers.title: APUF-SNG: A Low-Cost Arbiter-PUF Stochastic Number Generator with Tunable Output Probability
papers.abstract: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes numerical values as probabilistic bit-streams and enables arithmetic operations using simple logic gates, offering a promising paradigm for low- cost, fault-tolerant, and highly parallel computation. However, the accuracy and efficiency of SC systems depend on the quality of the stochastic number generator (SNG). Conventional SNGs rely on pseudo-random or quasi-random generators, whose deterministic nature introduces periodicity, correlation, and bias, limiting achievable accuracy and robustness. This paper proposes a low- cost arbiter physical unclonable function (APUF)-based SNG that operates in near-metastable delay conditions to generate true- random stochastic bit-streams with controllable output probabilities. By selecting input challenges that drive the path delay difference toward a target value, the resulting output probability is governed by intrinsic device noise, eliminating the need for conventional random-number generators and comparator-based SNGs. The proposed design inherits the low hardware overhead and statistical independence properties of the APUF structure. A probabilistic model and a challenge selection method are developed to characterize and control the stochastic behavior. An 8-stage APUF-SNG matches the 1% mean absolute error of state- of-the-art true-random SNGs at 1024-bit streams and occupies 116μm^2 in 45nm, 2.5x and 7x smaller than the TRNG-based and Sobol-based generator designs, respectively.
papers.authors: Shelby Williams, Mehran Moghadam, M. Hassan Najafi, Sercan Aygun, Arman Roohi, Gourav Datta

papers.title: A Model Obfuscation and Controllable Authorization Scheme for Deep Learning as a Service
papers.abstract: Developing deep learning models requires substantial computational and data resources, making them core intellectual assets for enterprises. As Deep Learning as a Service (DLaaS) increasingly extends to edge computing environments, models deployed on third-party devices face growing threats from reverse engineering. Existing model protection methods often depend on specialized hardware or incur substantial computational overhead, while lacking effective mechanisms for controlling model usage. There is therefore a need for lightweight solutions that combine model protection with controllable authorization. To address this challenge, we propose KeyObf, a model obfuscation and controllable authorization scheme for DLaaS. KeyObf efficiently protects model parameters and architecture through model obfuscation while binding parameter recovery to user keys, ensuring that only authorized users can perform inference correctly. By integrating a key-based mechanism into the obfuscation framework, KeyObf unifies model protection and controllable authorization. Experimental results demonstrate that KeyObf preserves the inference accuracy of authorized users, rejects inference requests when credential authentication fails, and increases the difficulty of recovering model information under the evaluated reverse-engineering conditions. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a lightweight approach to model protection and controllable authorization in third-party deployment scenarios.
papers.authors: Nianyun Song, Haodi Wang, Yu Guo, Xiaohua Jia

papers.title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
papers.abstract: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.
papers.authors: Andrew Lowy

papers.title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications
papers.abstract: Agentic coding tools turn a specification into a running web application, so their defaults for authentication, sessions, input validation, and dependencies become its security posture. This study asks whether appending a fixed block of OWASP-aligned security requirements to the prompt changes what such tools produce, by how much, and with what side effects. Each of 100 frozen specifications was realized four times: two agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) crossed with two prompts sharing a byte-identical functional core, without (A) and with (B) the security block. A fixed static and dynamic pipeline scanned the 400 applications, yielding 6,721 triaged findings, analyzed with count and logistic mixed models and with a dependency diff. The block cut findings per application by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally through both tools, and roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B applications carried more high-severity dependency advisories. Adjusted for that surface the advisory rate did not rise (flat per application, 18% lower in aggregate), while high-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Security-focused prompting is therefore an inexpensive and portable improvement, but it enlarges the dependency surface that has to be audited against it, an effect of library selection rather than of the security requirements themselves.
papers.authors: Darko Andročec

papers.title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
papers.abstract: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.
papers.authors: Ethan Rathbun, Jonathan Nöther, Christopher Amato, Alina Oprea, Goran Radanović

papers.title: Enabling Verifiable Output Lineage for Virtualized ML Workload Execution
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) property attestation lets a model provider demonstrate properties of their models and datasets to verifiers, and trusted execution environments (TEEs) have emerged as its most practical mechanism. However, existing TEE-based systems attest only a static snapshot of the TEE's initial configuration, leaving run-time behavior unauditable. Proof of execution (PoX) architectures close this gap by requiring the prover's root of trust to also demonstrate that (1) the attested operation actually executed and (2) the claimed outputs were affected only by that operation. Existing PoX designs, though, target microcontrollers and rely on hardware features unavailable in server-grade TEEs, so they cannot be applied directly to ML workloads. We present EVOLVE, a software-based PoX framework for server-grade TEEs. EVOLVE mediates an operation's writes and control flow to track whether a requested ML operation executes without violation. It binds the execution status to measurements of the operation's inputs and outputs, enabling verifiers to assess run-time behavior through ML property attestation. We implement EVOLVE on Intel TDX as a Rust module within its virtual firmware, with policy checks built on primitives formally verified in F*. Our evaluation shows that EVOLVE is versatile across diverse ML applications on unmodified hardware, provides formal guarantees for its policy checks. EVOLVE incurs per-request run-time overhead on average ranging from 1.07$\times$ (for decision trees) to 2.13$\times$ (for multi-layer perceptrons).
papers.authors: Prach Chantasantitam, Adam Caulfield, Sujaya Maiyya, N. Asokan

papers.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
papers.abstract: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.
papers.authors: Ivan Brugere, Junqi Jiang, Saumitra Mishra, Sumitra Ganesh

papers.title: SecretSifter: A Runtime Secret-Detection Engine for Live Web Traffic
papers.abstract: Credentials embedded in client-delivered web artifacts, such as minified JavaScript bundles, webpack chunks, server-side-rendered state objects, and JSON or XML API responses, form a runtime attack surface that repository-time (shift-left) secret scanners do not observe, because the credential enters the served artifact at build time or at runtime, after every source-code gate has passed. This paper presents SecretSifter, an open-source runtime secret-detection engine that inspects live web traffic and reports secret-grade credentials at the point they are delivered to the browser. The engine combines format-anchored and context-gated detection rules, semantic key-name extraction, Shannon-entropy scoring, and dedicated detection of hardcoded CryptoJS/AES material across the full served surface. SecretSifter ships as three editions over one shared detection core: a Burp Suite extension, a Chrome extension, and a standalone Windows and macOS desktop application, with a Bearer-authenticated REST and MCP interface for automation. On a 198-value benchmark of real production client-exposed values (GT-198), the deterministic detection stage reached 79.8% recall at 86.8% precision in default configuration, the highest F1 of any system evaluated. The detection core is released under an open-source (MIT) license, and a de-identified reproducibility bundle and a public synthetic demo target are provided.
papers.authors: Hemanth Gorijala

papers.title: STEGOGUARD-LM: Evaluating End-to-End Protection Against LLM Covert Channels
papers.abstract: A defense that disrupts hidden messages may still provide little protection if its detector rarely triggers an intervention. We present StegoGuard-LM, a controlled framework for evaluating defenses against covert messages in large language model outputs. We examine token-rank and synonym channels, with Unicode concealment as a structural control, and track messages through detection, intervention, and recovery. Deterministic rewriting prevented full recovery of 103 of 104 synonym-encoded messages when applied unconditionally, but only one when intervention depended on a detector set to limit false alarms. In a four-round replay on a 48-response subset, an attacker selecting from a fixed catalog recovered more bits by switching channels, although paired gains were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Randomized rewriting showed no sustained advantage in this pilot. A more sensitive detector improved protection but modified about one-third of clean responses. These findings show how uneven detection can undermine effective rewriting and why protection must be evaluated alongside attacker adaptation and intervention on legitimate text.
papers.authors: Martha Dimgba, George Williams

papers.title: POMA: Beyond Final Flags -- Process-Level Evaluation of Base LLMs in Vulnerability Exploitation
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from text generation to autonomous software-engineering execution, automated vulnerability exploitability verification has emerged as a vital frontier in software quality assurance and security validation. Existing security benchmarks, however, largely judge models by binary pass/fail outcomes or coarse stage milestones. Such outcome-centric scoring obscures fine-grained failure dynamics across long-horizon execution and conflates the intrinsic capability of a base LLM with external agent scaffolding. We present POMA (Pwn-Oriented Model Assessment), a process-level evaluation methodology and platform that isolates base LLMs under a unified execution baseline -- fixing task inputs, tool interfaces, target environments, feedback formats, and execution budgets -- while measuring intermediate states and transitions from runtime evidence. Evaluating four frontier base LLMs across 55 CTF Pwn challenges and 10 real-world vulnerability reproduction tasks exposes persistent capability attrition along the exploitation chain: from vulnerability knowledge to executable implementation, from client-side actions to verified target states, from failure localization to precise repair, and across iterative revisions. In real-world software, models further struggle to satisfy format, semantic, differential, and crash-identity constraints simultaneously. By pinpointing where execution chains break down, POMA provides an empirical foundation for trustworthy capability assessment and principled vulnerability-agent design. Our benchmark catalogs, process-measurement evaluator, and sample harness are publicly available at https://github.com/maple-pwn/poma-release .
papers.authors: Gufeng Zhang, Yiru Zhao, Shengyu Liu, Weichen Yan, Xingwang Xiang, Yiran Ma, Benxiao Tang, Lei Zhao, Jinxin Ma

papers.title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution
papers.abstract: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.
papers.authors: Zehao Liu, Huashuo Lei, Xi Lin, Haoang Li, Yuliang Chen, Huarui Zhang, Yifan Wang

papers.title: Conartist: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Computer-Using Agents against Multi-Step Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.
papers.authors: Jiaqi Rong, Yunchen Lu, Lihai Nie, Yan Jia, Tong Li, Zheli Liu

papers.title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.
papers.authors: Leizhen Zhang, Sheng Chen

papers.title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.
papers.authors: Ailin Barzegar, Khalil El-Khatib, Li Yang

papers.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
papers.abstract: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
papers.authors: Peter Horvath, Ilia Shumailov, Zhuoran Liu, Lukasz Chmielewski, Lejla Batina

papers.title: CyberDualEval: Measuring Dual-Use Cyber Risks in Frontier Language Models
papers.abstract: While frontier language models are becoming capable cybersecurity assistants, they also create a dual-use cyber risk: the same capabilities that help defenders identify and analyze vulnerabilities can similarly help attackers weaponize them. Existing cyber benchmarks measure either raw offensive capability or generic refusal behavior, overlooking the dual-use cyber assessment of preserving benign security utility while refusing assistance that materially advances misuse. We introduce CyberDualEval, a benchmark with 430 vulnerable tasks for measuring dual-use cyber risk in frontier language models. Each task is decomposed into three phases of increasing operationalization: security analysis, proof-of-concept generation, and exploit generation. To quantify the residual cyber risk, we annotate each task with a Task Weaponization Score that measures how much work remains to turn the resulting artifact into unauthorized cyber misuse. CyberDualEval assesses ten closed- and open-weight language models both on correct compliance and on task performance, developing four deterministic mechanisms for determining per-phase success on a large subset of the dataset. Our evaluation reveals that none of the existing frontier models effectively navigate helping with safe requests and refusing risky ones, characterized by being overly-cautious. On the other hand, recent open-weight models rarely refuse and demonstrate strong validated accuracy on risky requests.
papers.authors: Magnus Saebo, Francesco Piccoli, Maxwell Watson, Pranjali Thakur, Yangruibo Ding, Zhuo Zhang

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Classifiers for Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection Using Feature Reduction
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems can improve IoT security, but high-dimensional traffic features and imbalanced datasets may reduce model reliability and deployment feasibility in resource-constrained environments. This study presents a lightweight binary IoT intrusion detection framework using an approximately balanced CICIoT2023 derived dataset, feature reduction, and comparative machine learning evaluation. The original multi-class attack labels were converted into two classes: Benign and Malicious. To reduce class bias, malicious traffic was randomly undersampled to obtain an approximately balanced binary dataset. Information Gain Ratio and Gini Decrease were then used to rank traffic features and generate reduced feature subsets of 38, 30, 20, 10, 5, and 3 features. Five machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest(RF), Decision Tree(DT), Naive Bayes(NB), Logistic Regression(LR), and Support Vector Machine(SVM), were evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. The results show that Random Forest achieved the strongest overall performance. In particular,the 20-feature subset achieved accuracy of 99.1% and MCC of 0.982, matching the full-feature model while reducing feature dimensionality by approximately 47.4%. The 10-feature subset also maintained strong performance with accuracy of 98.9% and MCC of 0.979, reducing the feature space by approximately 73.7%. These findings demonstrate that balanced binary classification and progressive feature reduction can preserve detection effectiveness while improving lightweight IDS feasibility.
papers.authors: Shaker Nawasra

papers.title: Mitigating Nested GTP Attacks: A Closed-Loop eBPF Defense for 5G and Beyond Networks
papers.abstract: The evolving cellular networks continue to rely on the legacy GPRS Tunneling Protocol-User Plane (GTP-U) to encapsulate and route user data traffic across the data plane. Recent security research demonstrated that nested GTP-U (GTP-in-GTP) payload vulnerabilities enable a diverse range of attacks on victim users. To address this vulnerability, in this paper, we propose a closed-loop extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and eXpress Data Path (XDP) defense to detect and mitigate nested GTP-U attacks in 5G and beyond networks. The proposed framework contains three components: an in-kernel XDP Detection and Drop Module (XDP-DDM), a user-space User-Plane Telemetry Agent (UP-TA), and a multi-threaded Control-Plane Mitigation Orchestrator (CP-MO). We implement and evaluate the proposed defense on a sliced 5G testbed integrating Free5GC, UERANSIM, and Containerlab. Experimental results indicate that the XDP-DDM detects and drops malicious nested GTP-U packets at line rate, while the UP-TA and CP-MO asynchronously report and revoke the attacker's network access, respectively. Under a 10,000 packets-per-second cross-slice nested GTP-U flood, the proposed solution preserves the baseline performance of the victim slices while introducing minimal overhead. We also show that the proposed solution has minimal impact on the user's throughput and round-trip time.
papers.authors: AbdulAziz AbdulGhaffar, Ashraf Matrawy

papers.title: Operational Assurance for LLM-Based Systems under Governance Opacity
papers.abstract: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. The framework incorporates mechanisms to move from general, CVSS-inspired severity metrics toward contextualized operational risk assessments that take into account user profiles, industrial domains, and organizational knowledge. In addition, the proposal strengthens practical auditability through digitally signed explainability reports (signed XAI reports), designed to support verifiable traceability, continuous monitoring, and operational accountability in LLM-based sociotechnical systems.
papers.authors: Pedro Pinacho-Davidson

papers.title: More Is Never Less: Affordable Robustness to Additive Attacks via Monotone Multiple-Instance Learning
papers.abstract: Static malware detectors that represent each sample as a bag of extracted features, such as permissions, API calls, or imported functions, are cheap to deploy and remain state-of-the-art under temporal drift and in selective classification. Yet, attackers can evade them by adding benign-looking content that outweighs malicious evidence. Canonically, detectors encode the presence of a few thousand features, selected during training, as sparse multi-hot vectors over a fixed vocabulary. Features that emerge after training remain invisible. We show that linear models and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) over this input are sum-pooled set models in disguise. Sum-pooling lets added benign features cancel malicious evidence. Instead, we cast malware detection with set-shaped static features as a multiple-instance learning (MIL) problem. To this end, we propose MalSets, which uses max-pooled Deep Sets models with a monotone head to ensure that any malicious evidence remains undiluted; thus, more is never less. Under MIL, a general text encoder maps any feature string to an embedding, thus eliminating the long-standing out-of-vocabulary problem at test time. Max-pooling retains the malicious evidence regardless of how many benign features an attacker adds. Since max-pooling can only grow when features are added, constraining the head alone makes the malware score monotone under additions, even against a white-box attacker adapted to this architecture. While monotone detectors are never evaded by state-of-the-art black-box or white-box attacks, they often significantly pay for this robustness in clean performance since benign features cannot count as evidence. However, by combining a non-monotone set encoder with max-pooling and a monotone head, MalSets maintains the robustness of prior monotone classifiers while achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.authors: Alexander Herzog, Shae McFadden, Lorenzo Cavallaro

papers.title: SoK: Splitting the Trigger or Adding Attackers? Disentangling Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Distributed backdoor attacks split a trigger among several federated learning clients, so that the backdoor appears only in the aggregated model. Since DBA, a line of work has reported that such attacks are stronger, more persistent, and stealthier than a single attacker with the full trigger. We systematize this literature and test this belief. We code nineteen primary studies and fifteen papers that evaluate against DBA. The reported advantage is rarely measured against a complete trigger delivered by the same attackers, and none of the fifteen evaluations tests whether individual pieces remain effective. We then run 875 paired federated runs that separate adding attackers from splitting the trigger. In our image experiments, adding attackers raised attack success in every seed of all 30 cells where we measured it, by 7.5 to 83.4 percentage points on average. Splitting the trigger among the same attackers had a smaller effect, and its sign depended on the piece layout, the allocation, and the attackers' local training. With DBA's compact layout, splitting lowered attack success on CIFAR-10. A larger penalty on small CNNs vanished once the attackers trained longer, and an FCBA-style allocation gained a few points. Widely separated pieces helped on CIFAR-10, its grayscale version, and GTSRB. No model required all pieces. Neural Cleanse suppressed single pieces together with the full trigger, but split backdoors with separated pieces survived it better than complete ones. We derive reporting requirements for attack and defense evaluations.
papers.authors: Zhuotao Lian, Qingkui Zeng, Weiyu Wang

papers.title: Targeted In-Context Poisoning of Tabular Foundation Models: An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict the label of a query row conditioned on a context of labelled rows, without training on them. Drawn from operational data, the context becomes an attack surface. We study targeted in-context poisoning in its simplest form: an attacker with write access to the context's source places exact copies of a target row there with the wrong label. On 30 OpenML datasets for binary classification, one such poison row flips on average 53% (TabICL) and 65% (TabPFN) of the predictions correct without attack, and three poison rows flip almost all. The same copy with the true label flips almost none, and performance on the remaining rows hardly changes. Predictions flip by two routes: in TabICL, the target row's embedding rotates towards the mean of the wrong class; in TabPFN, the poison row pulls genuine rows of the wrong class along. The TFMs thus infer soundly, but from forged evidence. Predictions of trained models flip as well: almost always for a random forest, for CatBoost as often as for the TFMs, hardly for a logistic regression. New with TFMs is not the kind of vulnerability but the timing: the data take effect at the moment of prediction, not through training, and a poison row in a live context can be deleted afterwards. Three established requirements must therefore cover the context: access control for its source, traceability per prediction, which can also deter, and validation at prediction time. A detection mechanism shows how such validation can work.
papers.authors: Adem Alparslan

papers.title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.
papers.authors: Mehrdad Khodapanahandeh, Selin Unal, Berkay Kemal Balioglu, Alireza Khodaie, Beren Semiz, M. Emre Gursoy

papers.title: Cross-Boundary Vulnerability Management for SDVs: A Traceability Architecture at the ISO/SAE 21434 and EU Cyber Resilience Act Interface
papers.abstract: A software-defined vehicle depends on products that sit under different EU regimes. The type-approved vehicle and the systems, components and separate technical units made for it fall under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, which makes UN R155 mandatory; Regulation (EU) 2018/858 does so for R156; and ISO/SAE 21434 supports the management system R155 requires. Chargers, companion apps, aftermarket devices and many backends may fall under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) instead, whose reporting duty in Article 14 has applied since 11 September 2026. Neither side defines how a vulnerability found on one reaches the other's risk process. We contribute a four-question classification procedure, a five-regime traceability matrix, a reference architecture with four handoff paths and three boundary findings. On 75 classified products from a frozen public-source corpus, the procedure yields 47 Periphery, 11 Core, 1 Other and 16 Boundary products, three of them outside both the CRA and compulsory R155. Because UN R10 lets an electronic sub-assembly be approved as a component, the texts leave a second reading open, and we report both counts. Under it, 22 aftermarket devices become components, Periphery falls to 25 and 25 products sit outside both regimes. Seven retrospective walkthroughs suggest that, for third-party products, vulnerability information stops in the vehicle manufacturer's own inventory, triggers or exploitation assessment, and that no provision obliges a product maker to tell a vehicle manufacturer: the only defined two-way route is a contract. No reviewed source establishes a case that reached an Article 14 clock.
papers.authors: Krishna Teja Medam

papers.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.
papers.authors: Pascal Joos, Michael Pradel

papers.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
papers.authors: Honghao Feng, Shanhan Qu, Kai Tong, Shuquan Man, Huiping Zhuang

papers.title: Persistent Jailbreak Backdoor Attack
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) to produce helpful and harmless responses. However, an attacker can plant a jailbreak backdoor in an LLM such that adding a universal trigger word or phrase to a harmful prompt elicits attacker-desired responses.
