Existing jailbreak backdoor attacks induce distinct behaviors on backdoored inputs and safety samples (harmful prompts paired with refusal responses), making the backdoors susceptible to subsequent safety alignment and advanced defenses. In this paper, we propose a persistent jailbreak backdoor attack that reduces the divergence between clean and trigger-conditioned continuations during LLM decoding, making backdoored samples difficult to distinguish from safety samples. We also introduce a deferred-response mechanism that postpones harmful generations, further disguising the backdoor behavior. We evaluate our attack, PJBack, on eight LLMs from five model families, ranging from 7B to 70B parameters. PJBack achieves an average attack success rate of 93.9% and bypasses all seven evaluated defenses while preserving benign utility. In contrast, five existing backdoor attacks either achieve limited attack success or fail to withstand the evaluated defenses.
papers.authors: Haichuan Zhang, Xinyu Sun, Shih-Chieh Dai, Zhiyuan Zhong, Guanhong Tao

papers.title: Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Hidden AI-Directed Text on GitHub
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now triage issues, review pull requests and pick up tasks inside GitHub repositories, and to do so they read text that anyone with a GitHub account can write. This makes GitHub a prime surface for indirect prompt injection, in which instructions embedded in untrusted content steer a model that later processes it. Prior work has demonstrated such attacks against agents on GitHub in controlled settings, but how often they occur in practice, who deploys them, and for what purpose remain unknown. We present the first large-scale empirical study of AI-directed hidden text on GitHub. We analyzed roughly 145 million issues, pull requests, comments and README files, detected text that GitHub does not render to a human reader but that an agent receives in full, and filtered it with a two-stage LLM classification, a template provenance check and an exhaustive manual review. We identify 2,281 validated findings in issues, pull requests and comments (16 per million items), and AI-directed hidden text in the READMEs of 107 repositories. We find a heterogeneous ecosystem of four uses: attacks on other parties' agents, defensive text that restricts agents, content override that steers what they write, and first-party orchestration, in which projects coordinate their own agents through hidden markers. Attacks are rare (about one in 3.3 million items) but aimed at maintainers' own triage, review and CI agents. Orchestration accounts for two thirds of the findings in issues, pull requests and comments, grew fivefold in four months, and forms a control channel that anyone who can comment can imitate. Replayed offline against five models we tested, the attacks succeed against one small, fast model in 19% of cases, and against none once HTML comments are stripped. We release our detection tool and every finding.
papers.authors: Gabi Nakibly, Zvika Babo

papers.title: Development of an Effective Federated Learning-Based Defense System Against Phishing Attacks on Mobile Platforms
papers.abstract: Phishing remains one of the most pervasive and damaging cyber threats, exploiting both technical flaws and human behavior to compromise sensitive data. We present a privacy-preserving, real-time defense that analyzes full webpage source code on mobile platforms. Our system combines a lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for end-to-end feature extraction with a Federated Learning (FL) framework that updates models collaboratively on user devices without transferring raw data-supporting regulatory compliance and personalization. Evaluated on a large and diverse dataset, the model attains 86.02\% accuracy, 90.35\% precision, 80.64\% recall, and 92.78\% ROC-AUC. While some centralized, classical approaches may report higher accuracy, our design emphasizes a practical balance among accuracy, user privacy, and real-time performance on resource-constrained devices. We further demonstrate an end-to-end integration within the open-source Lightning Android browser, achieving real-time detection with low computational overhead. This work shows that privacy-first, AI-driven phishing detection is both feasible and scalable across mobile and IoT settings, delivering robust protection while keeping user data on-device.
papers.authors: Eren Dogan, Busra Buyuktanir, Gozde Karatas Baydogmus, Kazim Yildiz

papers.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.
papers.authors: Haichuan Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhong, Shih-Chieh Dai, Xinyu Sun, Guanhong Tao

papers.title: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Agent skills are reusable packages that extend a large language model (LLM) agent with scripts, third-party dependencies, and natural-language instructions. An agent builds a skill's arguments from user requests and untrusted external content, so a flaw left by a benign author can escalate a prompt injection to code execution. Existing studies target malicious skills or a single attack vector, and none tests whether an agent can reach such flaws. We present the first registry-scale empirical study of the supply chain attack surface arising from unintentional vulnerabilities in agent skills, over all 48,682 skills in ClawHub. The study covers two carried-over risks, dependencies and first-party code, and two agent-native ones, install instructions and credentials printed to stdout. We screen all skills by static analysis, manually review all 3,428 cases flagged by the four main detectors, and test reachability by running sampled flagged skills in a sandbox and with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection. First, dependency risk carries over in a different form: 49.6% of the skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE, and unlike npm packages, which mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% of them are born vulnerable, already exposed at publication. Second, few of these CVEs are reachable: agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of the affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. Third, a live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of the sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs, and the payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Hence, registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell.
papers.authors: Kaixuan Li, Wenbo Guo, Sen Chen, Yang Liu

papers.title: Pretzel: Compact Lattice Signatures from Module-LWE and Module-SIS
papers.abstract: We present Pretzel, a lattice-based signature scheme in the style of ML-DSA. Across parameter sets targeting NIST security categories 2, 3, and 5, its signatures are 52-59% smaller than ML-DSA's, it signs and verifies faster in all three categories, and its quantum security proof needs fewer assumptions. Across all three parameter sets, Pretzel produces smaller signatures than SHUTTLE (Ming et al., ASIACRYPT 2026), the recent state of the art for iterative rejection sampling from Module-LWE. At category 3, for example, Pretzel's 1361-byte signatures are 14% smaller than SHUTTLE's 1589 bytes. Unlike the quantum analyses of ML-DSA and SHUTTLE, Pretzel's security proof in the quantum random oracle model needs no self-target assumption: it relies only on Module-LWE and Module-SIS. Like SHUTTLE, Pretzel builds on Gartner's iterative rejection sampling (CRYPTO 2025). Its sampler keeps the response exactly on its target distribution after every update, which allows a substantially narrower mask than SHUTTLE's. Its verifier also enforces an additional bound on the response coefficients. This bound lets the security proof adapt Poremba's LWE-phase technique (ITCS 2023) to Module-LWE and rely on Module-LWE and Module-SIS alone.
papers.authors: Alberto Centelles Hidalgo, Justin Thaler, Markos Georghiades

papers.title: LatPRE: Compact Lattice-Based Proxy Re-Encryption with Security against Honest Re-Encryption Attacks
papers.abstract: Proxy re-encryption (PRE) allows a proxy to transform ciphertexts for other recipients without learning their plaintexts. It is a versatile cryptographic tool enabling a wide range of real-world applications, e.g., email forwarding, file sharing, and digital identity management. For these applications, security against honest re-encryption attacks (HRA) is essential: decrypting re-encryptions of some ciphertexts originally under a public key should not help break other ciphertexts under the same key. However, existing lattice-based approaches incur substantial ciphertext overhead or impose restrictions such as private proxy state or encryption requiring receiver's secret key. In this work, we present LatPRE, a compact single-hop HRA-secure PRE scheme based on the standard module learning with errors (MLWE) assumption. To this end, we make two technical contributions: (i) a novel generic framework for HRA-secure PRE based on a new hint-CPA security notion and hint-assisted re-encryption simulation; and (ii) tighter spectral bounds for honestly sampled leakage matrices in Matrix Hint-MLWE, whose hardness follows from standard MLWE under suitable parameters. Our results substantially reduce the required Gaussian masking widths, thereby enabling a compact lattice instantiation. We believe both contributions to be of independent interest. Finally, we implement LatPRE in C and evaluate parameter sets targeting 128-bit security and supporting up to 2^40 source encryptions and 2^20 outgoing rekeys per key. For 256-bit messages, re-encrypted ciphertexts occupy only 1.8-2.8 KB, and re-encryption takes about 0.2-0.3 ms on a standard PC. Compared with the state of the art, LatPRE achieves around 23-37 times smaller re-encrypted ciphertexts and 7-9 times faster re-encryption. To demonstrate its practicality, we also integrate LatPRE with Proton Mail's open-source framework to build a hybrid post-quantum encrypted email-forwarding prototype.
papers.authors: Hongxiao Wang, Mengting Yao, Ron Steinfeld, Muhammed F. Esgin, Amin Sakzad, Jian Weng

papers.title: A Two-Party Threshold Signature Scheme for Aigis-sig
papers.abstract: Aigis-sig uses Fiat--Shamir with aborts. Its rejection step depends on the full response, which complicates threshold signing. We present ThAigis-2P, a two-party threshold signature scheme whose outputs are accepted by the unmodified Aigis-sig verifier. The parties sample their secret shares independently from the Aigis-sig key distribution, subject to a spectral screening condition. Each party samples masks from a scaled hyperball and performs rejection sampling locally. The protocol runs K candidates per attempt. The spectral screening condition bounds the secret shift for every challenge and contributes approximately one bit of conditioning loss to the security reduction. The protocol has a three-round interactive mode and a preprocessing mode that exchanges commitments offline and requires one online round trip per attempt using committed salts and single-use records. In the random oracle model, the security analysis relates unforgeability to AMLWE under the Aigis-sig key distribution, MLWE under hyperball distributions, and the unforgeability of native Aigis-sig. The preprocessing mode also assumes a rollback-resistant state service. Experiments with a single-process C reference implementation based on PQMagic yield success probabilities of 0.22--0.25 per candidate and above 0.92 per attempt with K = 10. All 39,000 generated threshold signatures pass Aigis-sig verification. Canonical lossless encoding reduces partial response sizes by 21/%--25/% relative to transmitting raw coefficients. The evaluation covers all three Aigis-sig parameter sets and measures computation in a single-process prototype.
papers.authors: Li Wang, Tihong Qin

papers.title: How to Hash and Commit Real Values with Dynamic Precision
papers.abstract: When hashing or committing real values (represented by floating-point numbers), traditional cryptographic hash functions and commitment schemes have to first convert the real values to integers or finite ring elements. Such solutions suffer from several drawbacks. The schemes do not support dynamic choices of precisions. More generally, hashing or committing algorithms lose the efficiency and flexibility of directly working on real numbers. In this paper, we define and construct cryptographic hash functions and commitment schemes with dynamic precision choices and native real number arithmetic. Our main contributions are: 1. Providing the definitions of the real value collision resistant hash function (RVCRH) and commitment for real numbers, formalizing the notions of dynamic precision choices in the hashing, committing, and opening algorithms. 2. Defining the continuous analogs of the Short Integer Solution Problem (CSIS) and proving their hardness based on the worst-case hardness of lattice problems. We then construct RVCRHs and compressing commitment schemes with dynamic precision and native real arithmetic from CSIS problems. 3. Constructing a statistically binding additively homomorphic commitment scheme that supports real number arithmetic from the Continuous Learning With Errors Problem (CLWE). As an application, we provide a Sigma protocol for proving the knowledge of real numbers from CLWE. We also show that additively homomorphic commitment schemes for real values are unlikely to be compressing by showing a partial impossibility result for achieving such schemes.
papers.authors: Binyi Chen, Yilei Chen, Zhenghao Guan, Wenjie Li

papers.title: Post-Quantum Self-Updatable Pseudonyms for Conditional Privacy-Preserving Authentication in VANETs From Lattice-Based Credentials
papers.abstract: Authentication in vehicular networks must hide the sender and still allow an authority to identify it when needed. Schemes in which a vehicle derives its own pseudonyms avoid authority contact after registration, but known constructions rest on assumptions that quantum computers break. We present L-SUPA, a lattice-based scheme of this kind. The credential contains a binary key, and the pseudonym of an epoch is a vector of rounded inner products of that key with public pseudo-random vectors; because the rounding is an exact integer relation, the statement that a pseudonym is the rounding of the signed key fits, together with possession of a credential, inside the presentation proof of a practical lattice anonymous-credential system. Messages are signed with a fresh FN-DSA-512 key bound to the pseudonym, and a tracing authority separate from the issuer identifies a sender by scanning stored keys. The relation raises the presentation proof from $79.6$ to $81.4$ KiB and its verification time by about $3\%$; on one desktop core a presentation verifies in $0.15$ s, the time of about $4500$ message-signature verifications, and a message signature verifies in $0.033$ ms. A presentation adds $0.32\%$ to the message bytes of a one-hour epoch at $10$ Hz for $722$-byte messages, the most favorable rate, and messages of one vehicle are linkable within an epoch. The analysis states, goal by goal, whether we have a reduction, a conditional reduction, or a sketch; under the generic hybrid the presentation-layer M-LWE and LWR terms leave margins of about $80$ and $176$ bits for $2^{30}$ vehicles over ten years (no claim of $128$-bit anonymity).
papers.authors: Rui Xiao, Xiaoying Jia

papers.title: CycloSPDZ: Efficient MPC over 2-Power Cyclotomic Rings mod \(2^k\) for Dishonest Majority
papers.abstract: Most multi-party computation (MPC) protocols support arithmetic over finite fields or integer rings. Polynomial arithmetic in applications such as convolution evaluation and distributed key generation motivates extending these protocols to the 2-power cyclotomic rings $R_k=\mathbb{Z}_{2^k}[X]/(X^N+1)$, where $N$ is a power of two. However, no native protocol is known for actively secure computation over these rings with a dishonest majority. In this work, we present an information-theoretic MAC that is homomorphic over $R_k$ and requires only a small increase in coefficient bit length. We apply this to construct CycloSPDZ, an actively secure MPC protocol for a dishonest majority in the preprocessing model that has efficiency comparable to the state-of-the-art field-based convolution protocols in Convolutions in Overdrive (PoPETs 2023). We also construct an efficient preprocessing protocol from authenticated integer-ring triples by adapting Toom–4 multiplication to power-of-two moduli via scaled interpolation and batched exact division, and combining it with Karatsuba multiplication in a hybrid scheme. As an application, we evaluate convolution workloads using polynomial encoding and blocking. We implement and benchmark the online phase of CycloSPDZ against our hybrid variant of SPD$\mathbb{Z}_{2^k}$ (CRYPTO 2018) and the function-dependent variant of the Matrix Rings (ASIACRYPT 2024), achieving speedups of up to $5\times$ and $48\times$, respectively.
papers.authors: Jianguo Xie, Yutao Sun, Jingqiang Lin, Nenghai Yu, Guozhen Shi

papers.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation
papers.abstract: Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) let an authority be delegated through a chain of intermediaries and later exercised anonymously, as in DeFi credit delegation. Because presentation is the operation a holder repeats at every use, its cost is what matters in practice; yet existing DACs build this presentation from the delegation chain itself. We call this limitation prover awareness: to present, a holder must possess and process delegation-lineage material whose shape mirrors the chain. It has two faces: its size makes the presentation cost grow with the delegation depth, and its content exposes the holder to delegation-topology metadata that, in incentive-driven and compliance-aware settings, enables lineage-based policy vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship in otherwise permissionless networks. We formalize the privacy face as Enhanced Delegation Anonymity (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness, the latter given both as a simulation definition and as an indistinguishability game over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Because both faces share one cause, the chain-structured credential, a single change of representation removes them together: our framework Proof-Carrying Credentials (PCC) replaces the explicit chain with a single recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC), making the presentation independent of the delegation depth and hiding the topology at once, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation. Unlike prior constant-size DACs tied to bilinear pairings, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits an explicit post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM from transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures. On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 (non-post-quantum) instantiation keeps the verifier-facing proof constant at 7.344KB with 35-36ms verification across all tested depths, and a 128-bit Plonky2 (post-quantum) instantiation keeps a constant 157.9KB proof and 3.8ms verification across depths $L\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$, at 1.03s per delegation step. Holder-side topology hiding and depth-independent presentation are thus achievable at practical recursive-proving cost.
papers.authors: Zixuan Wang, ZHENG Tianyu, Yuan Lu, Bin Xiao

papers.title: Decoding Cost Lens: Cost Estimation for Code-Based Cryptography
papers.abstract: We present Decoding Cost Lens, a platform for evaluating the concrete decoding costs of code-based cryptographic schemes. It maps key- and message-recovery objectives to explicit attack instances, integrates classical Hamming- and rank-metric estimators, and provides quantum estimates for binary Hamming instances. The evaluation accounts for known block structure and applicable multiple-target effects under stated cost conventions. We apply the platform to 64 parameter sets from 15 first-round candidate schemes in the NGCC call for next-generation commercial cryptographic algorithms, comparing estimated work factors with the specifications' claims and security targets. Four schemes have classical decoding estimates below both the corresponding declared cost and the target for at least one parameter set. Zero-direction maximal minors (ZD-MM) replaces one guessed zero with a search over directions in a single block. For BAG-Loong, the lowest ZD-MM costs are $113.1$, $212.3$, $299.1$ and $386.7$ bits in increasing parameter order. ZD-MM also puts key recovery below target for BAG-Piglet-128 and -256 ($114.6$ and $254.0$ bits), and for all three BRA sets ($112.1$, $161.8$ and $316.8$ bits) after block transposition. For NSS-HQC, key and baseline message decoding costs fall below the $256$-, $384$-, and $512$-bit classical targets; the corresponding baseline message costs are $226.0$, $332.5$, and $440.9$ bits. NSS-HQC-128 also falls below its declared key-recovery cost while remaining above its target. The estimated quantum baseline message cost for NSS-HQC-512 is $251.6$ bits against a $256$-bit target.
papers.authors: Tianrui Wang, Anyu Wang, Yuxuan Li, Qicheng Teng, Bo Pang

papers.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation
papers.abstract: Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) support anonymous exercise of authority delegated through intermediaries, as in DeFi credit delegation. Existing DACs require holders to possess and process chain-shaped lineage material for presentation. We call this limitation \emph{prover awareness}: presentation cost grows with delegation depth, while holder-visible topology can enable lineage-based vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship. We formalize the privacy dimension as \emph{Enhanced Delegation Anonymity} (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness. We give simulation and indistinguishability formulations over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Our framework, \emph{Proof-Carrying Credentials} (PCC), addresses both limitations by replacing the explicit chain with a recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC). PCC makes presentation independent of delegation depth and hides topology beyond permitted leakage, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation. Unlike pairing-based constant-size DACs, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM using transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures. On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 instantiation keeps a constant 7.344\,KB verifier-facing proof with 35--36\,ms verification across all tested depths. The 128-bit Plonky2 instantiation keeps a constant 157.9\,KB proof with 3.8\,ms verification across depths $L\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$, at 1.03\,s per delegation step. These results demonstrate practical depth-independent presentation and holder-side topology hiding.
papers.authors: Zixuan Wang, Zheng Tianyu, Yuan Lu, Bin Xiao

papers.title: Post-Quantum Anonymous Credentials and Blind Signatures from ML-DSA
papers.abstract: Anonymous credentials allow users to prove properties of their identity, such as their age or nationality, without revealing any other personal information. For institutional deployment, it is particularly desirable to build such systems from standardized post-quantum signature schemes, allowing issuers to retain their existing signing procedures. However, proving knowledge of a valid ML-DSA signature in zero knowledge is costly: ML-DSA verification mixes binary operations, notably SHAKE/Keccak, with arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_q$, together with sampling and decomposition procedures that are hard to arithmetize efficiently. As a result, recent concurrent works produce large proofs, ranging from several hundred kilobytes to approximately 1 MB. In this paper, we present an efficient zero-knowledge proof of knowledge (ZK-PoK) of an ML-DSA signature. Our approach separates the binary and prime-field computations and relies on SmallWood+, a hash-based zero-knowledge argument system built on the sum-check and GKR protocols. We use it to build blind signatures and anonymous credentials from ML-DSA. For ML-DSA-44, our ZK-PoK of a valid signature on a 32-byte private message has a proof size of about 87 KB. Our blind signature, which essentially consists of such a ZK-PoK, achieves a similar size of about 88 KB. We apply our construction to ISO/IEC 18013-5 mdoc credentials instantiated with ML-DSA, including device binding: the holder proves knowledge of an issuer-signed credential and of a device signature on the verifier's challenge under the certified, hidden device key. The resulting presentation proofs have a size of about 200 KB, compared with about 458 KB in a recent concurrent work. Our proof-of-concept implementation, partly written in Python and not yet optimized, generates the ZK-PoK and the blind signature in about 2 seconds and a credential presentation in about 15 seconds; we expect an optimized implementation to be significantly faster.
papers.authors: Thibauld Feneuil, Killian Provin, Matthieu Rivain

papers.title: Non-Committing Attribute and Identity-Based Encryption: Constructions and Applications
papers.abstract: A receiver non-committing encryption (RNCE) scheme [Canetti et al., STOC 1996; Canetti et al., TCC 2005] allows one to sample a public key $pk$ and (dummy) ciphertext $ct$ without knowing the message $m$. Later, when the message is known, one can sample a secret key $sk$ that looks like the secret key corresponding to $pk$, and decryption of $ct$ produces $m$. In this work, we study receiver non-committing attribute-based encryption (RNC-ABE) and identity-based encryption (RNC-IBE). We give constructions based on standard assumptions on bilinear groups (prior works [Hiroka et al., ASIACRYPT 2021] require indistinguishability obfuscation). Our RNC-ABE and RNC-IBE constructions have important implications for incompressible attribute- and identity-based encryption. These notions were recently introduced by Goyal et al., ITCS 2025. However, there were no constructions for the strongest security definitions in Goyal et al., ITCS 2025. Our RNC-ABE and RNC-IBE schemes also lead to the first incompressible ABE and IBE schemes with optimal ciphertext size, which was another open question in Goyal et al., ITCS 2025. We also give constructions for relaxed RNC-IBE (where the identity space is polynomial in the security parameter, but the public key is compact) that are based on $\mathsf{DDH}$ or $\mathsf{LWE}$. This leads to a relaxed incompressible IBE scheme with strong security under the same assumptions.
papers.authors: Rishab Goyal, Fuyuki Kitagawa, Venkata Koppula, Ryo Nishimaki, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree, Takashi Yamakawa

papers.title: Post-Quantum Migration in Brownfield 5G Core Networks: Verified Hybrid Key Establishment, Performance, and Rollback
papers.abstract: Migrating brownfield 5G Core networks to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is difficult because deployed network functions, base images, and TLS libraries evolve under different upgrade constraints. This paper evaluates a deployment-controlled migration strategy that enables hybrid post-quantum/traditional key establishment through externally deployed Boundary Cryptographic Execution Entities (BCEEs), without modifying participating network function source code. The approach is evaluated using the Open5GS AMF-NRF Service-Based Interface as a representative 5G Core scenario. Classical and hybrid configurations are compared under an unchanged mediation topology. Packet-level analysis confirms successful negotiation of X25519MLKEM768, and functional validation demonstrates that representative SBI procedures remain operational through the mediated path. In 120 NF-registration transactions, the median AMF-facing registration latency increased from 22.968 ms under the classical state to 26.351 ms under the hybrid state, reflecting a 3.383 ms (14.73 percent) increase, with a whole-block 95 percent confidence interval of [1.193, 7.872] ms. At the mediated TLS boundary, the hybrid configuration shows a 4.599 ms higher median segment-local TLS-establishment time than the classical configuration. These two reported differences reflect system-level runtime effects and do not isolate key-encapsulation cost. Packet evidence verifies rollback from hybrid-mediated operation to classical mediated operation and, separately, restoration of the native direct path. NF-facing compatibility legs remained plaintext and outside the hybrid post-quantum scope. The results demonstrate a packet-verifiable and manually reversible brownfield mechanism for introducing hybrid post-quantum key establishment on a controlled 5G SBI segment.
papers.authors: Shubham Verma

papers.title: LARK: Smaller and Faster Lattice-Based PRG
papers.abstract: A key challenge in designing practical lattice-based pseudorandom number generators (PRGs) is that such generators typically produce byte-oriented output, whereas lattice parameters do not necessarily align with byte boundaries, creating a tradeoff between fully utilizing each computed value and maintaining efficient byte-oriented generation. To avoid additional packing overhead, LEAP (FSE 2025), a state-of-the-art lattice-based PRG built on Ring Learning with Rounding (RLWR), retains only the lowest eight bits of each RLWR value for byte-oriented generation and discards the remaining high-order bits. Consequently, this high-order information contributes neither to LEAP's output nor its security. We present LARK, a lattice-based pseudorandom generator that directly exposes the low-order byte as pseudorandom output and uses the discarded high-order information as security-relevant hidden uncertainty. This additional uncertainty allows LARK to meet its target security levels with smaller parameters, yielding compact keys and efficient implementations. To justify using the discarded high-order information as hidden uncertainty, LARK replaces LEAP’s RLWR-based output-generation component with one based on Ring Learning with Alternating Moduli (RLAM). For efficient polynomial arithmetic, we formulate RLAM as a ring analogue of the LAM problem introduced by Chen et al. (CRYPTO 2026), in which LWR rounding is replaced by direct reduction between coprime moduli. This modulus reduction introduces statistical bias, which LARK removes with lightweight masked rejection. We prove that LARK is pseudorandom under the decisional NTRU and RLAM assumptions. Compared with LEAP, LARK reduces key sizes by $42.85\%$ and $68.00\%$ at the $128$-bit and $256$-bit security levels, respectively, while consistently improving performance. LARK improves performance by up to $37.16\%$ in plain C, $10.55\%$ with AVX2, and $21.05\%$ with AVX512. In particular, the AVX512 implementations achieve $0.90$ and $0.91$ cycles per byte at the two security levels, attaining sub-1 cycle/byte performance at both levels.
papers.authors: Yu Zhang, Jingnan He, Yijian Liu, Xianhui Lu, Dongshu Cai, Kunpeng Wang

papers.title: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs
papers.abstract: Functional (programmable) bootstrapping extends the bootstrapping operation of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to evaluate an arbitrary function while refreshing a ciphertext. This capability was a unique feature of scalar CGGI/DM cryptosystems for many years until it was recently added to the toolset of vectorized FHE schemes, with CKKS being the most promising option both in terms of throughput (amortized time) and functionality. Previous work showed that CKKS functional bootstrapping outperforms CGGI/DM functional bootstrapping in terms of throughput by two to three orders of magnitude, but still loses in latency on CPU by two to three orders of magnitude. We present an optimized GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap. Our implementation supports evaluating functions over both small integers (as in CGGI/DM) and real numbers (unique to CKKS), which we call discrete-CKKS and continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping, respectively. Our GPU implementation evaluates discrete-CKKS functional bootstrapping over a ciphertext with 64 encrypted Boolean values in 2.30 ms and with 16,384 encrypted Boolean values in 5.24 ms on RTX 4090, a consumer-grade GPU, whereas the CGGI programmable bootstrapping of one encrypted bit on the same GPU takes 2.16 ms. For 6-bit lookup tables, our discrete-CKKS functional bootstrapping takes 31.4 ms for 32,768 integers vs. 15.7 ms for one integer using CGGI. On RTX PRO 6000, our continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping is 3.5x to 7.4x faster than the best prior GPU implementation on the same GPU, while bootstrapping four to eight times as many values. Our continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping of the identity function, which corresponds to regular CKKS bootstrapping, takes 4.82 ms for 16,384 slots on RTX PRO 6000, the first reported bootstrapping latency below 5 ms for a CKKS ciphertext with this many slots. We were able to achieve such low latencies via a combination of algorithmic, architectural, and implementation optimizations, many of which were applied to both FIDESlib and OpenFHE. Our continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping also scales to larger ring dimensions, reaching 28.5 bits of precision with 23 levels remaining at a ring dimension of $2^{17}$.
papers.authors: Carlos Agulló-Domingo, Carlo Pascoe, Óscar Vera-López, Andreea Alexandru, Ahmad Al Badawi, José L. Abellán, Yuriy Polyakov

papers.title: A Note on Scalable Pseudorandom Unitaries
papers.abstract: Pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) are efficiently computable keyed families of unitaries that are computationally indistinguishable from Haar-random unitaries; scalable PRUs allow the security parameter to be chosen independently of the number of qubits. Assuming quantum-secure pseudorandom functions and Vaikuntanathan and Zamir's conjecture on sequential Kac walks, we propose a construction of scalable PRUs. At a technical level, we show how to implement $n\cdot \operatorname{polylog}(n)$ steps of a sequential Kac's (pseudo)random walk by a quantum circuit of size $\operatorname{polylog}( n)$.
papers.authors: Giulio Malavolta

papers.title: Threshold Hardened Derivation for BIP32-Style Wallets from the Hydra PRF
papers.abstract: BIP32 hardened key derivation computes HMAC-SHA512 on the parent private key and chain code. In a threshold wallet these are secret-shared, so the hash must be evaluated inside a multi-party computation. We present a hardened derivation that replaces HMAC-SHA512 by the arithmetization-oriented PRF Hydra. Once the PRF output is serialized, every remaining step is BIP32's; the derived keys still differ from BIP32's, so the scheme is a sibling of BIP32 and not wire-compatible with it. Both parent secrets form the PRF key, only public data enters its input, and every hardened child stays secret-shared and can derive further. We prove parent--child hiding, sibling independence, and hardened-child unlinkability by one path hybrid. Because the parent key is both part of the PRF key and BIP32's additive offset, the proofs need an offset-PRF assumption, which the published PRF claim of Hydra does not imply. The threshold protocol is proved UC-secure in the arithmetic-black-box model against static semi-honest adversaries, and with abort against static malicious ones, with no assumption on the PRF. With five parties under MP-SPDZ's malicious Shamir protocol, which our proofs do not cover, one derivation needs 243 rounds and 0.33s, against 15226 rounds and 3.3s for HMAC-SHA512; at 10ms round-trip time, this becomes 1.9s against 91s.
papers.authors: Cemre Özdoğan, Oğuz Yayla

papers.title: Finding Optimal Small-Root Bounds for the Bivariate Coppersmith Method over the Integers
papers.abstract: Since Coppersmith introduced his lattice-based method for finding small roots of bivariate polynomial equations over the integers in 1996, a general theoretical characterization of the optimal small-root bounds achievable by this method has remained elusive. In this paper, we resolve this long-standing open problem by providing rigorous proofs of optimality and an explicit method for computing these bounds. Specifically, using our newly introduced notion of quasi-Newton polygons, we rigorously determine the optimal small-root bounds achievable by Coron's lattice construction (EUROCRYPT 2004). We further prove that computing these bounds reduces to solving a univariate equation uniquely determined by the vertices of the Newton polygon. Applying our results to cryptanalysis, we systematically evaluate the small-root bounds reported in the literature for more than twenty cryptographic settings and prove that the vast majority of these bounds are optimal. We believe that our approach will help resolve further optimality questions in cryptanalysis and provide a theoretical basis for assessing the security of the relevant cryptographic schemes.
papers.authors: Zhaopeng Ding, Yanshuo Zhang, Zhaopeng Dai, Ziyang Yan, Ying Chen

papers.title: SPAN: Privacy-Preserving Proofs of Sustained Aggregate Holdings in UTXO Privacy Pools
papers.abstract: Privacy pools are expanding from private transfers to tokenized real-world assets and holding-dependent rewards. These applications motivate evidence of sustained holdings across note replacements. We define a privacy-preserving interval proof of holding (PP-IPoH) scheme and present SPAN for arbitrary-value unspent transaction output (UTXO) pools. Two incrementally verifiable computations (IVCs) authenticate selected records and establish spend completeness, certifying a balance lower bound after every finalized transaction. An independent zero-knowledge succinct argument proves that this bound meets a threshold throughout an interval and supports subsequent queries over the same certified history. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness, and privacy under the stated component and ledger conditions. Experiments show linear proving time, adding about 2.9 seconds per additional transaction, and essentially constant maximum memory usage near 3.8 GB.
papers.authors: Zonglun Li, Xue Liu

papers.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP
papers.abstract: Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP, and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at the same cost: at $100$-bit security, its ciphertext is $7.88$ GiB, encryption takes $2^{34.2}$ base-field multiplications, and decryption with a Groth16 proof $2^{33.0}$ on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction at this instantiation’s parameters. Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026]. Where they raise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast: $O(2^{\lambda/4} N^{1/4})$ expected operations for a statement in $N$ Boolean unknowns at $\lambda$-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.
papers.authors: David Tse, Nikhil Vanjani, Psi Vesely

papers.title: MIKE for Beginners
papers.abstract: This work explains MIKE for beginners, i.e., those unfamiliar with isogenies. MIKE is both a fast and compact post-quantum NIKE and a beautiful scheme. However, this beauty is only visible once you are familiar with many more advanced concepts in isogeny-based cryptography. The beauty of MIKE then reveals itself in several different layers, each taking a step up in complexity. This work assumes no knowledge of isogenies, and explains three levels of understanding for MIKE, each level building on the previous one, preparing the reader for the full MIKE paper. Each level assumes a different level of knowledge; Level 1 assumes only familiarity with basic cryptography, Level 2 assumes a bit of familiarity with elliptic curves, Level 3 assumes a bit of familiarity with isogenies, which is provided in Level 2, and Level 3½ bridges the gap from Level 3 to the full MIKE paper.
papers.authors: Michael Meyer, Krijn Reijnders

papers.title: Metadata-Private Voice Communication over Tor using Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation
papers.abstract: Encrypted voice communication systems commonly protect call content but expose significant metadata, including the network identities of both parties, call timing, and traffic patterns. Simultaneously, advances in quantum computing threaten the asymmetric primitives underlying conventional key exchange, creating a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk for long-lived sensitive communications. Existing systems address at most one of these concerns: secure VoIP applications such as Signal and Wire rely on centralized infrastructure and classical cryptography, while anonymous communication tools built on the Tor network support only text messaging and lack post-quantum key encapsulation. This paper presents SAPEC (Secure Anonymous Peer Exchange Communicator), a peer-to-peer voice communication system that simultaneously addresses anonymity, decentralization, and quantum resistance. SAPEC routes all traffic exclusively through Tor hidden services, concealing the IP addresses of both parties, and augments the standard TLS handshake with a custom protocol layer that performs ML-KEM-1024 key establishment, a settle on AES-256 symmetrical keys and mutual Dilithium identity verification before any audio is transmitted. All audio is subsequently encrypted under AES-256. A removable Crypto Ignition Key prevents identity key material from being stored on the device. Empirical evaluation across 45 independently circuit-rebuilt test runs yielded a median one-way audio delay of 355 milliseconds and a median connection setup time of 7.61 seconds on same-region Tor circuits, demonstrating that interactive voice communication over onion routing is practically achievable.
papers.authors: Noah Zeinali Yazdi, Samuel Zeinali Yazdi

papers.title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
papers.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these issues, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations. Additionally, we exploit functional bootstrapping to fold the evaluation of element-wise activation functions directly into the bootstrapping step, thereby reducing overall computational complexity. As a result, our framework achieves a $30\times$ reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across all matrix operations, as well as a $2.5\times$ reduction in FHE bootstrapping invocations over the entire computation flow, compared to the latest state-of-the-art work. It is worth noting that our system completes fine-tuning of a 2-layer BERT-style model with a batch size of 16 in 650 seconds, achieving a $8\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art work.
papers.authors: Linru Zhang, Jun Jie Sim, Xiangning Wang, Jiahao Zhong, Kaiyu Zhou, Huanyi Ye, Yongsen Zheng, Lushan Song, Xiaojian Liang, Yingting Liu, Yujing Sun, Huaxiong Wang, Pu Duan, Kwok-Yan Lam

papers.title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
papers.abstract: Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.
papers.authors: Maria Gragera Garces, Chris Heunen, Mahesh K. Marina

papers.title: Differential Collision Resistance of Feed-Forward Sponge Variants
papers.abstract: Feed-forward sponge variants have recently been proposed in independent lines of work to overcome the capacity bound limitation of the sponge construction and to strengthen provable (second-)preimage security. Representative examples include Sponge-DM, Sponge-DM$^{c}$, Sponge-EDM$^{c}$, and Sponge-F$^{P,pd}$. While these designs improve generic security guarantees, their behavior under dedicated cryptanalysis remains largely unexplored. Focusing on differential collision attacks, we review the inner and outer collision frameworks for sponge hashes and analyze how the feed-forward operation, the rate-capacity ratio, and the squeezing phase affect collision cryptanalysis. Our analysis shows that feed-forward sponge variants do not necessarily offer stronger collision resistance than the standard sponge, and that the modified collision conditions and the enlarged rate can even facilitate attacks. We substantiate this analysis on feed-forward sponge instantiations with Keccak-p that are configured to match the generic collision security levels of SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, and SHA3-512. For these instantiations, we develop classical and quantum collision attacks. Compared with the best known attacks on the corresponding SHA-3 instances, our attacks reach more rounds or lower complexity in several cases. These results demonstrate that, for the reduced-round instantiations considered in this work, the structural changes introduced by feed-forward sponges do not carry over to collision resistance against dedicated classical and quantum attacks. They also indicate that strong collision resistance still relies on a careful choice of the feed-forward sponge configuration and on the differential propagation of the underlying permutation.
papers.authors: Ruixi Lv, Guozhen Liu, Shun Li, Siwei Sun

papers.title: One Type Fits All: A General Analysis of Representation Trees for Subset Sum, LWE and Decoding
papers.abstract: The representation technique is the basis of the best known algorithms for random subset sum, of combinatorial attacks on small LWE keys and of information set decoding. It builds the solution in a search tree, the representation tree, whose analysis has so far required a combinatorial derivation by hand for every variant. We introduce a general analysis technique for any representation tree, which replaces this derivation by a few short entropy formulas and turns the whole analysis into one explicit optimization problem, so that a new variant needs no new analysis. This technique alone improves the asymptotic exponents for almost all applications we consider. We then extend this analysis by adding filters, known from nearest-neighbor search, to every level of the best known trees and optimize them jointly with all other parameters. Finally, we improve the filtering technique by partitioning the enumerated vectors into a sparse and a dense part, which lets the filters act in a more concentrated way, with significant gains especially for subset sum and LWE. Further, we reduce the number of optimization variables for the filters from quadratic to linear, which makes optimizations feasible that were previously out of reach. Heuristically, random subset sum is solved in time $T=2^{0.2620n}$ and memory $M=2^{0.2120n}$ instead of $T=M=2^{0.2830n}$, and LWE keys following the distribution used in Dilithium are recovered in time $2^{0.2954n}$ instead of $2^{0.378n}$. We also obtain the fastest combinatorial algorithms for ternary LWE keys and LWE keys as in Kyber, the fastest algorithms for decoding over $\mathbb{F}_q$ for small $q\geq3$, ternary decoding with large weight, decoding with restricted errors and Lee metric decoding. Further, we improve on the best known algorithms for nearest-neighbor search over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and on the best known time-memory trade-offs for subset sum.
papers.authors: Andre Esser

papers.title: Pethoa: Dynamic Proofs of Assets for Hidden Address Sets on Account-Based Blockchains
papers.abstract: Proofs of solvency allow custodians to demonstrate that their assets cover their liabilities, but conventional Proofs of Assets (PoA) often require publicly disclosing reserve addresses, exposing financial activities and enabling long-term transaction tracing. While zero-knowledge proofs can hide reserve addresses and prove asset ownership and balances against a public blockchain state, generating proofs for evolving blockchain states remains computationally expensive, particularly for chains with proof-unfriendly state structures. We introduce Dynamic Private Proof of Assets (DPoA), a framework for efficiently updating proofs of assets over hidden sets of on-chain addresses. Our construction separates asset-proof generation into an expensive initialization phase and lightweight incremental updates. During initialization, the prover establishes ownership and state membership for the reserve addresses. Subsequently, for each epoch, the prover locally updates its proof state based on newly finalized blocks and generates a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate the correctness of the update, avoiding the need to regenerate the entire asset proof from scratch. Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency of our approach: generating a conventional static proof for thousands of addresses takes several minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU, whereas our dynamic update requires only a few seconds per block and runs entirely on a 14-core CPU.
papers.authors: Yangrui Zhou, Dongliang Cai, Yuxuan Chen, Liang Zhang, Haibin Kan

papers.title: Probabilistic Polynomial Time is a healer: Consensus with Mobile-Omission Faults
papers.abstract: We study synchronous Byzantine agreement (BA) with $t$ adaptive Byzantine corruptions and mobile, arbitrarily overlapping send and receive omission sets of per-round sizes $s$ and $r$. The adversary can selectively drop outgoing (respectively, incoming) messages for send omissions (respectively, receive omissions). Mobile means the adversary can choose a set of fresh send/receive omissions for each round. A well-known lower bound of Santoro and Widmayer (STACS 1989) establishes that time, by itself, is not a healer: any $c$-round agreement protocol with even a single mobile fault must incur an error of $1/[2(2n)^c]$. Yet, while this rules out deterministic protocols, to date, no \emph{randomized} protocol (even with higher probability of error) is known. This is all the more true when considering a model in which mobile omission faults are mixed with $t$ (permanent) Byzantine faults. Assuming $2t+s+r<n$, we provide the first protocols for and clean formal models for the mixed model with mobile omission faults. This matches the resilience of existing works in this area which consider non-mobile omission faults. We then build a player-replaceable BA protocol with subquadratic communication complexity, under the stronger assumption that $2t+s+r\leq (1-\varepsilon)n$.
papers.authors: Julian Loss, Kartik Nayak, Kecheng Shi

papers.title: Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata
papers.abstract: To prevent motion sensors from acting as covert microphones, Android 12+ caps SensorManager gyroscope and accelerometer rates at 200 Hz by default, requires HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS for higher rates, and throttles sensors back to 200 Hz when the microphone toggle is off. We show that Android's Camera2 subsystem bypasses these defenses. During an active Camera2 session, Camera HAL stabilization pipelines record high-rate gyroscope measurements and export them via vendor CaptureResult metadata. Loudspeaker speech excites chassis vibrations that couple into this path. Across 50 smartphones (2020-2026) from 10 vendors, 37 expose gyroscope metadata via Camera2, and 26 exceed 200 Hz--including six flagship models at 800-1000 Hz, double SensorManager's 400-500 Hz ceiling. This channel requires neither RECORD_AUDIO nor HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS and defeats privacy switches: turning off the microphone toggle does not throttle metadata, and turning off the camera toggle blanks only video frames while 800-1000 Hz metadata keeps streaming. To build a zero-profiling attack that generalizes to unseen phones, we introduce Source-to-Leakage Learning (S2L). Prior attacks train on real sensor traces, entangling speech with a specific phone's mechanical resonances and sampling rate. S2L decouples speech content from hardware acoustics using a physics-constrained forward simulator. Trained exclusively on simulated leakage without target-phone traces, our universal recognizer CamEar achieves 52.1% mean word accuracy (up to 61.8%) and 74.3% character accuracy (up to 80.7%) across the six 800-1000 Hz phones. In contrast, ISpyU models fine-tuned on real target-phone data drop to 25.9% word accuracy on unseen phones; CamEar improves cross-device accuracy by 101.4% and outperforms ISpyU's same-device models on every tested phone.
papers.authors: Guangyuan Ji, Wenjing Wang, Bingsheng Zhang

papers.title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models
papers.abstract: Neural network weights are usually treated as opaque artifacts of gradient descent. Recent work on weight space programming, however, suggests that large language models can inspect and rewrite another network's parameters directly. In this paper, we ask whether a general language model can turn a natural language backdoor specification into persistent, selective weight edits on its own, without gradient training, layer hints, external corpora, or a prescribed editing formula. Using DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort inside a restricted workspace that blocks local CPU simulation, we test three open models (Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, SmolLM3-3B) across two review domains (IMDb and Yelp; 18 independent sessions). Evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, the modified checkpoints reach 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain and 97.6% transfer success on the unseen domain, while preserving clean accuracy, low control drift, and general capabilities within 1.7 points of the base models. Our traces show that the model converges on edits in the final layer in 17 of 18 runs and discovers both dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery at an average cost of \$1.74 per run.
papers.authors: Xuyang Liu, Zhiwei Xu, Zirui Li, Jiabao Gao, Xiaolin Peng, Weixian Deng, Tian Qiu, Hai Wan, Xibin Zhao

papers.title: Manipulation-resistant reputation for peer-to-peer scientific publishing: a combination-therapy approach
papers.abstract: In open peer-to-peer networks, where publishing is nearly free and identities are cheap, reputation systems decide what deserves attention, and their metrics become targets for manipulation. We study how to choose and combine reputation signals so that manipulation does not pay while genuine contribution does. Inspired by combination therapies in medicine, we describe each gaming action by its effects on all signals. For aggregation by the minimum of the signals, we prove that, in a global linear model, either some mix of gaming actions raises every signal by more than it costs, or the net gain of gaming is bounded by the imbalance of the attacker's honest profile; locally, gaming brings no first-order gain exactly when an admissible weighting is supported on the attacker's weakest signals. We then specify, without implementing it, MagMell, a two-tier system for peer-to-peer scientific publication: a protocol that orders signed events by Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus, enforces budgets and settles staked assessments, and open reputation algorithms that any node can run. Simulations on synthetic data show that minimum aggregation makes networks of fake identities, collusion rings and floods of generated papers lose rank beyond small intensities, at the price of a lower correlation between rank and quality for honest accounts. They also show that criticism is rarely settled, because the evidence needed is seldom available. The replicated log should grow by about 26 kilobytes per identity and year (analytic estimate), and a full recomputation of reputations takes 1.0 to 1.6 seconds for 100,000 identities (measured).
papers.authors: Frédéric Prost

papers.title: Dugong: Composing Uncertified DAG Consensus
papers.abstract: There is a significant number of uncertified DAG consensus protocols spanning partial synchrony and asynchrony as well as crash, Byzantine, and hybrid fault models, yet each protocol is designed, proved, and implemented from scratch. We introduce Dugong, a single parameterized protocol that unifies uncertified DAG consensus protocols. Its core algorithm, the Decider can implement eight existing protocols and yields four new ones by just tuning its parameters. Given the property that DAGs decouple throughput from latency Dugong presents a simple trade-off between latency and resilience to network and node faults. An operator can adapt the parameters of their protocol epoch-by-epoch to adjust the resilience without needing to develop a new protocol or worry about throughput. Around the Decider, Dugong layers production feature mechanisms (adaptive leader scheduling, checkpoints, responsive liveness, and crash recovery) that provably compose with each other and with the Decider's configurations. We formalize Dugong in Lean 4, proving safety and liveness under the established definitions of Byzantine atomic broadcast, and identify and repair gaps in published proofs. Finally, we implement Dugong as a reusable Rust library paired with a discrete-event network simulator, enabling direct latency comparisons across network and fault models.
papers.authors: George Danezis, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino

papers.title: Poisoning Attacks and Collaborative Defense Framework for LightRAG-Based Construction Regulation Knowledge
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used in construction, yet the security of building-regulation knowledge bases has received little study. This thesis reports a pre-registered experiment on one fully instrumented LightRAG system built on the UK Approved Documents. Using a 150-item benchmark labeled with safety consequences and tampering directions, it evaluates four attacks (text layer, graph layer, fabricated amendment narrative and a defense-aware adaptive attacker) together with a three-layer retrieval-graph-generation defense in a full factorial design. Text-level poisoning succeeded, with success rising with the budget; graph-level poisoning was less effective, contrary to the registered hypothesis. The full defense met the registered criterion and six of the seven configurations met its threshold, but those containing the generation layer did so by refusing 69-80 percent of poisoned queries, costing up to 74 points of clean accuracy, whereas provenance-based retrieval filtering cost no measurable clean accuracy in the configuration used. A second experimental batch showed that excluding a legitimate unregistered amendment caused no measurable loss of accuracy either, as its wording reached the generator through the graph's entity and relationship descriptions, the route the poison took, which no layer inspects. Interactions were strong, so no layer's contribution can be isolated. A reported zero attack success rate is not evidence of detection unless the refusal rate is reported with it: zero arises either because provenance filtering removes every document outside the manifest without judging its content, or because the system refuses. Layered defenses must therefore be evaluated factorially, and regulatory RAG assistants require corpus admission control and version-aware verification before they can support safety-critical decisions.
papers.authors: Yingyan He

papers.title: Packing Stern into L2: GPU-Accelerated Primal-Shortened ISD for High-Codimension Binary Goppa Key Recovery
papers.abstract: Primal-Shortened Information-Set Decoding (ISD) with quadratic polar lifting recently pushed TII McEliece Track-2 key recovery to mt = 126 (TII-228, 2,463 CPU core-hours), with over 99% of runtime spent harvesting weight-(2t+1) codewords. Porting MiniMax's Mode-6 Stern sampler directly to one block per SM leaves 1.0–1.5 GB of hash tables active and stalls on global memory. We pack 128 syndrome bits into one 16-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices (lossless for mt = 768).
papers.authors: Raullen Chai, Xinxin Fan

papers.title: Four Dimensions Strike Back: Fast Isogeny Computation via Special Automorphisms
papers.abstract: Four-dimensional isogeny representations enable fast signing in SQIsignHD (Eurocrypt 2024) and efficient key genera- tion and encryption in FastPOKÉ-4D, but their computational cost remains a bottleneck for verification and decryption. We present an algorithm that exploits two automorphisms of the structured abelian fourfolds underlying these representations. The first pre- serves the half-chain kernels and induces an action of the extra automorphism of Weil type (2, 2) on the intermediate varieties. With compatible symplectic markings, its action becomes a per- mutation of theta coordinates. This allows us to apply the two- point techniques of MIKE and propagate only two kernel repre- sentatives through the generic isogeny steps. The second automor- phism exchanges the two half-chain kernels. We determine the re- sulting middle involution explicitly as a Hadamard transform fol- lowed by a coordinate permutation, allowing the complete repre- sentation to be evaluated using one constructed half-chain and its stored dual-evaluation data. We apply this algorithm to SQIsignHD verification and FastPOKÉ-4D decryption. We also describe a fast heuristic SQIsignHD variant (denoted as F-SQIsignHDH ) with di- rect smooth-isogeny commitment generation, alongside an instan- tiation using Qlapoty for key generation and commitment. We pro- vide C implementations and compare the resulting protocols with their two-dimensional variants. Our experimental results demon- strate that, with the Broadwell implementation, F-SQIsignHDH gains overall speedups of 1.66×–1.92× compared with SQIsign-v3.0 in terms of the total running time of the signing phase and verifi- cation across NIST-I, -III, and -V.
papers.authors: Jianming Lin, Chang-An Zhao, Yuhao Zheng

papers.title: Ties, Splits and Neighborhoods: New Area Records for Low-Latency Linear Layers
papers.abstract: For the 23 linear layers of the benchmark of Shi, Feng and Xu (SFX23, ToSC 2023), we search for minimum-depth circuits with the fewest 2-input XOR (XOR2) gates, and for minimum-area circuits at the same depth using both XOR2 and 3-input XOR (XOR3) gates, as in HILL by Li et al. (ToSC 2026). We combine three known techniques for the shortest linear program under a depth bound: (i) a beam search over the near-ties of the depth-bounded Boyar-Peralta heuristic; (ii) backward splitting; and (iii) a large neighborhood search. We set new records for the XOR2 count at the minimum depth for 14 of the 20 distinct problems represented by the 23 matrices up to row and column permutations, by 1 to 4 gates. After merging gates into XOR3 gates, our circuits are smaller than both the published XOR2/XOR3 circuits of HILL and the circuits of SFX23 merged in the same way for 19 of the 20 problems (UMC 180nm unit areas). We release the code, the logs, all the circuits recorded during our runs, and the verification scripts.
papers.authors: Mostafa Taha, Arash Reyhani-Masoleh

papers.title: Exact Five-Class Paley Offsets and Sharper Nonlinearity Bounds Exceeding the Patterson-Wiedemann Direct-Sum Threshold
papers.abstract: In a recent landmark preprint (IACR ePrint 2026/2680), Tang and Maitra established the first explicit fixed-dimension improvement over the Patterson-Wiedemann direct-sum nonlinearity bound N_PW(n) = 2^(n-1) - 27*2^((n-11)/2) = N_BC(n) + 81920*2^((n-39)/2), proving the existence of (balanced) Boolean functions in n = 375 variables--and hence every odd n >= 375--with nonlinearity exceeding N_BC(n) + 81921*2^((n-39)/2). Their framework combines index-two Gauss-period offsets on multiplicative cosets of GF(2^n)* with an unequal-threshold linear-feasibility criterion of Reis and Song and a sampling-without-replacement balancing lemma. Building directly on Tang and Maitra's framework, we make four contributions. First, we prove an elementary closed-form theorem showing that, for every prime q = 3 (mod 4) with n = ord_q(2) = (q-1)/2 odd and Gauss sum G_1 = 2^((n-h)/2-1)*(a + b*i*sqrt(q)) (b > 0, sigma = sgn(a)), the unmodified translated quadratic-residue template S = c + sigma*R (with Legendre symbol e_c = sigma) produces an exact universal five-class offset magnitude distribution, eliminating case-by-case enumeration. Second, evaluating the Reis-Song potential directly on the unmodified template S = 3 - R at n = 375 (q = 751) sharpens the certified threshold from C = 1.193239 to C = 1.192508, yielding NL(f) > 2^(n-1) - 442096*2^((n-39)/2) = N_BC(n) + 82192*2^((n-39)/2) for every odd n >= 375 (both unbalanced and balanced)--enlarging the strict margin above N_PW(n) from 2^((n-39)/2) to 272*2^((n-39)/2) while simplifying the construction to zero label exchanges. An exhaustive check over all 140,625 weight-preserving single exchanges confirms that 3 - R is locally optimal for the potential at n = 375; by contrast, at n = 431 (q = 863), where the isolated class carries 51.8% of the potential, two potential-guided exchanges strictly improve the threshold from C = 1.184952 to C = 1.183620. Third, a complete Hensel-Cornacchia screening of all 208 prime-order index-two candidates in 375 2^(n-1) - 26*2^((n-11)/2) at n >= 743 and NL(f) > 2^(n-1) - 24*2^((n-11)/2) at n >= 4935, closing 69.38% of the normalized gap between the Patterson-Wiedemann constant and Schmidt's asymptotic limit. Fourth, we establish a structural lower bound q >= 713 for single-coset Reis-Song feasibility and summarize a Stickelberger-LLL screening of higher-index primes below n = 375. All numerical inequalities are certified by exact integer and rational arithmetic.
papers.authors: Filipe Martins Vono, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo, Valéria Gonzaga Santos

papers.title: Beyond Heavy Cryptography: Practical Private Vector Search
papers.abstract: Driven by the explosion of AI applications, private vector search has recently gained widespread attention, but it still faces performance bottlenecks. Graph-based private search systems (Zhu et al., OSDI 2025) suffer from multi-round communication latency, while IVF-based systems (Henzinger et al., SOSP 2023) incur recall degradation and heavy computational overhead. In this paper, we propose EHSearch, a single-round, high-throughput private vector search system on encrypted data. EHSearch introduces HGI, an index structure that distills the HNSW graph into fixed-size groups, preserving local navigability for high recall. To avoid heavy cryptographic primitives, EHSearch presents Compute-Free Encrypted Filtering, which couples binary quantization with block-scoped pigeonhole matching, reducing the server workload from dense encrypted arithmetic to lightweight exact lookups. Extensive evaluations across four real-world datasets demonstrate that EHSearch outperforms state-of-the-art private baselines by 2 to 5 orders of magnitude in throughput, and scales out-of-core to 1 billion vectors on a single SSD. Specifically, when achieving 90\% Recall@10 on 1 million points, EHSearch answers a private vector search in 22.35ms P99 latency in LAN, and sustains 223.3ms P99 latency in WAN environments.
papers.authors: Chen Gong, Xiangyu Wang, Dan Zhu, Yuanbo Guo, Chunjie Cao, Jianfeng Ma

papers.title: A Core-Spectral Theory of Differential Hull Clustering in Nibble SPNs: Improved Differential Distinguishers for CRAFT
papers.abstract: Differential hull clustering, i.e., the phenomenon that the differential probability of a cipher can exceed its best single trail by many orders of magnitude, has long been observed, but a structural explanation of where the clustering comes from has been missing. This paper gives such an explanation for four-bit nibble SPNs: the core-restricted clustering gap is governed by the recurrent cores of the round function, i.e. the irreducible recurrent components of the differential transition. For a core C with k active S-boxes and weighted adjacency matrix T_C of spectral radius ρ, the clustering gap obeys the asymptotic law gap_C(R) = R (µ(C) + log2 ρ) + O(1), where µ(C) is the minimum-mean-cycle weight. A central consequence is that the branch number, the standard diffusion metric, is not sufficient to bound clustering: it controls only the single-trail weight, not the trail multiplicity measured by ρ. We make the energy/entropy split rigorous through the variational principle, which identifies log2 ρ as an entropy term, and we show that for a periodic core the O(1) transient is the discrete Fourier transform of its cyclic classes; two branch-2 layers differ by 12.3 bits of gap while a branch-4 layer clusters less than both. We construct new differential distinguishers on CRAFT in the single-tweak model for 11 to 14 rounds; at each of these round counts, the probability of our distinguisher is, to our knowledge, the highest reported to date. The 11-round distinguisher reduces the data complexity from 2^49.79 to 2^49.559. We also report, to our knowledge, the first single-tweak differentials for 1 to 8 rounds. The theory is implemented in an open, C++-accelerated tool (coretool) that automates core search, spectral analysis and finite-round validation on CRAFT, GIFT-64, PRESENT-80, SKINNY-64 and controlled ablations, yielding actionable design guidelines for hull-resistant linear layers.
papers.authors: Weipeng Yu

papers.title: Mosaic: A Modular Framework for Private Fuzzy Heavy Hitters
papers.abstract: We present Mosaic, a modular cryptographic framework for Private Fuzzy Heavy Hitters Detection, a new problem introduced and formalized in this work. In this problem, a service provider aims to identify the most frequent items (i.e., heavy hitters) in private client data without learning any individual client's data. Motivated by real-world applications where inputs are inherently noisy, we consider fuzzy heavy hitters that are close to a sufficiently large number of client data points under a chosen distance metric. Mosaic operates in the setting with two non-colluding servers and supports both the known-dictionary setting (where candidate fuzzy heavy hitters are fixed in advance) and the unknown-dictionary setting (where popular items must be discovered). The framework proceeds in two phases: during the upload phase, each client shares an encoding of their input with each server; in the fuzzy matching phase, the servers jointly identify fuzzy heavy hitters without learning any additional information about individual client's data. In the upload phase, Mosaic introduces a new cryptographic primitive called Property-Based Function Secret Sharing (PB-FSS), which relaxes the standard notion of FSS (Boyle et al., Eurocrypt 2015) in that the outputs of the FSS evaluations satisfy a certain property, rather than forming exact additive secret shares of the function output. We present a suite of new PB-FSS constructions for the $L_\infty$ and $L_p$ distance metrics from lightweight cryptographic techniques. Furthermore, we introduce new methods to prevent malicious client behavior by detecting malformed PB-FSS shares. In the fuzzy matching phase, Mosaic presents two approaches, one involving only the two servers, and one involving an additional trusted dealer to improve efficiency. All parties are assumed to be semi-honest during the fuzzy matching phase. Finally, we implement Mosaic and evaluate it using real-world trace data from a ride-sharing service. In one scenario, Mosaic servers discovered over a thousand of the most popular ride start locations among 21 thousand users within 30-90 seconds. On the user side, the protocol requires only lightweight computation (as low as 0.14 millisecond) and communication (as low as 9 KB).
papers.authors: Gayathri Garimella, Peihan Miao, Eileen Nolan, Phuoc Van Long Pham, Siddarth Sitaraman

papers.title: Fake-Hiding Deniable Secret Sharing from One-Way Functions
papers.abstract: Deniable secret sharing (DSS), introduced by Canetti et al. (TCC 2025), considers an adversary who coerces or bribes shareholders into revealing their shares. Shareholders are either fakers, who submit fake shares of a target message, or snitches, who reveal their real shares. Fake hiding, the strongest security notion considered in their work, ensures that the adversary cannot tell whether any submitted shares are fake. We focus on their coordinated shareholder-specified setting for threshold DSS, where fakers coordinate and choose the target fake message. When the fakers form a strict majority but remain unqualified to reconstruct the secret, Canetti et al. rule out information-theoretic fake-hiding DSS and give a construction based on indistinguishability obfuscation. In this regime, we construct a DSS scheme with statistical fake hiding and computational privacy from one-way functions alone, and prove that one-way functions are also necessary for such schemes. We further define a property that strengthens fake hiding by guaranteeing deniability even when the fakers' original shares are revealed, and call it strong fake hiding. We show that public-key encryption is necessary and sufficient to construct DSS schemes satisfying this property.
papers.authors: Kengo Sasaki, Yusuke Yoshida, Keisuke Tanaka

papers.title: Do Alice and Bob Dream of the Oracle? Wishful Cryptanalysis
papers.abstract: For two millennia, offense and defense have forged cryptographic security boundaries. Tools automated calculation and search, while humans drove discovery. Foundation models now mark a shift from automated computation to intelligent scientific discovery. Because cryptanalysis rests on exact mathematical definitions and immediately executable truth, it offers a proving ground for autonomous intelligence to move past security reliant on scarce human attention and explore structures beyond human working memory. Unguided models stall between two opposite traps: authority hallucination, where they surrender whenever prior literature declares a route blocked, and reasoning hallucination, where they produce subtle, unverifiable flaws. Closed platforms and generic agent loops further impede sustained open inquiry. We introduce wishful cryptanalysis, a harness-agnostic methodology that pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification against error. Agents first compress reduced-scale theory within provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically. They then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory.
