Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models with minimal human intervention beyond targets and compute, this paradigm yielded novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES. These include breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released alongside an early-preview open-source workbench (agent-framework). Extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era, we envision an Open Oracle, an open and auditable public infrastructure that frees cryptographers to legislate security goals, challenge assumptions, distill theory, and co-design resilient standards.
papers.authors: Guoxiao Liu, Keting Jia, Hongbo Yu, Zongyue Wang, Tianshuo Cong, Junfeng Fan, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang

papers.title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".
papers.authors: Ahaan Dabholkar, Harshvardhan Patel, Michalis Polychronakis, Saurabh Bagchi

papers.title: Suspected Until Inspected: Neuro-Symbolic Detection of Broken Access Control in Server-Side Web Applications
papers.abstract: Broken access control (BAC) has topped the OWASP Top 10 since 2021. Unfortunately, a decade of detectors still leaves a gap on every front. Static analyzers are tied to one language or framework, dynamic testers cover only the endpoints they manage to exercise, and LLM-based auditors leave the final verdict to an error-prone model. In this paper, we design and implement FLINT, a neuro-symbolic framework that detects BAC in server-side web applications without language- or framework-specific rules. Our key insight is to separate the proposal from the verdict -- an LLM may flag any data access as needing a guard, but only a symbolically verified check can clear it. The neural component enumerates every endpoint and distills each, via demand-driven code slicing, into an authorization certificate whose claims are all grounded in cited code. The symbolic component verifies each claimed check through origin tracing and a lattice-based interprocedural dataflow analysis, so that no access is cleared on the model's word. When applied to popular real-world open-source applications, including Gitea, Grafana, and Strapi, FLINT detected 112 zero-day, exploitable BAC vulnerabilities, 30 of them in projects with over 20,000 GitHub stars. We have responsibly disclosed all of them to the developers. Mattermost, for example, has already confirmed our report and is assigning a CVE identifier.
papers.authors: Chengyao Yang, Zifeng Kang, Dongqi Han, Shihong Zou

papers.title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models via Perceptual Image Editing
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.
papers.authors: Haoyang Xu, Christian Iha, Colbren Fujimoto, Yingfei Dong, Rui Ning, Liuwan Zhu

papers.title: Extracting Next Generation Access Control Policies from Natural Language Using LLMs: An Intermediate-Representation Approach with Back-Translation Verification
papers.abstract: Organizations write access-control rules in natural language, but NIST's Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) needs them as a formal policy graph. Large language models (LLMs) can automate this translation, but their output can break the format, add rules the text does not state, or drop conditions. We present NGAC-IR, which follows model-driven engineering (MDE). First, the LLM fills in an intermediate representation (IR), a JSON template that records who may, must or must not do what, on which resource and under which condition; a grammar keeps the output within this template. Second, a compiler that uses no LLM converts the IR into an NGAC policy graph and links each rule to its source sentence. Third, a back-translation check writes each rule in English and asks an LLM whether the source sentence states it. On four public datasets, all outputs could be compiled, compared with 95.5% without the grammar, and 95.7% were faithful to their sentence. NGAC-IR outperforms two published methods on all four datasets: the LLM-based Code4Policy in exact match and faithfulness, and the rule-based extractor of Abdelgawad et al. in rule type. The back-translation check sent 10.5% of sentences to human review and found 26 of the 31 errors. To test enforcement, we deployed the compiled policies in NIST's Policy Machine: they gave the expected decision for all 390 access requests, and the tested obligations were carried out. On one local server with open-weight models, all 714 sentences take about 20 minutes and 0.35 kWh, at zero API cost.
papers.authors: Ayesha Habib, Huixiang Zhang, Waiz Haider

papers.title: Evaluating CNF/SMT Encodings for SAT-Based Differential Cryptanalysis of Lightweight Block Ciphers
papers.abstract: This study evaluates three encoding methods for automated differential cryptanalysis: (1) SMT formulations (using CVC), (2) standard CNF, and (3) size-optimized CNF (via Logic Friday). We assess these using four SAT/SMT solver types: single-core (CryptoMiniSat-v5, CaDiCaL), multi-core (Treengeling), and massively parallel Mallob—novel to cryptanalysis. Encoding-solver combinations are tested on seven lightweight block ciphers representing distinct design philosophies: SPECK-32 and CHAM-64 (ARX structure), SIMON-32 (AND-RX structure), PRESENT, GIFT-128, and MIDORI-64 (4-bit S-box in SPN structure), and LBLOCK (Feistel structure). For each cipher, SAT/SMT instances targeting specific rounds/differential weights were generated, with wall-clock solving time, parallel efficiency, and modeling effort measured. Our results establish criteria for optimal encoding-solver pairings that strike a balance between modeling simplicity and computational performance. Crucially, Mallob emerges as the state-of-the-art framework for large-scale automated differential cryptanalysis.
papers.authors: Marzieh Vahid Dastjerdi, Majid Rahimi, Iman Mirzaali Mazandarani, Sadegh Sadeghi

papers.title: Real Brakedown Performance: A Portable Scalar Baseline for Spielman-Code Polynomial Commitments
papers.abstract: Brakedown-style polynomial commitment schemes encode the rows of a coefficient matrix with a linear-time Spielman code and Merkle-commit the columns. New schemes are typically compared against the unoptimized LCPC and PolyCommit libraries. Conversely, the reported speedups of the AVX-512 encoder SIMD-Spielman over LCPC combine vector arithmetic with portable algorithmic and memory optimizations. We present RBP-LCPC, an optimized implementation of LCPC in portable stable Rust that integrates column-major batched encoding, right-to-left graph evaluation, lazy modular reduction and cache-aware slicing. Its incremental structure isolates the contribution of each optimization. On both x86-64 and AArch64, its compiled hot kernels contain no vector arithmetic. With LCPC's code and prime, its encodings, Merkle roots and proofs match those of LCPC bit-for-bit. On an AMD Zen 5 server with one thread and N = 2^16 to 2^28 coefficients, RBP-LCPC encodes 8.14-9.06x faster than LCPC under its default build configuration. SIMD-Spielman, measured on the same server, remains 1.59-4.44x faster up to N = 2^26. Commit achieves a smaller speedup of 5.21-5.95x over the default LCPC configuration (4.48-5.95x across both default and tuned configurations), because column hashing then accounts for over a third of single-threaded commit time. Prove and verify are 1.83-7.61x and 2.65-5.36x faster than under the default LCPC configuration across thread counts and sizes, and single-threaded PCS setup is 1.31-1.44x faster. The accompanying artifact reproduces all baselines and measurements from fixed source revisions.
papers.authors: Jipeng Zhang

papers.title: Improved GGM Witness-Encryption Bypassing Rank Gap
papers.abstract: Hair and Sahai construct witness encryption in the classical prime-order generic-group model using a designed matrix space with a growing rank gap. We retain their encryption mechanism while replacing the minimum-rank requirement with a lower bound on the min-entropy of $Mr$ for nonzero matrices $M$ that do not permit witness extraction, where $r$ is the short random vector used in encryption. A matrix with substantial concentration has a column factorization from a finite family of short rational patterns. One list of linear forms evaluated at powers of a public random seed preserves all these patterns simultaneously, except with exponentially small probability, and therefore suffices in place of their multiple folded lists. For a quadratic verifier encoding with $N$ Boolean variables, using $t=\lceil\log N\rceil$ forms gives one-bit ciphertexts of $\widetilde O(N^5)$ bits and optimized decryption using $\widetilde O(N^4)$ group queries. For sufficiently large $N$, distinguishing advantage on false instances is at most $N^{-\log N}$ against classical generic adversaries making at most $N^{\log N}$ group queries. Correctness error is $2^{-\Omega(N)}$, simultaneously for all valid witnesses of a ciphertext. At these same security and correctness guarantees, a beneficial reparameterization of Hair--Sahai's deterministic construction gives ciphertexts of $\widetilde O(N^6)$ bits and, with the same decryption optimizations, $\widetilde O(N^5)$ group queries.
papers.authors: Charanjit S. Jutla

papers.title: A Practical Collision for 36-Step SHA-512
papers.abstract: We give a colliding message pair for SHA-512 reduced to 36 steps, starting from the standard initial value. The first such pair was published by Yuan and Yu on 18 November 2026 (ePrint 2026/3005); we found ours independently four days later. The previous practical record had been 35 steps. The attack is not new. It uses the 36-step differential characteristic and the memory-efficient two-block framework of Li et al. (ePrint 2026/1120), whose estimated time complexity is $2^{66.2}$. Our contribution is to make it practical by: (i) counting the degrees of freedom and the uncontrolled conditions more precisely; (ii) re-solving $(A_0, E_4)$ on the fly for each first block, which makes the cost of the first block negligible; and (iii) a meet-in-the-middle lookup on 19 bits of $E_{16}$ whose table fits in the GPU's L2 cache. The collision was found after about 3 hours of wall-clock time on three NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (one RTX 5090 and two RTX PRO 6000), i.e. about 8.9 GPU-hours; Yuan and Yu report a similar expected cost and found their pair on 8,960 CPU cores in 16.9 hours. At the compression-function throughput we measured on the same hardware, this equals about $2^{49.2}$ evaluations of the 36-step compression function. The measured stage-by-stage pass rates agree with the cost model; for example, the step-22 survivors that also satisfy $\delta W_{23}$ number 9, against 9.3 expected. We verified the pair with an independent implementation, and independently re-measured the tail probabilities on $2\cdot 10^{10}$ generated message pairs.
papers.authors: Junhong Huang

papers.title: Coppersmith’s Method for Bivariate Modular Equations: Optimal Small-Root Bounds
papers.abstract: In 1996, Coppersmith established the classical small-root bound for univariate modular equations, which was subsequently proved to be asymptotically optimal within the standard Coppersmith framework. In contrast, a general theoretical characterization of optimal small-root bounds for bivariate modular equations, together with a method for computing them, has remained elusive. The main difficulty is that the additional degrees of freedom introduced by a second variable turn shift selection into a complex combinatorial optimization problem. We prove that, for standard triangular shift constructions in Coppersmith’s method, optimal small-root bounds for bivariate modular equations admit a unified characterization and can be computed effectively. To this end, we introduce a class of geometric objects called quasi-Newton polygons, which provide an exact geometric characterization of these optimal bounds and yield a method for computing them. This result extends the theory of optimal small-root bounds for Coppersmith’s method to the general bivariate setting, marking its first breakthrough beyond the univariate case in three decades.
papers.authors: Zhaopeng Ding, Yanshuo Zhang, Zhaopeng Dai, Ziyang Yan, Ying Chen

papers.title: Chosen-Ciphertext Security for Nested Proxy Re-Encryption with Restricted Key Exposure
papers.abstract: Proxy re-encryption (PRE) allows an authorised proxy to re-encrypt ciphertexts for another recipient without learning their plaintexts. We construct a single-hop PRE scheme with restricted chosen-ciphertext security (rCCA2). For a given honest delegator, an adversary that obtains an outgoing re-encryption key cannot also obtain re-encryptions to corrupted recipients. We revisit the nested encryption of Ivan and Dodis (NDSS 2003) with the encrypted delivery of the inner secret key described by Ateniese et al. (ACM TISSEC 2006). A recipient can recover this key from one authorised delivery and use it to decrypt inner ciphertexts sent to others. Encrypting each inner ciphertext under an independent public key of its intended recipient gives a scheme secure against restricted honest re-encryption attacks (rHRA). To obtain rCCA2, we use CCA2-secure public-key encryption, authenticate source ciphertexts and encrypted inner secret keys with strongly unforgeable signatures, and protect inner ciphertexts with deterministic authenticated encryption during re-encryption. We instantiate rCCA2 using hybrid public-key encryption with ML-KEM, ML-DSA signatures, and AES-SIV, and give key and ciphertext sizes. A packet-level OpenPGP prototype forwards the session key in a separate envelope and verifies decryption of the same encrypted body by the original and forwarding recipients.
papers.authors: Haotian Yin, Jie Zhang

papers.title: Which Masks Are Worth Testing? Key-Dependent Correlation and Symmetry in Lightweight Block Ciphers
papers.abstract: A mask that scores well on average over keys can behave differently on the weakest quarter of keys. Determining which masks differ in this respect can itself require many correlation evaluations. We study both questions. For an 11-round CRAFT differential--linear instance, an alternative output mask increases the measured mean signed correlation by factors of 1.69 to 1.86 over the published reference across four tweak settings. A separate fixed-budget experiment leaves the difference in rejection rates inconclusive. For local linear sections, a measure-preserving relabeling of effective keys certifies when several masks share an absolute-correlation histogram. In a common four-cipher benchmark this reduces elapsed time by factors of 2.85 to 4.94 for an all-equal input mask within individual column types. Sharing between two PRINCE column types gives a further gain even for an all-distinct input. Finally, exhaustive effective-key populations for MIDORI64 and QARMA64 let us measure the cost of choosing among 81 masks from a sample. RMS and lower-quarter scores have disjoint optimal sets in five of six cases. In one QARMA64 case, restricting a 32-key sample to 36 orbit representatives increases mean loss relative to the lower-quarter optimum by 2.66 percentage points. At an equal budget of 2,592 mask--key values, evaluating the 36 representatives on 72 keys instead of all 81 masks on 32 keys reduces mean loss by 4.16 points on that input. A corresponding MIDORI64 comparison gives a 17.52-point reduction.
papers.authors: Alireza Gholizadeh Shahrbejari, Reza Ebrahimi Atani

papers.title: Authority Without Priority: The Revocation Trilemma and the Price of Stablecoin Freezes
papers.abstract: Stablecoin contracts let issuers freeze an address, but a freeze is an ordinary transaction that block producers order like any other, so a transfer submitted after it can still execute first. We define the missing guarantee as $\textit{revocation priority}$: once a restriction is submitted, no prohibited operation submitted later takes effect before it. We prove a trilemma: with revenue-maximizing block producers, no blockchain platform can provide revocation priority together with immediacy, which makes a transfer’s effects usable upon inclusion, and neutrality, which rules out preferential inclusion or ordering for any sender. Ethereum keeps immediacy and neutrality and gives up revocation priority. Using USDT and USDC freezes on Ethereum from 2017 to 2026, we examine how issuers and their targets compete for execution order. In one case, a freeze had long been pending when a transfer submitted after it executed first. The competition has escalated from fee bidding to private submission to execution delegated through intent-based orders. Overall, the issuer pays more for order than its target. These patterns follow from the two sides’ incentives, which we model as a Tullock contest. In equilibrium the issuer outbids its target but cannot buy certainty. Stricter freeze obligations thus strengthen its incentive to integrate into ordering infrastructure, at the expense of neutrality.
papers.authors: Di Wu, Yuman Bai, Shoupeng Ren, Xinyu Zhang, Yiyue Cao, Yuheng Wang, Xuechao Wang, Huan Huo, Wu Wen, Jian Liu

papers.title: TreeOnion: Efficient Private Retrieval of Tree Paths
papers.abstract: Private information retrieval (PIR) lets clients retrieve entries from a public database hosted on a server without revealing which entries are retrieved. Traditionally, the database is assumed to be an array or a key-value store, and the client has the index or keyword of the entry it wishes to retrieve. However, in practice, the database can have a more complex structure. An important example is when the database is organized as a tree, and the client wants to retrieve all nodes along a root-to-leaf path. Notably, retrieving a Merkle proof is a natural instance of this problem, as is done in applications such as certificate transparency and blockchain systems. We present TreeOnion, a single-server scheme that allows clients to privately retrieve a path of nodes from a public database organized as a tree. For small node sizes, the communication and computation costs of TreeOnion are comparable to the costs of privately retrieving a single node from the same database. Compared with alternate approaches, TreeOnion is strictly better in both communication and computation, and is at least an order of magnitude better in one of the two metrics.
papers.authors: Pranav Shriram Arunachalaramanan, Chenyang Zhang, Yue Chen, Ling Ren

papers.title: AnimalFarm: Auditing the Generation and Detection of Hateful Images Featuring Anthropomorphic Characters
papers.abstract: Anthropomorphic non-human characters have long been used to convey hateful messages targeting human groups, from Nazi-era propaganda to recent AI-generated imagery on social media. However, the safety risks posed by such imagery remain largely unexplored. We thus conduct the first systematic study of hateful image generation and detection involving anthropomorphic non-human characters. We construct a benchmark from conservatively screened source scenes, covering five character types and three image generation tasks: text-to-image generation, image editing, and conversational image generation. Across 14,250 scheduled queries, image generation systems produce images for 92.1\% of queries, of which 95.9\% contain hateful content. We further collect 4,370 hateful images and evaluate five popular hateful-content detectors. Even the strongest detector, GPT-5.5, identifies only 73.9\% of hateful images, while most detect fewer than 58\%. Our analysis reveals that existing detectors often misclassify hateful images as benign when their main subjects are non-human characters. We explore two effective mitigation approaches: a training-free pipeline that maps non-human characters back to human representations before classification and a detector fine-tuned for this type of hateful content. These approaches achieve F1 scores of 0.962 and 0.979, respectively. Our findings expose significant safety gaps in both image generation and hateful-content detection. Disclaimer: This paper contains hateful text and imagery.
papers.authors: Junjie Chu, Ye Leng, Mingjie Li, Yiting Qu, Michael Backes, Yun Shen, Yang Zhang

papers.title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed. Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.
papers.authors: Nathan Nour Houlamy, Mattia Favretto, Earlence Fernandes, Mauro Conti

papers.title: Too Fast to Doubt? Skipping Reasoning Leaves Jev-like Models Vulnerable
papers.abstract: Fast decision models offer low-latency actions and explicit confidence estimates. We audit four state-of-the-art decision models on 1,440 paired synthetic browser tasks, injecting false conclusions or evidence interpretations through external comments. Across models, clean accuracy averages 91.0%, yet two-shot attack success reaches 81.2%. Mean expected calibration error rises from 2.6% on clean inputs to 36.7% under conclusion poisoning and 36.1% under evidence poisoning. Clean accuracy and calibration therefore do not ensure reliable decisions under injection. We further compare GPT-6 Luna and Luna Decisions, which share the same base model, on 48 matched tasks. With a chain of thought averaging fewer than 30 reasoning tokens per response, low-effort GPT-6 Luna answers 95.83% of poisoned inputs correctly, versus 38.54% for native Luna Decisions, while mean selected-generation latency increases from 0.29 to 1.94 seconds. These results expose a sharp latency-robustness trade-off: skipping reasoning for sub-second speed leaves fast decision models substantially more vulnerable to deceptive web content.
papers.authors: Yue Li, Hao Wu, Zenan Fu, Xiao Li, Fengyuan Xu, Sheng Zhong

papers.title: Isonomy: Isolating Every Request from Timing Side Channels at Nearly Full-Sharing Throughput in Multi-Instance LLM Prefill
papers.abstract: Many long prompts share a prefix, and reusing its cached keys and values saves prefill computation. A cache hit, however, makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix, so providers share the cache only within an account. Under least privilege, even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other requests' prompts in the same account. This matters because agents send unreviewed requests carrying private data, resellers pool users behind one account, and creden-tials can be stolen. Isonomy therefore isolates each request by default and lets requests opt into explicit sharing groups. Rather than give up reuse, it keeps one cache shared across accounts and hides only hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group. We target deployments where clients cannot observe one another's load, because there it suffices to hide these hits in the request's own timing. On three commercial APIs, our listeners could not distinguish added prefill work from a short request beyond measurement noise. Built on vLLM, Isonomy's gateway applies the deployment's routing rule to load and visible cache entries only, which yields the instance where the request would run if hidden hits missed. On that instance, the prediction mode estimates when the first token would be ready from the queue and the visible prefix, and gates its release. The execution mode instead reserves the work a hidden hit skips and fills it with other requests' prompts where possible. In direct-probe tests on two, four, and eight instances with every request isolated, both modes kept the upper bound on a probe's advantage within measure-ment noise at both prefix lengths. At saturation, the prediction mode retains 0.98 of unprotected sharing's throughput on two workloads with account labels, whereas isolation by account retains 0.95, or 0.80 where more reuse crosses accounts.
papers.authors: Bowen Sun, Chaowei Xiao

papers.title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
papers.abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.
papers.authors: Feng Huang, Qiang Huang, Yue Gao, Mei Zhang, Bin Liu, Lihua Ju, Xinhao Wei, Yongfeng Huang, Yu Qing, Yunqi Zhang

papers.title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
papers.abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.
papers.authors: Ali Yousefi, Nikos Komninos, Hafizul Asad

papers.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.
papers.authors: Chong Tian, Yu Wang, Steve Liu, Qirong Ho, Xiuying Chen

papers.title: "More Than You Expect!": Leakage-Abuse Attacks on Encrypted Vector Search
papers.abstract: Vector databases support semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embeddings, queries, and record labels may contain sensitive information. Although encrypted vector search protects these contents, some schemes expose records retrieved together across queries. We identify semantic neighborhood leakage, whereby co-retrieval relationships derived from access patterns reveal semantic categories of encrypted records and queries. We present SAGE (Semantic Access-pattern Graph Exploitation), a passive, persistent leakage-abuse attack that infers record labels and query categories from access patterns. SAGE builds a weighted co-retrieval graph and offers two variants requiring different auxiliary knowledge. SAGE-Dist matches anonymous spectral groups to semantic categories using estimated class proportions and refines labels via optimal transport, without known record labels. SAGE-Known combines graph-based label propagation with spectral-group anchor voting using a small set of known labels. We evaluate SAGE on four text and image datasets. With 1% known record labels, SAGE-Known achieves up to 84.3% mean record-label accuracy and outperforms the strongest corresponding baselines on all four datasets. With only estimated class proportions, SAGE-Dist achieves 66.9% record-label accuracy and 68.1% query-category accuracy on AG News, exceeding the strongest corresponding baselines by 21.8 and 41.9 percentage points, respectively, though performance varies across datasets. Experiments with a real-world DCPE implementation (Fuchsbauer et al., SCN'22) show that semantic leakage persists under encrypted approximate retrieval. These findings expose privacy risks even when vector contents remain protected.
papers.authors: Yang Zhang, Ruiqi He, Xiaoqian Sun, Siyi Lv, Zheli Liu

papers.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
papers.abstract: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.
papers.authors: Sandeep Dhuri

papers.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.
papers.authors: Sean Maxwell

papers.title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
papers.abstract: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.
papers.authors: Zibin Lin, Taotao Wang, Shengli Zhang

papers.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.
papers.authors: Minda Zhao, Yue Zhang, Mengyu Wang

papers.title: Mjolnir: Finding and Reproducing Vulnerabilities in Root-of-Trust Firmware and RTL with Project-Grounded Agents
papers.abstract: A root of trust (RoT) anchors secure boot and attestation for the system above it, so a bug in RoT firmware or hardware undermines every layer that trusts it. LLM agents now find real vulnerabilities in general-purpose software, but RoT code presents two challenges. First, many security-relevant bugs depend on project-specific trust boundaries and fault-injection countermeasures rather than generic vulnerability patterns, and may cause no crash. Second, without RoT hardware, agents must exercise RoT inputs through the project's own hardware model, mocks, or RTL testbenches. We present Mjolnir, an agentic pipeline that supplies each project's threat model and design conventions to discovery and skeptical review agents, and reproduces surviving findings as proof-of-concept tests in the project's own toolchain. We evaluate Mjolnir on six firmware and RTL targets in Caliptra, OpenTitan, and OpenPRoT. On Caliptra's runtime firmware, it reaches 83.3%-100% precision across three models under blind expert labeling, including 100% on Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 66.7%-78.6% for four single-agent baselines on the same model. On 34 known security-relevant bugs in Caliptra's core firmware fixed after the models' training cutoffs, it finds 10 with Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 7 for the best baseline, and 17 with Gemini 4 Argon versus 12. Across our evaluation scans, maintainers have confirmed 64 of Mjolnir's findings as previously unknown security-relevant bugs: 37 across three models on Caliptra's runtime firmware and 27 across single scans of the other five targets.
papers.authors: Collin MacDonald, Carl Lundin, Stephen Herwig, Miguel Osorio, Timothy Trippel

papers.title: Proactive Defense Benchmark against Deepfake Generation
papers.abstract: Despite the proliferation of proactive defenses against deepfakes, the lack of a unified evaluation protocol precludes fair comparison and masks critical vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically assesses disruption, robustness, and transferability encompassing pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Our extensive analysis reveals that fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes, often leading to conflicting interpretations when relied upon individually. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental trade-off where peak white-box performance signals overfitting, and we introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct generator-induced identity bias. By exposing these blind spots, we establish a rigorous standard to guide the development of genuinely generalizable protections. Project page is available at: https://proactivedefensebenchmark.github.io/
papers.authors: Joonhyuk Baek, Wonjune Seo, Jae-yun Kim, Saerom Park, Hoki Kim

papers.title: Railroads as Cyber-Physical Systems: Cybersecurity Implications of Increasing Automation -- Threats, Consequences, and Operational Resilience
papers.abstract: Objectives: Rail automation improves train protection, traffic management, inspection, and operational efficiency but increases dependence on software, communications, remote access, and external providers. This paper examines its impact on railroad cyber-physical system security and operational resilience. Methods: A narrative review synthesizes railroad automation literature, OT security guidance, FRA and TSA materials, and documented rail cyber incidents. Automation functions are mapped to exposed assets, attack vectors, and operational consequences, focusing on signalling, communications, onboard systems, remote access, and human oversight. Findings: Automation shifts rail risks from isolated mechanical failures toward interconnected cyber-physical dependencies. Key vulnerabilities involve train detection, positioning, signalling, grade crossings, remote diagnostics, vendor access, and AI-enabled monitoring. Cyber incidents can cause operational disruption, supply-chain impacts, and national-security risks, even when fail-safe mechanisms prevent catastrophic outcomes. Novelty: The paper introduces a rail-specific taxonomy connecting automation functions, cyberattack pathways, operational consequences, and resilience requirements, framing cybersecurity as an operational rather than purely IT concern. Practical Applications: The framework supports security-by-design procurement, IT/OT segmentation, secure remote access and software updates, degraded-mode planning, trusted recovery, and human oversight. Operators and regulators can use it to assess automation deployments and mitigate cyber risks.
papers.authors: Syed Owais Athar, Mohsin Kamal, Aemal Khattak, Muhammad Naveed Aman

papers.title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Conventional indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks hijack an LLM agent's workflow through malicious instructions embedded in retrieved external content. The growing adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) exposes another attack surface: tool descriptions supplied by third-party MCP servers. Attackers can manipulate this metadata to induce malicious argument generation during tool calls. The challenge is to ensure that the modified descriptions still appear benign to both LLMs and users. Existing IPI attacks, however, struggle to achieve both high attack success and low detectability in this setting. To address this challenge, we propose GRAFT, an LLM-based optimization method for crafting adversarial tool descriptions. Specifically, GRAFT uses a masking mechanism to identify argument-relevant token positions for targeted injection. It then iteratively refines candidate descriptions using dynamic mutation strategies proposed by an LLM, guided by the agent's tool choices and generated arguments. We evaluate GRAFT on three public datasets against several attack baselines. The results show that GRAFT achieves higher attack success while maintaining low detection rates across five filter-based defenses. It also bypasses several existing IPI defenses. Even under an adaptive defense trained on GRAFT-generated injections, GRAFT remains more effective than the baselines.
papers.authors: Shih-Chieh Dai, Xinyu Sun, Haichuan Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhong, Guanhong Tao

papers.title: Exploring Early Vulnerability Analysis via Automatic Identification of Vulnerability-Introducing Commits
papers.abstract: Developing effective vulnerability analysis techniques requires high-quality datasets that capture how vulnerabilities appear and evolve in real software codebase. Existing datasets, however, typically label as vulnerable only the code immediately preceding vulnerability-fixing commits (VFCs), overlooking the earlier versions in which vulnerabilities were first introduced and subsequently evolved. This practice limits both dataset coverage and our understanding of whether current detectors can identify vulnerabilities during their early, latent stages. In this paper, we present three manually annotated datasets of vulnerability-introducing commits (VICs) based on recent CVEs and widely used open-source projects. We further propose D-SZZ, a data state-aware VIC identification framework that analyzes security-fixing patterns and performs vulnerability scope slicing to recover the semantics implied by a fix. Experimental results demonstrate that D-SZZ outperforms existing SZZ and LLM-based baselines in identifying VICs. In addition, we evaluate six representative vulnerability detectors and find that models trained only on pre-VFC code struggle with original vulnerabilities, while incorporating early-stage samples improves detection performance. We also show that D-SZZ improves downstream vulnerable-version identification, and use it to uncover 16 inaccurate affected-version records in the NVD, all of which were officially confirmed and updated.
papers.authors: Weiliang Qi, Shu Wang, Youpeng Li, Ela Guo, Xinda Wang

papers.title: Enhancing Metaverse Security using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework
papers.abstract: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.
papers.authors: Esha Kuppanda, Shalaka Mahadik, Pranav M. Pawar, Mithun Mukherjee, Raja Muthalagu

papers.title: A Unified Framework for Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection and Alert Correlation
papers.abstract: A Security Operations Center (SOC) plays a critical role in detecting, correlating, and responding to modern cyber threats. However, SOCs continue to face challenges related to alert overload, fragmented detection capabilities, and limited collaboration between analysts and automated systems. These issues often result in delayed incident response, analyst fatigue, and an increased risk of overlooking sophisticated, multi-stage attacks that unfold gradually across different layers of the network. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a unified framework for network traffic classification and alert correlation through the use of signature rules, machine learning, and sequential pattern mining algorithms. The solution was evaluated in a controlled testbed environment emulating realistic, multi-stage attack scenarios, including malware exploitation, lateral movement, reconnaissance, and data exfiltration. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in detecting and correlating complex attack behaviors, while providing analysts with actionable insights in line with a human-in-the-loop approach to SOC operations.
papers.authors: Miguel Silva, João Vitorino, Daniela Pinto, Eva Maia, Ivone Amorim, Isabel Praça

papers.title: BinXSight: Fast Binary Program Summarization via Hierarchical Modular Decomposition
papers.abstract: Binary code summarization (BCS) is crucial in fields such as cybersecurity. Particularly, program-level BCS can quickly provide a comprehensive overview of an entire stripped binary without in-depth manual reverse engineering. However, a binary often contains numerous functions with complex interactions, making it challenging to extract its functionality efficiently. Moreover, existing methods focus solely on function-level without considering contextual information, limiting their applicability to program-level analysis. Towards comprehensive and fast program-level BCS, we propose BinXSight, an LLM-powered framework based on hierarchical modular decomposition. Specifically, we first propose binary graph, a new data structure composed of four graphs, to comprehensively represent a binary. Then, based on the binary graph, we hierarchically decompose functions into modules and select the most significant ones. Finally, BinXSight generates a program-level summary from these module summaries. We evaluate BinXSight on stripped binaries across various sizes, fields, platforms, and architectures. Results show that BinXSight outperforms baselines by 23.18% to 46.99%, and summarizes a binary with about 3K functions in 24.3 seconds on average. In addition, a user study with 27 experts shows that BinXSight's high-quality summaries help users quickly understand the whole binary. Our case analysis on recent real-world malware further demonstrates its practical utility.
papers.authors: Zhijie Liu, Zhipeng Xue, Zhipeng Gao, Pengfei Jing, Zixiong Qin, Sen Nie, Shi Wu, Liang Feng Zhang, Yutian Tang

papers.title: Adaptively Secure Batched IBE from LWE
papers.abstract: We construct the first adaptively secure (epoch-based) batched identity-based encryption (BIBE) scheme from the learning with errors (LWE) assumption in the plain model. In addition to achieving adaptive security, we obtain significant efficiency improvements over existing lattice-based constructions. The public parameters, batch keys, and ciphertexts have sizes independent of the batch size, and setup requires no prescribed batch-size bound, unlike other lattice-based constructions. The authority generates batch keys from short, publicly computable digests. Encryption time is independent of the batch size, while decrypting an entire batch takes time linear in its size, including public preprocessing. We first give a plain-model generic construction from laconic function evaluation and tagged one-key functional encryption. Building on this generic construction, we then exploit the linear structure of laconic encryption to obtain a more efficient algebraic construction using tagged inner-product functional encryption. Using receiver non-committing encryption, we further obtain an adaptively secure variant in the random oracle model that avoids noise flooding in the laconic encryption component in our plain-model construction and permits a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio for that component. Finally, we give a generic transformation from BIBE to threshold BIBE using threshold fully homomorphic encryption. The transformation preserves adaptive security against static corruptions and requires only one round of communication for batch-key generation after a trusted setup.
papers.authors: Jiaqi Cheng, Pratish Datta

papers.title: Post-Quantum Adaptive Multiparty NIKE
papers.abstract: Non-interactive key exchange (NIKE) is a fundamental cryptographic primitive that enables a group of users to establish a shared secret key without any interaction. Constructing multiparty NIKE for groups larger than three has proven notoriously difficult, with all known constructions requiring indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) or multilinear maps. A major challenge in this area is achieving adaptive security, where the adversary chooses the target set of users after observing the system's public keys and can dynamically corrupt honest users, without incurring a sub-exponential loss in the security reduction. The only known construction up to this point has been that of Koppula, Waters, and Zhandry (TCC 2022), which relied on polynomially secure iO and a q-type assumption over pairing-free groups. In this work, we present the first adaptively secure multiparty NIKE schemes from standard, static, and post-quantum polynomial assumptions. More broadly, we develop new techniques that allow us to construct adaptive multiparty NIKE from polynomially secure iO and either of Ring LWE, DDH or even cryptographic group actions. Specifically, we introduce a new abstraction called Key-Accumulative PRFs (KA-PRFs), which captures the structure common to all of the aforementioned algebraic assumptions, and construct our NIKE scheme from polynomially secure KA-PRFs and polynomially secure iO. Our scheme supports an unbounded number of honest and malicious users, where the party size and the number of dynamic corruptions are fixed at setup.
papers.authors: Shafik Nassar, Brent Waters

papers.title: Shifting Dark Matter: Two-Query Key Recovery on a Post-Quantum OPRF
papers.abstract: At the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, Aranha et al. proposed a maliciously secure post-quantum oblivious pseudorandom function (OPRF) from Crypto Dark Matter. Its strong PRF is $F_k(x) = B \cdot \mathrm{vec}(k \cdot \mathrm{elt}(E(x))) \bmod 3$, where the key $k \in \mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ multiplies a systematic encoding $E(x)$. In this paper, we show that a client that follows the protocol recovers the key from two chosen queries. Multiplication by $\alpha^{-2}$ commutes with the key multiplication and acts on the polynomial basis as a shift, up to a correction from two bits. We prove that input pairs whose encodings differ by the factor $\alpha^2$ correspond to the binary solutions of six linear systems over $\mathbb{F}_3$. For the proposed parameters, we found such a pair in 146 seconds. After a guess of two bits, the outputs give a full-weight ternary syndrome decoding instance whose 164 equations almost always determine the other 254 bits of $k \cdot \mathrm{elt}(E(x))$. Counting memory in list elements, we estimate time and memory complexities of $2^{67.3}$ and $2^{51.8}$, or $2^{69.9}$ and $2^{33.3}$, both far below the claimed 128-bit security. For a 64-bit security target, the whole attack recovered the key with $2^{34.39}$ operations, matching our cost model. A dense field modulus does not prevent the attack. For 128-bit inputs, a non-systematic code of length at least 160 heuristically removes such pairs, and a public $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear mixing of the output removes the linear structure of the key recovery.
papers.authors: Hanbeom Shin, Insung Kim, Seokhie Hong, Dongjae Lee

papers.title: Fuzzy Private Set Intersection with Large Databases via Locality-Sensitive Hashing
papers.abstract: Many query workloads require privacy-preserving similarity joins: parties, each holding a private database, may want to learn which of their records are close to records in the other party's database under a distance metric, without leaking anything beyond this information. Fuzzy private set intersection (fuzzy PSI) is a cryptographic primitive that addresses this problem. In this setting, a client and a server hold sets $X$ and $Y$, respectively, and the client learns the subset of points in $X$ that are "close" to points in $Y$. Fuzzy PSI has many use cases, including biometric authentication, password breach monitoring, contact tracing, regional-outbreak monitoring, and machine-learning label matching. Despite growing interest in fuzzy PSI, many existing schemes still require communication costs and client computation linear in the server's set size $|Y|$. Consequently, these protocols do not scale well to the unbalanced setting, where $|X| \ll |Y|$, as is common in many client-to-server applications. In this work, we propose an efficient fuzzy PSI protocol for the unbalanced setting. At its core is a fuzzy probabilistic data structure (fuzzy PDS), which generalizes prior work by combining locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) with compact filters, enabling tunable false-positive and false-negative rates while ensuring efficient queries. Building on techniques from unbalanced PSI, we combine oblivious pseudorandom functions and private information retrieval with our fuzzy PDS to support private and communication-efficient approximate matching. We instantiate the protocol with an LSH for the $L_2$ metric and evaluate it on two real-world workloads: regional-outbreak monitoring and machine-learning label matching. Our results show significant reductions in communication and runtime compared with state-of-the-art fuzzy PSI schemes, with gains that increase as the server database size $|Y|$ grows.
papers.authors: Francesca Falzon, Andreas Athanasiou, Laura Hetz, Tjitske Ollie Koster, Evangelia Anna Markatou

papers.title: LaTSEC: Lattice-Based Threshold Signatures with Native Non-Interactive Identifiable Abort and Compact Per-Party Storage
papers.abstract: We present $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$, a three-round lattice-based threshold signature scheme with native non-interactive identifiable abort. Each party holds one small-norm signing share and is associated with one public abort key, against which its partial signature is verified directly, without zero-knowledge proofs or an additional interactive protocol. Prior lattice-based threshold signatures that identify misbehaving parties rely on one of three mechanisms: zero-knowledge proofs, an additional interactive protocol, or an everywhere-short secret sharing scheme in which each party holds multiple signing shares, each with its own public abort key. Compared with schemes that use the third mechanism, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ substantially reduces per-party storage. The construction uses $\mathsf{SEC}$, a recent ramp everywhere-short secret sharing scheme based on lossless expanders that gives each party a single short share. We prove correctness, identifiable-abort security, and threshold unforgeability under the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ and $\mathsf{MSIS}$ assumptions. The unforgeability proof introduces the Repeated-$\boldsymbol{A}$ Matrix Hint-MLWE problem, a new variant of $\mathsf{MLWE}$ with hints that captures the complete tuple of correlated public abort keys. We rigorously prove that this new variant admits a reduction from the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ problem. For 60 parties at 128-bit security, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ tolerates up to 6 corrupted parties, and, empirically, a randomly chosen set of at least 46 parties can sign with probability at least 0.99. Each party holds one signing share of about 14.3 KiB and is associated with one 24-KiB public abort key.
papers.authors: Muhammad Arzaki, Muhammed F. Esgin, Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, Amin Sakzad, Ron Steinfeld

papers.title: On the Hardness of LWE with Trapdoor Hints and Applications to Fuzzy Cryptography
papers.abstract: Learning with Errors (LWE) and its variants have revolutionized modern cryptography, enabling a wide range of applications that previously seemed out of reach. In recent years, there has been growing interest in hinted variants of LWE, in which the adversary receives carefully structured side information, and these assumptions have further expanded the cryptographic toolkit. In this work, we study a natural hinted LWE assumption that we call LWE with Trapdoor Hints. Concretely, we consider the hardness of distinguishing an LWE sample $(\mathbf{A},\, \mathbf{s}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{e}^{\mathsf{T}} \bmod q)$ from uniform even in the presence of a full-rank homogeneous trapdoor $\mathbf{T}$ for $\mathbf{A}$. We show that when the error $\mathbf{e}$ is drawn from a Gaussian distribution that is only slightly wider than the decoding radius associated with $\mathbf{T}$, this problem remains hard under the standard LWE assumption. We then present two compelling applications of this problem that were previously out of reach: First, we construct the first Euclidean-ball obfuscator from LWE satisfying distributional virtual black-box security. Our construction achieves the functional preserving property, reusability, and distributional VBB security, assuming the obfuscated inputs are drawn from a suitable LWE-compatible distribution such as a discrete Gaussian. To the best of our knowledge, such a notion was not previously known even assuming indistinguishability obfuscation. As a byproduct, we resolve the open question posed by Fuller, Meng, and Reyzin (Asiacrypt 2013) concerning using lattice trapdoors to construct computational fuzzy extractors supporting the Euclidean metric and with drastically larger error tolerance. Second, we introduce a new primitive that we call Threshold Difference Revealing Encryption (TDRE), which can be viewed as a public-key, two-input analogue of fuzzy extractors. Standard fuzzy extractors are highly effective for fuzzy authentication, but they are fundamentally asymmetric and do not directly support the task of comparing two independently encoded, hidden biometrics. We believe that TDRE can help fill this important conceptual gap in current techniques for fuzzy cryptography.
papers.authors: Divesh Aggarwal, Aayush Jain, Huijia Lin, Yuetian Wu

papers.title: BOCCHI: Compact Blind SNARK via Malformation-Tolerant Ciphertext Aggregation
papers.abstract: Blind SNARKs combine fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) with cryptographic proofs to enable verifiable computation over encrypted data, and can substantially outperform SNARK-over-FHE approaches in efficiency. However, ciphertext openings in existing constructions can inflate proofs to tens or hundreds of megabytes. We present BOCCHI, a compact and efficient blind SNARK that addresses this bottleneck by committing to ciphertexts natively and opening them through a few aggregates. To establish soundness even for malformed ciphertexts, we introduce canonical binding and a lightweight noise filter that achieves it with optimal error, tools that may be of independent interest. We further formulate this transformation as a Commit–Aggregate–Check (CAC) compiler and show its effectiveness on two systems with different PIOPs (GKR and Fractal). At $2^{22}$ constraints, BOCCHI produces a 6.57 MB proof in 115.3 seconds, 9.3× smaller and 2.54× faster than Phalanx. Its proof is the smallest among five baselines. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/BOCCHI-Artifacts.
papers.authors: Ye Yu, Kexi Huang

papers.title: Hardware/Software Co-Design of ML-DSA with Random Delay Insertion Against Correlation Power Analysis
papers.abstract: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) recently led to the standardization of the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA). Standard software implementations of ML-DSA on embedded devices are exposed to physical side-channel attacks, since the power consumption of the circuit depends on the processed secret data and allows key recovery via Correlation Power Analysis (CPA). In addition, protecting these implementations in software introduces large latency overheads. In this paper, the physical vulnerability of ML-DSA is considered focusing the study on embedded microcontroller and System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms. The computational cost of software countermeasures, validated via Test Vector Leakage Assessment (TVLA), is evaluated on both architectures. An Hardware/Software co-design implemented on a Zynq-7000 SoC is then proposed to overcome the software execution bottleneck. The vulnerable pointwise Montgomery multiplication is offloaded to an Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI4-Full) hardware accelerator that integrates a 16-bit Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) for Random Delay Insertion (RDI), preventing CPA trace alignment. Experimental results demonstrate a 13.4× speedup over the software-protected SoC implementation. The proposed architecture reduces the protected signing latency to 42.80 ms, achieving an execution time close to the 40.64 ms of the unprotected software implementation, while the dynamic power dissipated by the hardware accelerator in the programmable logic is limited to 33 mW.
papers.authors: Salvatore Coppa, Ettore Napoli

papers.title: A Transparent Post-Quantum Zero-Knowledge Argument for R1CS
papers.abstract: We construct a transparent, post-quantum zero-knowledge argument of knowledge for R1CS. Satisfiability of $n$ constraints is reduced by two masked sumchecks to linear claims on a committed short vector; every field element the prover reveals is uniform. The witness is committed row-wise with Module-SIS (Ajtai) commitments; evaluation claims are proven by folding the rows with monomial challenges, whose differences have short scaled inverses, so that the extraction norm grows only singly exponentially in the folding depth. The row commitments and partial evaluations are moved into the witness of a LaBRADOR proof and replaced by two short outer commitments, so the proof has size polylogarithmic in $n$. The verifier runs in time $\tilde O(\sqrt n)\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)$ plus $T_\mathrm{circ}$, the time to evaluate the multilinear extensions of the constraint matrices, which we bound for data-parallel circuits. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness of the interactive protocol, and classical zero-knowledge in the programmable random-oracle model, and give parameters from a Core-SVP estimate. The concrete verifier cost at $n=2^{20}$ exceeds that of checking the circuit directly; the gain is asymptotic. Soundness of the Fiat--Shamir compiled protocol and a quantum-oracle zero-knowledge bound are not proven.
papers.authors: Vu Hung Tung

papers.title: A Key Recovery Attack on TRIKE Based on Decoding Failures
papers.abstract: TRIKE is a code-based Key Encapsulation Mechanism submitted to the Next-Generation Commercial Cryptographic algorithms (NGCC) standardization program currently run in People's Republic of China. TRIKE, similarly to other Quasi Cyclic Moderate Density Parity Check (QC-MDPC) code-based KEMs such as BIKE, is built with a decryption procedure which recovers a sparse error vector (i.e., the message) given its syndrome (i.e., the ciphertext) through a secret sparse parity-check matrix, employing an iterative bit-flipping decoder. Differently from BIKE, TRIKE employs a QC-MDPC matrix with a different structure, allowing them to improve the decoding, and hence the decryption, time. In order to guarantee IND-CCA security, the code length is chosen in order to reduce the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) below $2^{-\lambda}$, where $\lambda$ is the bit security level; such a DFR is estimated with extrapolation techniques. In this work, we show that the QC-MDPC codes employed in TRIKE are affected by the so-called near codewords phenomenon. We provide a lower bound on the DFR given by such near codewords, showing that the DFR of TRIKE is significantly higher than the required value for all parameter sets. This alone constitutes a breach of IND-CCA security requirements. We propose a key recovery attack based on near codeword-induced decoding failures. For NGCC security level $1$, $\lambda=128$, the attack requires less than $2^{80}$ (random) ciphertexts and lowers the hardness of the static key recovery step down to $2^{65.52}$ bit operations. We validate our attack strategy and complexity estimation on a toy parameter set with extrapolated DFR below $2^{-80}$, recovering the secret key with $2^{29.50}$ decryption queries.
papers.authors: Alessandro Annechini, Alessandro Barenghi, Gerardo Pelosi

papers.title: Recovering HQC Secret Key from Distance Spectrum using Side-Channel Attack
papers.abstract: HQC is a code-based key encapsulation mechanism selected for standardiza- tion by NIST. It uses sparse secret vectors in a quasi-cyclic structure, where GJS-style attacks can exploit correlations between private syndrome weight and the secret-key distance spectrum. However, HQC decapsulation does not directly manipulate any syndrome, leaving open whether any such attack could be performed in practice. In this work, we present the first practical end-to-end side-channel attack against HQC that recovers the secret key through error-weight leakage and distance-spectrum reconstruction. We identify two sources of leakage in the Reed–Muller decoder under different attacker capabilities. In a chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA), we exploit the ExpandAndSum function by imposing a zero message, whereas in a known-ciphertext attack (KCA), we target the FindPeaks function without modifying the legitimate encapsulation procedure. We provide a theoretical characterization of the Hadamard coefficients manipulated by FindPeaks, establishing a direct relationship between the highest peak and the error weight under a sufficient decoding condition, while showing that the remaining coefficients also depend on the error pattern. We develop profiled side-channel attacks to estimate the error weight and construct a soft distance spectrum of the secret key. To recover the key from imperfect in- formation, we introduce a simulated-annealing reconstruction algorithm that, in simulations, reduces the number of required error-weight observations by approxi- mately 5.8× compared with the state-of-the-art SSV26 method, with substantially lower reconstruction times. Our experiments on an ARM Cortex-M4 implementation of HQC-1 demonstrate end-to-end secret-key recovery in both attack settings. In the CCA setting, our algorithm achieves a 93.5% success rate with 40 000 decapsulation traces, compared to 200 000 traces for SSV26, and recovers the secret key in all 200 trials with 100 000 traces. Most notably, in the more restrictive KCA setting, our approach recovers the secret key in all 200 trials using 1 000 000 traces, whereas the reconstruction algorithm from SSV26 fails to recover the key in any of the 200 trials, even with 1 300 000 traces.
papers.authors: Magali Salom, Angélique Lopez, Valentin Vasseur, Gabriel Zaid

papers.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
papers.abstract: Remark. This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle $\mathcal{O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{\mathcal{O}}=\mathsf{BQP}^{\mathcal{O}}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathcal{O}} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{\mathcal{O}} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{\mathcal{O}} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{\mathcal{O}}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{\mathcal{O}},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In more detail, we show that there exists a classical oracle $\mathcal{O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{\mathcal{O}} = \mathsf{BQP}^{\mathcal{O}} =\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathcal{O}}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{\mathcal{O}}$ but the following primitives exist relative to $\mathcal{O}$, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025). (1) Pseudorandom states (PRS) with classical keys. (2) Pseudorandom functions (PRF) with (copy-protected) quantum secret keys, and thus also pseudorandom unitaries (PRU) with quantum secret keys, (3) Public-key encryption (PKE) with a (copy-protected) quantum decryption key, classical public keys and ciphertexts, (4) Signature schemes with quantum signing keys and either classical verification keys and quantum signatures or quantum verification keys and classical signatures, (5) Collusion-resistant public-key quantum money (PKQM) with classical verification keys.
papers.authors: Alper Cakan

papers.title: Concretely Efficient Byzantine Agreement and Interactive Consistency for Honest Majority
papers.abstract: We consider two of the main notions of round-efficient Byzantine agreement (BA): expected constant rounds and early stopping. Randomized protocols can terminate in an expected constant number of rounds, while early-stopping protocols terminate in a number of rounds that depends only on the actual number $f\le t$ of corrupted parties. Recent works achieve both guarantees at once, but at a high concrete cost: assuming PKI, for the optimal threshold $t<n/2$, the previous protocol with the smallest expected round complexity needs $37$ rounds in expectation and $15f+29$ in the worst case. In this work, we present a BA protocol for $t<n/2$, secure against an adaptive adversary assuming a PKI, that terminates in $18$ rounds in expectation and in at most $8f+18$ rounds in the worst case. Moreover, our protocol has the following optimistic feature: if no party is corrupted and all inputs agree, every party outputs after a single round. Our protocol is natively multi-valued and does not rely on random oracles. At the core of our result is a new randomized BA protocol in which a successful leader election leads to agreement within the same phase. We extend our results to Byzantine broadcast, obtaining a protocol that has $19$ rounds in expectation and $8f+19$ in the worst case, and to interactive consistency (IC), retaining the same round complexity while providing an optimistic fast path in which all parties output after only 2 rounds when everyone is honest. We do so by directly parallelizing our BB protocol, instead of using a generic IC compiler, for which, at $t<n/2$, the best known bounds are more than $4000$ rounds in expectation and $184f+730$ in the worst case.
papers.authors: Michele Ciampi, Pouyan Forghani, Yun Lu, Vassilis Zikas

papers.title: Anonymous C2PA: Feasibility of Large-Scale Anonymous Image Provenance
papers.abstract: High-quality AI-generated images are easy to create and near-indistinguishable from real photos, heightening the need to reliably establish image authenticity. The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) has developed a technical standard under which cameras and editing software cryptographically sign the images they create, along with metadata and edit history. The standard is widely deployed in products by Google, Sony, Adobe, and others. However, C2PA offers no anonymity for signers. Signed images can be linked to a specific device or person, creating serious surveillance risks. C2PA also lacks formal security definitions, making it difficult for other systems to build on it with provable guarantees.
