We formalize C2PA v2.5, and then we derive and formalize security and privacy properties desirable for an ideal anonymous image provenance system. Our primary building block for formalization is ring signatures, which let users sign on behalf of a group while staying anonymous within it. We give a new construction of shrinkable ring signatures that supports arbitrary subrings; this can be used to revoke compromised keys by "shrinking'' these keys out of existing signatures. Prior work supported only a small, fixed set of subrings. In our formalization, we find that several desiderata for an anonymous image provenance system are fundamentally incompatible. In particular, we prove that shrinking ring signatures requires work linear in the number of signatures shrunk, and in some settings, linear-sized public evidence; both are impractical at a global scale. We then explore the resulting trade-off space and analyze candidate systems making different choices among the strength of authenticity guarantees, network access requirements, and post-quantum security. Our work answers calls for a more private image provenance system and identifies several paths toward practical solutions.
papers.authors: Kelsey Merrill, Sarah Scheffler

papers.title: Karu64: An Open RVA23 Processor with Vector Keccak Support
papers.abstract: Can a whole-permutation Keccak instruction provide useful post-quantum acceleration inside a general-purpose vector application processor, despite its 1600-bit state and limited register-file bandwidth? We present, to our knowledge, the first hardware implementation of the standards-track RISC-V Zvknhk Vector Keccak extension. We integrate it alongside other vector cryptography support into Karu64, a new open-source application processor supporting the RVA23S64 profile. The complete system boots Debian Linux on a VCU118 FPGA at 75 MHz, allowing realistic OpenSSL benchmarking. Architecturally, the vkeccak.vi instruction gathers the state once, performs the permutation, and returns it through existing vector registers. This gives it excellent performance and allows usage from unmodified Linux userspace. In ideal-memory RTL simulation, resident-state SHAKE128/256 absorption and squeezing are $79$ - $83\times$ and $105$ - $116\times$ faster, respectively, than Clang-generated vector-enabled C with Zbb and Zvbb extensions. FPGA measurements under Linux show end-to-end ML-KEM and ML-DSA operations gain $1.48\times$ and $1.65\times$, respectively, over hand-vectorized implementations, due to the central role of Keccak in these PQC standards. A NanGate45 synthesis comparison shows a 2.29 % core-area increment over the implemented ratified-crypto baseline. These results establish practical feasibility of the fixed-group instruction, connecting standards-track semantics to integrated hardware cost and measured application benefit in a working Linux system.
papers.authors: Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, Thomas Szymkowiak

papers.title: A Quasipolynomial Quantum Algorithm for the Vector Dihedral Coset Problem with Smooth Modulus
papers.abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for the vector dihedral coset problem over $\mathbb{Z}_q^n$, in which the goal is to recover $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{Z}_q^n$ given independent samples of the form $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(\ket{0,\mathbf{x}}+\ket{1,\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{s}}\bigr)$, for $\mathbf{x}\sim \mathbb{Z}_q^n$. When the modulus $q$ is $B$-smooth, the algorithm uses $n^{O(B^{1+o(1)}\log q)}B^{O(B^{2+o(1)}\log q)}$ samples and time. For $B = \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ and $q=\mathrm{poly}(n)$, this gives a quasipolynomial time- and sample-complexity. This extends the previously known quasipolynomial-time result for power-of-two moduli (Bonnetain, Naya-Plasencia, ASIACRYPT 2018; Bai, Jangir, Kirshanova, Ngo, Youmans, CRYPTO 2025). The algorithm proceeds by reducing the modulus one prime factor $p | q$ at a time. The key ingredient is a sieving procedure that clears the non-linear terms in the phase modulo $p$ via an algorithm of Ivanyos and Santha (TCS 2017) that finds non-zero $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{F}_p^\ell$ such that $\sum_{i \in [\ell]} u_i^d \mathbf{a}_i = 0 \mod p$ for degrees $1 \le d \le p-1$, given vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_\ell \in \mathbb{F}_p^n$ as input. The algorithm also applies to the extrapolated dihedral coset problem (EDCP) introduced by Brakerski, Kirshanova, Stehlé, and Wen (PKC 2018), which is known to be equivalent to LWE in the polynomial sample regime. However, our result does not yield a new attack on LWE in any regime, precisely because the known reduction from LWE to EDCP provides only polynomially many clean samples, whereas our algorithm requires quasipolynomially many samples. The main algorithm was obtained in a GPT-5.6 Sol conversation prompted by the author; the author is responsible for all statements, proofs, and correctness. Concurrent work of Boucher, Fouque, and Shen gives an algorithm with similar guarantees for prime-power moduli.
papers.authors: Aparna Gupte

papers.title: Complexity-Theoretic Consequences of Zero-Knowledge with Inefficient Simulation
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge ($\mathsf{ZK}$) protocols are one of the most fundamental cryptographic primitives. Classic results in the 1980s established that one-way functions (OWFs) suffice for constructing $\mathsf{ZK}$ for $\mathsf{NP}$ (Goldreich-Micali-Wigderson [JACM'91], Naor [CRYPTO’89], Hastad et al. [SICOMP’99]). Moreover, OWFs are, in fact, necessary for $\mathsf{ZK}$ for $\mathsf{NP}$, due to the classic result of Ostrovsky and Wigderson [ISTCS'93], which was recently strengthened by Hirahara and Nanashima [STOC'24]. But for many applications of $\mathsf{ZK}$, it suffices to consider a slight relaxation of the $\mathsf{ZK}$ property where the simulator is allowed to run in super-polynomial time (Pass [Eurocrypt'03]). Surprisingly, the results of Ostrovsky and Wigderson break once we allow even a slightly inefficient simulator. Indeed, a recent result by Baril and Haitner [CRYPTO'26] shows that, without efficient simulation, $\mathsf{ZK}$ does not imply one-way functions in a black-box manner. We show that two-message arguments with a (non-trivial) inefficient simulator imply the errorless average-case hardness of the Minimum Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity Problem ($\mathsf{MKtP}$) over the uniform distribution. The hardness of the same problem against two-sided error algorithms is known to imply OWFs (Liu and Pass, [FOCS'20]). As far as we know, this result is the first complexity-theoretic consequence of $\mathsf{ZK}$ with even just slightly super-polynomial-time simulation.
papers.authors: Gal Arnon, Noam Mazor, Rafael Pass, Jad Silbak

papers.title: A Note on the Unforgeability Hierarchy of Non-Interactive Threshold Signatures, with a Mechanisation in EasyCrypt
papers.abstract: Bellare et al. (CRYPTO 2022) define a hierarchy of unforgeability notions for non-interactive threshold signatures, TS-UF-0 to TS-UF-4 and TS-SUF-2 to TS-SUF-4. They prove that each notion implies the weaker ones and that TS-UF-0 implies TS-UF-1 with a loss of $\binom{ns}{t-1}$ for $ns$ servers and threshold $t$, and they separate every other pair of notions. Cremers, Peltonen and Zhao (2024) showed that TS-UF-4 does not imply TS-UF-3, and Bellare, Tessaro and Zhu revised the definitions in response. We give machine-checked proofs in EasyCrypt of the revised hierarchy, of the loose implication from TS-UF-0 to TS-UF-1, and of the attacks behind the separations. We also prove that the loss of $\binom{ns}{t-1}$ is optimal for an implication that holds for every scheme, up to the security of a signature scheme.
papers.authors: João Diogo Duarte

papers.title: Generic Construction of Public-key Encryption with Bidirectional Keyword Search
papers.abstract: Public-key Encryption with Bidirectional Keyword Search (PEBKS), proposed by Zhang, Qin, Dong, and Tian (Computer Standards & Interfaces, 2021), extends the functionality of Public-key Encryption with Keyword Search (PEKS) by allowing not only the receiver but also the sender to generate trapdoors for keyword search. In this paper, we identify a close relationship between PEBKS and Public-key Authenticated Encryption with Keyword Search (PAEKS). Leveraging the generic construction of PAEKS proposed by Li and Boyen (IACR Communications in Cryptology, 2024), which is based on Non-Interactive Key Exchange (NIKE) and symmetric-key Equality Predicate Encryption (EPE), we show that PEBKS can also be generically constructed from the same building blocks. While Zhang et al. proposed a concrete pairing-based PEBKS scheme, our generic construction yields PEBKS instantiations under a wide range of cryptographic assumptions, including pairing-free Diffie-Hellman assumptions, lattices, isogenies, and codes. Furthermore, we define Key Collision Resistance for EPE as a new security property required for proving Consistency of PEBKS. We prove that the Li-Boyen EPE construction based on a pseudorandom function (PRF) achieves this property if the underlying PRF is Key Collision Resistant. We also discuss the use of AES and HMAC as the underlying PRF in light of the key collision attack reported by Taiyama et al. (Asiacrypt 2024). Since Key Collision Resistance is likewise required for proving Consistency of PAEKS, our result complements the Li-Boyen generic construction of PAEKS and is of independent interest.
papers.authors: Riku Matsui, Keita Emura

papers.title: Short-Input Random Oracles (and PRFs) over Abelian Groups: New Generalisations and Better Bounds
papers.abstract: At Eurocrypt '26, Bhaumik et al. initiated a systematic study of short-input random oracles built from public random permutations over $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$. While their main focus was on length-preserving random oracles, they also proved that XORP, the expanding construction at the core of CENC (Iwata, FSE '06), is indifferentiable from a random function up to about $N^{2/3}$ queries for a permutation with domain size $N$ ($= 2^n$). We extend this study in several directions. For classifying short-input expanding random oracles, we introduce GXP, a family of constructions that use independent random permutations over an arbitrary abelian group of order $N$ to build a function with several output blocks, each the difference of two masked permutation outputs. GXP covers XORP with one or several permutations, LXoP (Dinur, Eurocrypt '25), and the widely-studied sum of two permutations. We study the security of GXP in both keyless and keyed settings. In the keyless setting, a recent preprint from Kim has shown that the sum of two permutations over $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ with a class of simulators called uniform simulators achieves a tight indifferentiability from a random oracle up to about $N^{3/4}$ queries. We build on this analysis, and prove that every member of GXP, over every finite abelian group, with arbitrary automorphism masks (under an extra width condition for some singular masks) and with unused permutation inputs, is indifferentiable up to about $N^{3/4}$ queries, for a uniform simulator with three trials and an acceptance coin. For admissible masks we give a sharper bound with explicit constants; other masks only add lower-order terms. The coin is necessary: without it, the simulator is distinguishable at about $N^{2/3}$ queries. Extending Kim's attack, with coset progressions in place of subgroups, we show that the exponent $3/4$ is tight for this simulator, for every family whose construction domain has density bounded below. In the keyed setting, we extend the Fourier-analytic method put forward by Bhaumik et al. in another recent preprint, and establish the pseudorandomness with advantage $O_w(q/N^{3/2})$ for every rigid-free member of GXP, with explicit constants and over every finite abelian group. Pseudorandomness is thus governed by rigid-freeness, a strengthening of admissibility: rigid pairs and non-admissible masks can both limit it to about $q/N$, while neither affects the indifferentiability exponent. The fork constructions ForkEDMD and ForkCENC of Dutta et al., and EDMD, in which the output of one permutation call becomes the input of all the other calls, are not members of GXP. A change of variables on the permutations turns each of them into a member with exactly the same security, so all our results apply to them as well.
papers.authors: Ritam Bhaumik

papers.title: LNRPIR: High Throughput PIR with Flexible Communication-Computation Trade-offs
papers.abstract: Private information retrieval (PIR) is a powerful cryptographic primitive with numerous applications. Recent works have largely pursued two different directions: minimizing online communication at the expense of high online computation costs, or achieving high server throughput while incurring substantial online communication overhead. In this work, we introduce LNRPIR, a PIR scheme that achieves high server throughput with moderate online communication overhead. LNRPIR also provides flexible trade-offs between communication and computation, addressing a gap in the trade-off space left by prior works. Our evaluation shows that LNRPIR retrieves a $256$-byte record from an $8$ GB database $2.541\times$ faster than VIA-C (S&P 2026), a state-of-the-art protocol in the client-hint model, with only $10.473$ KB of online communication. Furthermore, compared with InsPIRe (S&P 2026), a state-of-the-art protocol in the silent-preprocessing model, LNRPIR achieves $17.074\times$ lower online communication overhead for an $8$ GB database, while incurring only $1.885\times$ the online computation time of InsPIRe. LNRPIR primarily relies on three novel ciphertext conversion techniques: LWE-to-NTRU conversion, LWE-to-VNTRU conversion, and NTRU-to-RLWE conversion.
papers.authors: Liren Xu, Zhe Li

papers.title: SPECTRA: Sensor Provenance and Execution Through Recursive Arguments
papers.abstract: Autonomous systems plan and act on sensor data, yet existing integrity measures protect that data only after it has been produced. Signature- or proof-based schemes trust every processing stage that runs prior to the protection, so an attacker with privileged access can manipulate the data before any cryptographic measure applies. We propose SPECTRA, a novel, general sensor model that moves the trust boundary as close as possible to the analog domain while attesting every stage in the digital domain. We formally define the SPECTRA sensor by leveraging the recursive arguments of Non-uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC), define when a stage is attested, with the resulting trust boundary, and compare it to the state of the art, identifying a trust gap, where current solutions protect a single stage, or trust the whole sensor until the data leaves it. Furthermore, we instantiate SPECTRA for the camera pipeline (SPECTRA-CAM), with Bayer-compliant step circuit implementation, and evaluate it on CPU and GPU, from an embedded NVIDIA Jetson to high- end server hardware, over a wide range of frame sizes. Finally, we expose the limitations of the state of the art with Pipeline Ordering Shuffling Attacks, showing that merely reordering the pipeline stages can mislead downstream classifiers while the output still carries a valid signature. In the context of this attack we show why the state of the art falls short, and motivate the need to rethink sensor attestation from a data-centric perspective. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first image pipeline proven with NIVC, optionally in zero-knowledge, and the first image-based proof system evaluated directly on commodity embedded hardware, the NVIDIA Jetson, which proves frames up to 4K in under 6 GiB of memory. With GPU acceleration, its proving time on utility frame sizes is on average 3.1× lower than on its CPU, and on classifier-sized frames it stays within tens of seconds of server-grade hardware.
papers.authors: Marco Calipari, Paul Timke Contreras, Mohammad Hamad, Sebastian Steinhorst

papers.title: γ₁₁: Computational Certificates — the macadamias 0001, 0014, 0015, 0059 and 0052
papers.abstract: The macadamias are the ten perfect forms of rank 9 for which the proof of the Hermite constant $\gamma_{11}$ cannot be completed at rank 10. Four of them, 0001, 0014, 0059 and 0015, were treated at rank 11 by contact geometry in our previous work, and a fifth, 0052, by a gluing argument with a computer proof. To reduce dependency on pen-and-paper mathematical proofs and increase confidence in the announced results, this paper gives a second, machine-checked confirmation of these five cases. The new proof relies on computed certificates. A certificate counts only in general mode: it must hold for every lattice of rank nine that is admissibly marked by the form, and not only for the form itself. The certificate of a form is a tree of boxes over the space of its first gluings, every leaf of which is checked exactly, together with a ball of gluings around the rank-ten lattice stored with the form, on which some leaves rely. The ball comes from an exact theorem in which the gluing and the rank-nine member both move; the bound $\det L\ge 972$ follows from the inequality $\det L\ge\det M\,(4-\rho^2(M))$ between a lattice $L$ of rank 11, its primitive sublattice $M$ of rank 10 and the covering radius $\rho(M)$. For 0059 the ball uses a contact-cone certificate of degree three; for 0015, whose stored lattice has no margin, a sharper localisation and an off-mean covering bound, both proved here; 0052 needs no ball. We state what each program checks, give the checking algorithms, all in integer and rational arithmetic, including a parallel final verification of a tree, and describe the publicly available database that stores the certificates, with the commands that check each form again from the database, the build and the reproduction pack. Floating point is used to find certificates but never to accept them. The five certificates check again, by a second route, the proofs of these five cases in our previous papers; they do not replace them.
papers.authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache

papers.title: PC-DGS: A Pool-Certified Dynamic Group Signature Scheme Based on XMSS
papers.abstract: Hash-based group signatures provide a conservative approach to post-quantum anonymous authentication, but existing constructions often face a tension between stateless signing, compact signatures, and dynamic group management. This paper proposes PC-DGS, a pool-certified dynamic group signature scheme based on XMSS-certified WOTS+ one-time credentials. The main idea is to separate offline credential certification from online message signing: the group administrator uses XMSS to certify user-generated WOTS+ public keys, while users later sign messages using lightweight one-time WOTS+ credentials. This yields a signer-side stateful but public-verifier stateless design, reducing the communication overhead inherited from SPHINCS+-style constructions. To mitigate batch-level linkability, PC-DGS introduces a shuffled index-pool mechanism for randomized XMSS leaf allocation. To prevent malicious-administrator framing, each user registers a Merkle authorization root that binds the administrator to a pre-authorized set of user-generated WOTS+ public keys. We analyze PC-DGS under standard hash-based and authenticated-encryption assumptions and establish public-verifier anonymity, traceability, non-frameability, revocation correctness, credential-reuse detectability, and signer-side forward security for used credentials. Parameterized evaluation shows that PC-DGS achieves low-kilobyte signatures, with representative profiles ranging from about 1.5 KB to 5.4 KB.
papers.authors: Qiyan Sang, Lin Zhou, Huiyan Chen

papers.title: CKKS Acceleration for Next-Wave Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is a powerful cryptographic tool that enables computation directly on encrypted data without first decrypting it. It allows privacy-preserving computing where sensitive data is processed in the cloud or in other untrusted environments. Emerging functional bootstrapping and coefficient-based matrix-multiplication techniques offer opportunities to accelerate nonlinear and linear computations, respectively. However, there is still a gap between their theoretical advantages and achievable hardware performance gains. We present GEAR, an algorithm–architecture co-design for efficient FHE acceleration supporting recent CKKS advancements while preserving full conventional CKKS functionality for existing workloads. On the algorithmic side, we propose FusedFBS, a fused functional bootstrapping algorithm that combines coefficient-based matrix multiplication with grafting-enabled functional bootstrapping to enable high-precision, hardware-friendly FHE computation. On the hardware side, we propose the GEAR architecture, with a Modular Systolic Array and a Mixed-Radix Constant-Geometry NTT Unit, to accelerate key kernels. These mechanisms balance efficient execution with flexibility for evolving FHE algorithms, making it a versatile FHE accelerator. We demonstrate FusedFBS through encrypted Deep Learning inference. Across representative workloads, GEAR achieves more than 3000$\times$ speedup over the CPU baseline. Compared with state-of-the-art CKKS accelerators, it delivers significant speedup under similar area and power budgets.
papers.authors: Xuan Wang, Sanjay Deshpande, Jaehyung Kim, Jakub Szefer, Tajana Rosing, Patrick Longa

papers.title: Processor-Aware Quantum Time-Memory-Data Trade-Offs
papers.abstract: Time--memory--data trade-offs (TMDTOs) provide a fundamental framework for cryptanalytic attacks that balance preprocessing,memory, online computation, and available target data. In the quantum setting, Dunkelman et al. introduced quantum TMDTO attacks based on GroverMatch, obtaining the relation $N^2=T^{4/3}M^2D^2$ for multiple-target inversion using a single quantum processor. In this work, we introduce a processor-aware formulation of quantum TMDTOs by incorporating parallel quantum computation into the GroverMatch framework. We partition the flavour space across $K$ parallel quantum processors and use quantum counting to identify a promising local subspace, followed by Grover search within that subspace. Under an idealized parallel wall-clock model, we show that the online complexity becomes $ T_K = \frac{t^{3/2}}{\sqrt{K}} $, and consequently derive the processor-aware trade-off $ N^2 = T_K^{4/3}M^2D^2K^{2/3} $. The relation specializes to the previously known single-processor quantum TMDTO relation when $K=1$. We instantiate the framework for both Quantum Hellman and Quantum Rainbow constructions and show that, for fixed $N$, $M$, and $D$, parallelization reduces the online wall-clock time by a factor $\sqrt{K}$, at the cost of increasing the aggregate quantum work by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$. We further analyze the resulting trade-off against generic Grover search under both single-processor and equal-processor-budget comparisons. Our results provide a processor-aware characterization of quantum TMDTO attacks and clarify the trade-off between quantum hardware parallelism and online cryptanalytic time.
papers.authors: Aniket Ghara, Suman Pal, Prokash Kumar Kundu, Arpita Maitra

papers.title: Six Passes Are Enough: Security Proofs for NIST AES Key Wrap
papers.abstract: AES Key Wrap protects keys entering and leaving hardware security modules and keys exchanged through S/MIME, JOSE and PKCS#11. NIST standardized it as KW and KWP in SP 800-38F and is now revising that document. In twenty-five years the algorithm has received no security proof, and apart from a remark on very long messages, nothing published explains its six passes of AES. Its design breaks the assumptions of existing proofs in three ways. One AES key serves every step, whereas proofs for generalized Feistel networks assume independent round functions; the chaining value has only 64 bits, so collisions on it occur long before the birthday bound of AES and a proof cannot exclude them; and unwrapping runs the algorithm backward on adversarial ciphertexts, which the usual arguments handle only with independently keyed halves. We prove that if AES is a strong pseudorandom permutation (PRP), the six-pass wrapping function at the core of the standard is also a strong PRP, with main term $88\,\sigma^2/2^{128}$ for $\sigma$ semiblocks of data. KW and KWP are deterministic authenticated encryption schemes, with an additional term for guessing the 64-bit check value. Our main step is to sample the intermediate values of each message from both ends, forward from the input and backward from the output, and to join the two sides in the middle, which treats forward and inverse queries alike. Every bad event then involves at most two messages and needs two independent 64-bit collisions, which we count rather than exclude. The count needs only two passes on each side of the join and one for the join, so five passes give a bound of the same form and the sixth is to spare. Two passes, by contrast, can be distinguished from random with $2^{32}$ short queries. All bounds extend to many independent keys without a loss in the number of keys.
papers.authors: Yuwen Zhou

papers.title: A New Cryptanalytic Attack on an RSA Variant Arising from Cubic Pell Curves
papers.abstract: In 2024, Nitaj and Seck introduced an RSA-like cryptosystem defined by a public key $(N,e)$ and a corresponding private key $(N,d)$ satisfying $ ed-1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{2(a-1)} q^{2(b-1)} (p-1)^2 (q-1)^2}, $ where $N=p^aq^b.$ More recently, Seck and Tchapgnouo (DAM 2026) proposed a partial key exposure attack against the same scheme for the case where $N = pq$, assuming partial knowledge of one prime factor. Using a lattice-based method, they showed that, under some constraints, the private parameters $(d,p,q)$ can be recovered in polynomial time. In this paper, we further investigate the security of this construction by considering a dual-key scenario. Specifically, in the presence of two encryption exponents $e_1$ and $e_2$, with corresponding private exponents $d_1$ and $d_2$ satisfying $ e_i d_i - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{(p-1)^2(q-1)^2}, $ for $i \in \{1,2\}$, we prove that if the prime factors of $N$ share a certain number of least significant bits, and if $d_1$ and $d_2$ share an amount of their most significant bits, then the private parameters $(d_1,d_2,p,q)$ can be computed in polynomial time. Our method combines an extension of Coppersmith's small-root technique with lattice basis reduction, leading to improved bounds compared to existing single-key attacks.
papers.authors: Brahim Chnioune, Mohammed Rahmani, Abderrahmane Nitaj, Mhammed Ziane

papers.title: Beyond Leaderless: Randomized Consensus Against Mobile Crashes
papers.abstract: Many consensus protocols fail to terminate under attack from an adversary that has the power to move between replicas and repeatedly crash one of them, even in synchrony. We present Multi-Leader Fixed-View Simplex (ML-FVS) to defend against such an adversary while keeping the simple structure and good-case latency of Simplex consensus. Our protocol extends fixed-view Simplex with multiple leaders, each of which may broadcast a proposal. At the voting deadline, each replica votes on the set of proposals it has seen so far. A hidden threshold beacon revealed after the votes gives a priority order on the multiple leaders, resolving each vote to its highest-priority proposal. Our model combines permanent adaptive Byzantine faults with mobile crashes. For a constant crash budget and Δ-delayed Byzantine corruption, we obtain O(Δ) expected latency over repeated views whose leaders start honest. With immediate Byzantine corruptions, the protocol still achieves liveness. We also evaluate the protocol under random network delays and stochastic faults, finding that multiple leaders reduce view failures even when rational leaders delay their proposals to increase rewards.
papers.authors: Ittai Abraham, Kaya Alpturer, Pranav Garimidi, Joachim Neu, Tim Roughgarden, Ertem Nusret Tas

papers.title: Aggregating ML-DSA Signatures Without Recursion: A Cross-Field Argument for the Commitment Hash
papers.abstract: Consensus protocols must compress tens of thousands of signatures per block, yet ML-DSA (FIPS 204) signatures are kilobytes long and lack native aggregation. Aerie aggregates Falcon signatures into a single succinct proof per batch without recursion, using a sum-check-based polynomial interactive oracle proof (PIOP) over the Akita lattice-based polynomial commitment. Extending this approach to ML-DSA is challenging: the hash that its verifier recomputes from the response and hint takes seven Keccak-f permutations, or nine for ML-DSA-87, which are expensive over prime fields. We address this bottleneck by proving ML-DSA's algebraic and Boolean components over separate fields, supporting all three FIPS 204 parameter sets. A PIOP over a 64-bit prime field handles the lattice relation, hint verification, and range checks, while Flock proves Keccak over GF(2). We introduce a cross-field parity bridge to enforce bitwise consistency between the two commitments. Using seeded sparse matrices, the bridge detects any fixed nonzero difference except with probability below 2^-144.6, independently of batch size. The aggregate certifies that every signature passes FIPS 204 verification. In the classical random-oracle model, each Fiat-Shamir challenge incurs at most 2^-128 soundness error per query, as in Aerie, and aggregate unforgeability reduces to the strong unforgeability of ML-DSA. On 16 AMD Zen 5 cores with AVX2, our prover aggregates 32,768 ML-DSA-44 signatures in 2.68 s, at 49.2 bytes per signature. For ML-DSA-87, it takes 4.13 s at 82.7 bytes per signature. Against the Johnson-regime variant of Alloul26, a prime-field ML-DSA-87 aggregator, our prover is 43x faster and our aggregates are 1.8x smaller.
papers.authors: Jipeng Zhang, Jiaheng Zhang

papers.title: BEEP: IOPPs from List Decoding with Better Elimination of Pretenders
papers.abstract: We present an improved soundness analysis of the DEEP technique for linear codes (after a minor modification), which, unlike its predecessor, results in negligible error bounds for parameters typically used in practice. The modification consists simply in performing $m$ DEEP samples, instead of one. The resulting DEEP sampling error decreases exponentially with $m$, and in practice $m=2$-$5$ makes it tiny. The subsequent folding error is of $(\delta \cdot n +1)/|\mathbb{F}|$, for $\delta$ a proximity parameter and $n$ the code length. We modify typical code-based IOPPs with this technique, such as WHIR, Ligerito, Basefold, etc. As a result, we obtain code-based IOPPs that only require list decodability of the underlying codes, instead of Mutual Correlated Agreement (MCA), with smaller soundness errors than their counterparts. Since it does not rely on MCA for its soundness, this improved DEEP technique allows to use arbitrary linear codes in IOPPs with $\delta$ up to the Johnson bound. Additionally, this opens the door to using codes (e.g. perhaps Reed-Solomon codes) with $\delta$ beyond the Johnson bound, assuming the code is $\delta$-list decodable, even if it does not have the $\delta$-MCA property. Finally, we also provide an affine version of our improved DEEP analysis, where the folding challenges are affine polynomials instead of field elements, following [FS26,CWYZ26]. We provide a simple proof showing that, after the DEEP samples are done, the folding error with affine folding challenges is $2/|\mathbb{F}|$, which is smaller than the affine-MCA error from CWYZ26.
papers.authors: Remco Bloemen, Albert Garreta

papers.title: When Confirmation Tags Are Not Enough: Full Key Recovery from Ordinary Decapsulation Outputs in a HCR-KEM
papers.abstract: Reconciliation allows lattice-based key encapsulation mechanisms to derive a common secret despite noise. Yet confirming the resulting verifier word need not establish that the ciphertext itself is valid. This distinction matters when a design seeks to avoid full ciphertext re-encryption by checking only a confirmation tag. We introduce HCR-KEM, a source-available reconciliation-based research construction, to examine the security consequences of that choice. We recover all 1,536 secret coefficients using only ordinary 32-byte decapsulation outputs, without an explicit validity flag. Source-admitted unit-monomial ciphertexts keep 289 non-target verifier bits fixed, allowing locally predicted-key comparisons to isolate signed relations. A publicly checkable signed-graph certificate then enables complete reconstruction. Building on this structure, graph-aware peeling uses recovered coefficients to reduce the cost of subsequent ordered searches. In reference C experiments on 50 fresh matched keys, all 150 recoveries succeeded. Graph-aware peeling reduced mean online decapsulation calls from 4,382.54 for the depth-four scalar baseline to 3,565.18, an 18.65% reduction. To distinguish this leakage mechanism from cases where it does not arise, we also formulate a conditional reconciliation-independence criterion and examine the guaranteed-rejection branch of standard ML-KEM. Together, these results show why the security of a reconciliation-based KEM must be assessed from the ciphertexts it admits and the information exposed by its complete decapsulation interface, rather than from verifier-word confirmation alone.
papers.authors: Rafik HAMZA

papers.title: The Swell Protocol: Invite-Bound Hybrid Key Agreement, a Double Ratchet with an ML-KEM Epoch Ratchet, and a Signed Server Statement
papers.abstract: We describe the Swell Protocol, the end-to-end encryption protocol of the Swell messenger, as fixed by draft 3 of its specification. First contact uses an out-of-band invite code instead of a server-held prekey directory: a hybrid X25519/ML-KEM-768 handshake in the style of PQXDH, without prekey signatures, whose transcript is bound to the invite. Sessions then run the Double Ratchet with header encryption, extended by a post-quantum epoch ratchet: ML-KEM-768 exchanges carried inside the conversation renew an epoch key that is mixed into every message key, so that after a one-time state compromise confidentiality is restored against an adversary who is passive while healing, even if it later breaks every X25519 key. Sessions between existing contacts are started or repaired by link frames sealed under a static-static key. Groups fan out over pairwise sessions with identity-signed group states. Separately, the message relay publishes an hourly statement signed under a pinned key and kept in a hash-chained, append-only log meant to be mirrored by an external witness. We state the threat model precisely, including two admitted limits of forward secrecy, and we report symbolic analyses in ProVerif and Tamarin of simplified models, together with every attack those models found; there is no computational proof. The protocol has had internal review only; it has not undergone an independent security audit. We list the open problems and invite cryptanalysis.
papers.authors: Ilyas Akbar Almadani

papers.title: Early-Stopping Dishonest Majority Broadcast with Linear Rounds and Polynomial Communication
papers.abstract: Early-stopping Byzantine broadcast protocols adapt their round complexity to the number $f\le t$ of parties that are actually corrupted in an execution, where $t<n$ is the corruption threshold known to the protocol. For every $t<n$, Loss and Nielsen (Eurocrypt 2024) gave a protocol that terminates within $O(\min\{f^2+1,t+1\})$ rounds, using polynomial communication and a plain public key infrastructure (PKI). More recent work attains $O(f+1)$ rounds for every $t<n$ via exponential information gathering, but at the cost of exponential communication. It has therefore remained open whether $O(f+1)$ rounds can be achieved for every $t<n$ with polynomial communication and computation from a plain PKI. We resolve this question with a deterministic Byzantine broadcast protocol that is secure against a strongly adaptive rushing adversary. For every $f\le t<n$, all honest parties output and terminate within $O(f+1)$ rounds, using polynomial communication and computation. This matches the classical early-stopping lower bound of $\min\{f+2,t+1\}$ rounds up to a constant factor. Our basic protocol terminates within $14f+9$ rounds and communicates $O(\kappa n^7)$ bits, where $\kappa$ is the length of a signature. Two optimized variants improve both bounds: the first terminates within $5f+2\lceil\log_2(f+1)\rceil+10$ rounds and communicates $O(\kappa n^5)$ bits, and the second terminates within $5f+2\lfloor\sqrt f\rfloor+11$ rounds and communicates $O(\kappa n^4+n^{9/2})$ bits.
papers.authors: Renas Bacho, Kecheng Shi

papers.title: Cleve's Bound Is Tight: Optimally Fair Coin Flipping for Every Fixed Number of Parties
papers.abstract: Proof-of-stake chains, committee selection and lotteries draw public randomness from protocols whose participants may collude. Cleve [STOC 1986] showed that without an honest majority, aborting alone lets a coalition bias the outcome of any $r$-round $n$-party coin flip by $\Omega(1/r)$. Moran, Naor and Segev [TCC 2009] matched this bound for two parties, and later work came within a $\sqrt{\log r}$ factor of it for three. For four or more parties, the best known bias is about $r^{-1/2-1/(2^{n-1}-2)}$, which approaches the $r^{-1/2}$ of the simple majority protocol as $n$ grows. The obstacle is recovery: after an abort, the remaining parties must carry on without giving the coalition a fresh chance to bias the outcome. In the best earlier protocol they reconstruct a noisy copy of the current expected outcome, and with more than three parties this costs a power of $r$ at each level. We show that Cleve's bound is tight for every fixed number of parties. Assuming constant-round oblivious transfer and constant-round passively secure computation, we give an $n$-party $r$-round protocol over a broadcast channel whose bias against $n-1$ corrupted parties is $O(n^3 2^n / r)$. The protocol draws the outcome at the start and keeps it secret, and the coins it reveals form a random walk conditioned on that outcome. After an abort, the remaining parties reconstruct nothing: they start a new run whose outcome probability is a public table evaluated on bits they hold in secret-shared form. Our main technical result is that the entries of every such table stay within a factor of two of each other, however many aborts came before, so each level of recovery costs only a constant factor. The protocol therefore improves on majority for up to about $\frac{1}{2}\log_2 r$ parties, and a variant for any number of parties has an exponential factor set only by how many more parties are corrupted than honest.
papers.authors: Yuwen Zhou

papers.title: Registered Hierarchy-Based Signatures from Bilinear Groups
papers.abstract: Registration-based signatures (RBS) remove the trusted key generation center (KGC) of identity-based signatures, resolving the global key escrow problem: users generate their own secret state and publish public registration material, which a curator holding no cryptographic secrets aggregates into compact public parameters. Yet many scenarios need both registration to avoid key escrow across organizations and delegation for trust control within an organization. Delegated Reg-FE (ASIACRYPT'2025) realizes this hybrid trust model for encryption, but only for $2$-level hierarchies. In this work, we introduce registered hierarchy-based signatures (RHBS), which combines registration of root users with hierarchical delegation to non-root users in $L$-level hierarchies. We construct RHBS from BBG-based hierarchical signatures using three techniques: cross-term cancellation to remove the KGC, plus affine share compression and power-of-two groups with version tag to obtain the properties below. Our construction satisfies standard compactness, efficiency, and unbounded registration. It further achieves extra compactness for the common reference string, each root user's public registration material, and signatures. It also supports non-root key updates without re-delegation and public signature updates without re-signing when new registrations change the public parameters. We prove selective-identity unforgeability under the computational asymmetric $(L+1)$-BDHE assumption in the random-oracle model, even if all other root users are malicious. We implement our construction and compare its computational and storage costs with related schemes.
papers.authors: Jiamian Yan, Hong Yang, Ziyan Yuan, Borui Chen, Liang Zhang, Haibin Kan

papers.title: Impossibility Results for Single-Cut Full-Open Card-Based Protocols with Any Number of Cards
papers.abstract: Card-based protocols are cryptographic protocols using a deck of physical cards instead of electronic computers, where information is encoded into a sequence of face-down cards and decoded by opening the cards, and random operations are realized by shuffles of cards. In this research area, there are known impossibility results for protocol construction, but most of the existing results (except for one result for a specific function under a non-standard encoding rule) are conditional on the number of cards used in a protocol, i.e., just giving lower bounds for the number of cards. In contrast, in this paper we give impossibility results, unconditional on the number of cards, for some kind of protocols computing wide classes of functions. Technically, our result is given by deepening a recently explored connection between card-based protocols and combinatorics on words. Specifically, we consider card-based protocols with the following two properties: (1) just a single random cut is used as shuffles; (2) an opening operation is used just once, where all cards are opened at the same time. It has been known that an arbitrary function can be computed by slightly relaxing (1) to "a single shuffle" (not necessarily a random cut) or (2) to "a part of cards are opened". As opposed to them, in this paper we prove that for protocols satisfying both (1) and (2), for the case of symmetric Boolean functions and Boolean functions without redundant variables, the currently known protocols are essentially all of the possible cases; for any other function (in the sense of NPN non-equivalence), such a protocol is shown to be impossible regardless of the number of cards. We also partially extend the impossibility result to functions with non-binary outputs.
papers.authors: Koji Nuida, Kazumasa Shinagawa, Yasuhide Numata

papers.title: Does Witness Indistinguishability Require Cryptography?
papers.abstract: An interactive proof is witness indistinguishable ($\mathsf{WI}$) if the verifier cannot tell which of several valid witnesses the prover used. $\mathsf{WI}$ is a fundamental privacy guarantee that is implied by a number of central primitives, including zero knowledge ($\mathsf{ZK}$), batch arguments, and succinct arguments. Ostrovsky and Wigderson [OW93] showed that, assuming the worst-case hardness of $\mathsf{NP}$, $\mathsf{ZK}$ proofs for $\mathsf{NP}$ imply auxiliary-input one-way functions. This was recently strengthened by Hirahara and Nanashima [HN24], who showed that, under the same assumption, $\mathsf{ZK}$ proofs for $\mathsf{NP}$ imply standard one-way functions. For $\mathsf{WI}$, no analogous result was known; in fact, we do not known if cryptography is necessary for $\mathsf{WI}$ at all. One source of difficulty in proving a cryptographic implication from $\mathsf{WI}$ is the possible unconditional existence of witness canonicalization. More formally, an $\varepsilon$-witness canonicalization ($\varepsilon$-$\mathsf{WC}$) is a deterministic polynomial-time map that sends any valid witness $w$ for $x$, together with public randomness $r$, to an efficiently verifiable string that depends only on $x$ and $r$ (and not on the specific witness $w$), except with probability $\varepsilon$. Completeness and soundness hold perfectly (only canonicalization is allowed to fail). Indeed, if a valid witnesses for an $\mathsf{NP}$ statement can be efficiently mapped to a single canonical representation, then $\mathsf{WI}$ is trivial and requires no cryptography: the prover sends the canonical witness, and so reveals nothing about its own. We prove the following: 1. Let $L$ be an $\mathsf{NP}$ language that admits no $\varepsilon$-$\mathsf{WC}$ for some inverse-polynomial $\varepsilon$. Then, under a derandomization assumption, every constant-round (honest-verifier) $\mathsf{WI}$ proof for $L$ implies infinitely-often auxiliary-input one-way functions. The derandomization assumption can be avoided if one settles for canonicalization with negligible completeness and soundness errors. 2. Combining (a variant of) the above with a theorem of Bitansky, Kamath, Paneth, Rothblum, and Vasudevan [BKPRV24] yields analogous consequences for sufficiently compressing batch arguments and succinct non-interactive arguments. Since it is unlikely that $\mathsf{SAT}$ has a $\varepsilon$-$\mathsf{WC}$, even for constant $\varepsilon$, the above results establish that cryptography is necessary for designing $\mathsf{WI}$ proofs (or sufficiently compressing BARG/SNARGs) for $\mathsf{SAT}$. As far as we are aware, these are the first results establishing the necessity of cryptographic hardness for witness indistinguishability, BARGs, and SNARGs.
papers.authors: Gal Arnon, Noam Mazor, Rafael Pass, Jad Silbak

papers.title: SoK: A Unified Framework for Analyzing Coercion Resistance in Electronic Voting
papers.abstract: Electronic voting (E-voting) can improve the accessibility and efficiency of elections, but its reliance on electronic systems also introduces security and privacy threats. In remote e-voting, adversaries may observe voters' behavior and obtain some electronic information, making voters more vulnerable to coercion. Hence, coercion resistance is a security property of e-voting protocols which ensures that a voter can deviate from an adversary’s instructions. However, existing e-voting protocols establish coercion resistance under different assumptions about the protocol settings, such as election environments, trust assumptions, and adversarial capabilities. In particular, e-voting protocols involve diverse procedures and interactions, resulting in different protocol syntaxes. Consequently, it is difficult to determine whether their coercion resistance guarantees hold in practical election settings and which protocols provide stronger protection against coercion. In this work, we present a unified framework for systematically analyzing coercion resistance across different e-voting protocols. We introduce a unified syntax for e-voting protocols that captures diverse coercion-resistant protocols. This syntax provides a common execution model in which adversarial capabilities can be specified consistently across different protocols. Using our syntax, we systematically express existing protocols within this framework. We also adapt standard definitions of verifiability and ballot privacy of e-voting protocols to our syntax. Using these definitions, we compare the verifiability and ballot privacy of existing coercion-resistant e-voting protocols. We then extend existing definitions of coercion resistance to our unified e-voting syntax. We systematically classify coercion-resistance settings along five axes: corruption bounds, corruption modes, coercion phases, timing restrictions, and the number of coercion interactions. We establish implication relations among the resulting coercion resistance notions to characterize their relative strength. Using this classification, we evaluate existing e-voting protocols by proving the maximality of coercer-capability settings under which each protocol achieves coercion resistance. Our framework thereby enables direct and fine-grained comparison of coercion-resistant e-voting protocols under our common model.
papers.authors: Wonseok Choi, Won Kim, Changmin Lee

papers.title: Differential–Linear Distinguisher Search via Walsh Spectra over Low-Dimensional Mask Subspaces
papers.abstract: Searching for differential--linear (DL) distinguishers in ARX and AND--RX ciphers often requires empirical evaluation of multi-round middle correlations. Hourglass(-like) structures provide effective guidance by restricting middle differences and output masks to sparse forms. However, the corresponding low-weight output-mask position need not be the most favorable boundary for empirical middle-correlation evaluation. Exploring alternative boundaries may involve multi-bit output masks, whose numerous possible combinations make empirical evaluation expensive. We propose a spectral DL search framework for efficiently evaluating multiple middle output masks. We use Hamming-weight-one correlations to select low-dimensional output-mask subspaces and apply the fast Walsh--Hadamard transform to jointly evaluate all masks in each selected subspace using shared samples. Experiments on 32-bit ciphers show that HW1-guided subspaces can recover DL candidates with correlation estimates comparable to those obtained through full-state spectral evaluation. We integrate this approach with round-split selection, automated outer-trail search, and independent fixed-key evaluation of the retained middle correlations. Experiments on SIMON, SIMECK, SPECK, and CHAM yield DL distinguishers with improved round coverage or estimated correlations. In particular, we obtain a 36-round SIMON128 distinguisher under single-trail outer-component evaluation and a 39-round result through refined outer-component evaluation. Our results further show that evaluating multi-bit masks at alternative middle-output boundaries can reveal more readily detectable correlations or reduce reliance on single-trail approximations.
papers.authors: Chenlu Zheng, Liu Zhang, Zilong Wang

papers.title: Recovery Attacks on Distance-Preserving Encrypted Vector Databases
papers.abstract: Private retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems based on distance-comparison-preserving encryption (DCPE) are widely adopted in industry to protect sensitive embeddings while maintaining low-latency search. However, DCPE inherently leaks the relational geometry of stored embeddings by preserving relative distance comparisons across ciphertexts, making its security in practical deployments questionable. This paper demonstrates that the geometric structure DCPE preserves to enable nearest-neighbor search directly exposes the underlying data manifold to full database recovery from snapshots. We introduce two practical recovery attacks: (1) Attack A, which requires only a leaked snapshot, the public encoder, and an auxiliary candidate corpus, achieving 100\% record re-identification; and (2) Attack B, which requires no candidate corpus and uses a single known plaintext-ciphertext pair to resolve the secret scale in DCPE, reconstructing embeddings with 0.997 mean cosine similarity and restoring a functional search index. Furthermore, our evaluation indicates that existing defensive countermeasures offer minimal protection. Crucially, full-database reconstruction is computationally efficient, incurring an execution overhead that is even lower than that of the original encryption pass. Therefore, leaked DCPE snapshots must be treated as plaintext disclosures, underscoring the urgent need to explore and adopt truly secure cryptographic alternatives for private RAG.
papers.authors: Chen Gong, Xiangyu Wang, Dan Zhu, Bowen Zhao, Jie Li, Xinghua Li, Jianfeng Ma

papers.title: Nonlinear Invariant Attacks on Full CRAFT: Chosen-Tweak Key Recovery
papers.abstract: A nonlinear invariant is a Boolean function of the state that every round preserves, up to a constant, for a class of keys. It then relates plaintext and ciphertext with correlation one, whatever the number of rounds. Finding one is in general a problem about the whole state. We study a family of invariants of the tweakable block cipher CRAFT for which this problem splits into independent pieces. Each function reads half of the state linearly and the other half through components of the S-box, one nibble at a time, so that the condition for a round to preserve it becomes one small condition per S-box, read once from the algebraic normal form of the S-box. The family can therefore be analysed by hand and enumerated by computer. The simplest member uses a single quadratic component of the S-box and survives all thirty-two rounds on a class of $2^{108}$ keys. Allowing cubic components and a pattern that alternates between even and odd rounds yields an invariant that survives all thirty-two rounds for half of all keys, with suitably chosen tweaks. Both classes are determined exactly, and a computer classification shows that none in the family is larger. Since the conditions are periodic with the tweakey, these invariants pass any number of rounds, not only the thirty-two of CRAFT, so increasing the round count would not remove them. The invariants give key recovery. Almost every key of CRAFT satisfies a great many of them at once, and the classification yields a library of hundreds of thousands. Running the library against an unknown key and collecting the linear relations each invariant reveals recovers, for essentially every key, an average of 61.3 of the 64 low key bits with about $2^{14.5}$ chosen-tweak queries and negligible time. Over a sample of 5000 random keys every one was broken, the remaining search staying below the 124-bit security claim in every case. All programs and data that reproduce these results are available in a public repository.
papers.authors: Roberto Civino

papers.title: Classical Free-Start Collision Attacks on Full-Round AES-256-DM and AES-256-MMO
papers.abstract: Despite extensive cryptanalysis of hash modes based on the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), no classical free-start collision attack has previously been reported for full-round AES-256-DM or AES-256-MMO. In this work, we address this problem by extending the guess-and-determine (GD) rebound methodology. Our main technical contribution is a precomputation-based method for handling conflicts involving guessed variables in the GD procedure. By precomputing solutions to the corresponding systems of byte equations, such conflicts can be resolved in $O(1)$ online time. We further exploit triangular dependencies among controllable guessed variables to reduce the memory required for precomputation. Using this method, we construct classical free-start collision attacks applicable to both AES-256-DM and AES-256-MMO. For the full 14-round AES-256, the attacks require $2^{60}$ time and $2^{24}$ memory, providing the first classical free-start collision attacks on these full-round constructions. The same approach improves the time complexity of the full-round free-start differential $q$-multicollision attack from $q\cdot2^{67}$ to $q\cdot2^{60}$, with memory complexity $2^{24}$. We also obtain free-start collision attacks on the 12-round variants with time complexity $2^{54}$ and memory complexity $2^{24}$.
papers.authors: Liyuan Tang, Yanzhao Shen, Xiaoyang Dong

papers.title: Homogeneous rotation symmetric bent functions in twelve variables are quadratic
papers.abstract: Every homogeneous rotation symmetric bent Boolean function in twelve variables is quadratic. There are exactly sixteen such functions in labelled coordinates. The main step is to rule out degree four. The proof groups inputs according to which opposite coordinates agree. Walsh divisibility forces the restriction to each group to be quadratic. The squared Walsh sums of these restrictions must then fit a fixed total. This rules out one of the three possible restrictions on the diagonal and severely limits the other two. Explicit polynomial identities exclude the remaining possibilities. The classification and the coefficient characterization were formally verified in Lean 4.36.0. The appended supplement gives the identities, the case coverage, and instructions for verifying the calculations.
papers.authors: Filipe Martins Vono, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo, Valéria Gonzaga Santos

papers.title: Linear Cryptanalysis of ISO Standard SEED: Exact Trail Optima via Divide-and-Decide Search
papers.abstract: SEED is a block cipher developed by the Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and standardized in ISO/IEC 18033-3. For more than two decades, its best linear cryptanalysis has remained KISA's evaluation: a 5-round distinguisher and no key-recovery attack. In this paper, a new hierarchical certified search framework, called divide-and-decide (D&D), is proposed to determine exact optima of linear trails rather than heuristic upper bounds. D&D divides the trail space at two levels, followed by one decision. At the pattern level, the trail space is partitioned by the positions of trivial rounds, and whole patterns are eliminated before any solver call by the F-function spacing bound (FSB) for SEED, an analytic lower bound. At the layer level, each remaining pattern is divided into layers of integer cost, and the lowest layers are enumerated with a satisfiability (SAT) solver to obtain an incumbent trail. At the decision level, the weight beyond the integer cost is treated as an excess, and each remaining layer is closed by a single SAT decision model on this excess instead of being enumerated. For SEED, D&D gives the exact 3- to 7-round optima 18.830, 33.541, 43.472, 55.027, and 65.220, and shows that every 16-round trail has weight at least 112.980. The 6-round hull of weight 53.168 leads to the first linear key-recovery attack on 7-round SEED, and the 7-round hull of weight 63.391 extends linear distinguishers within the codebook from 5 to 7 rounds.
papers.authors: Haonan Hong, Kai Zhang

papers.title: Any Friend of Yours: Asynchronous Consensus with Unknown Participants from Local Trust
papers.abstract: Byzantine agreement protocols typically assume that all processes already agree on who participates and which failures must be tolerated. In an open system, reaching agreement on this information is itself a consensus problem. We avoid this circularity by presenting asynchronous protocols in which each process acts only on its own local trust. Each process declares quorums over the identities it knows and communicates by authenticated multicast. Processes need not know the number of participants or the trust assumptions of others, and we assume no trusted dealer, common reference string, or bound on the number of identities, including Sybil identities. Unlike Stellar and prior asymmetric-trust protocols, our protocols do not require a closed set of mutually trusting correct processes. Instead, their guarantees are characterized by depth, a fine-grained, failure-dependent measure of how well each process's trust matches the actual failures. We construct validated reliable broadcast, Byzantine agreement, agreement on a core set, and state machine replication in this model. The main technical ingredient for randomized termination is an approximate common coin based only on local trust.
papers.authors: Ignacio Amores-Sesar, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Juan Villacis

papers.title: Nonlinear invariants of CRAFT
papers.abstract: This note shows that the round function of CRAFT admits nonlinear invariants that activate only four S-boxes. These invariants extend to invariants of the full cipher that hold for $2^{120}$ out of $2^{128}$ keys and $2^{60}$ out of $2^{64}$ possible tweaks. Since there are four similar nonlinear invariants that hold under independent conditions on the master key, this yields nearly $2^{122}$ weak keys for the all-zero tweak. If 64 different weak tweaks can be chosen, then for at least half of the keys, one or more of these nonlinear invariants holds. Further invariants with a slightly different structure can also be found. The same invariants were found independently by Roberto Civino. These results imply that CRAFT is, for all practical purposes, insecure.
papers.authors: Tim Beyne, Michiel Verbauwhede

papers.title: TRAVESS: Traceable Threshold VSS with Publicly Verifiable Shares and Tracing Evidence
papers.abstract: Secret sharing protects a secret against coalitions below the reconstruction threshold, but it does not stop participants from selling their shares. Traceable secret sharing (TSS) holds participants accountable for such leakage: when a coalition packages its shares into a leaked program, called a reconstruction box, that recovers the secret given enough additional shares, a tracer can identify the traitors by querying this box on specially crafted artificial shares. Meanwhile, by allowing participants to verify that their shares are well-formed, verifiable secret sharing (VSS) addresses a different threat: a dishonest dealer distributing inconsistent shares. Boneh, Partap, and Rotem (CRYPTO 2024) posed the combination of TSS and VSS as an open problem, observing that share verification allows a reconstruction box to detect and reject the artificial shares used by their tracing procedures. We present TRAVESS, a threshold construction of traceable verifiable secret sharing. To our knowledge, it is the first construction to combine public share verification and reconstruction consistency with secrecy, tracer secrecy, non-imputability, and black-box traceability in the framework of Boneh et al. Our key idea is to use a trapdoor commitment scheme to enable the tracer to generate artificial shares that pass the same public verification as genuine shares. The tracer gains this capability without learning the secret, while the dealer remains bound to consistent shares. TRAVESS supports imperfect reconstruction boxes and produces evidence that anyone can verify using public information alone. We establish these guarantees in an ideal-functionality hybrid model.
papers.authors: Wenxing Duan, Huiran Zheng, Man Ho Au

papers.title: Batched Function Secret Sharing: Parallel Generation and Key Compression
papers.abstract: Function secret sharing (FSS) enables local evaluation of secret-shared functions and is an important building block for efficient secure computation, particularly for comparisons and private lookups. However, conventional tree-based distributed point functions (DPFs) and distributed comparison functions (DCFs) incur sequential dependencies during key generation and require $O(n\lambda)$-bit keys for fixed output length, where $n$ is the input length and $\lambda$ is the security parameter. We address these bottlenecks through parallel correction-word generation and compact key representation. By sampling the states along the target path in advance, we decouple correction computations across tree levels and enable their parallel generation. For compression, we give a shared-header batch representation under an explicit label-evaluation interface, using homomorphic seed expansion to reconstruct encrypted correction words locally. A uniform sublinear header bound makes the amortized key size approach $n+m$ bits per evaluator per function, where $m$ is the payload length. For 20-bit inputs, parallelization reduces the communication rounds for DPF and DCF from 72 and 1,048, respectively, to 13, while batched FSS requires only one round. Key compression reduces the key size to 1\% of that of conventional FSS schemes and achieves key-generation speedups ranging from $3\times$ to $40\times$.
papers.authors: Tianpei Lu, Keyu Ji, Yuntian Chen, Yuan Zhao, Shoumeng Yan, Bingsheng Zhang, Kui Ren

papers.title: Blind Deep-Learning Side-Channel Analysis of XTS-AES on a Commercial RISC-V Microcontroller
papers.abstract: The XTS-AES mode is widely deployed to provide storage encryption in embedded systems, where hardware accelerators are commonly used to protect sensitive firmware stored in external flash. Existing side-channel attacks against XTS-AES typically assume access to operation-level leakage, requiring precise segmentation of individual AES executions or exploiting implementation-specific temporal structures. Such assumptions are difficult to satisfy for commercial hardware accelerators, where cryptographic operations are tightly integrated and exposed only through coarse-grained leakage. This paper presents a blind side-channel analysis methodology for hardware XTS-AES implementations that operates directly on complete power traces without requiring operation-level segmentation or knowledge of execution boundaries. The proposed approach adapted the blind deep learning-based side channel analysis to recover the XTS-AES encryption key from full-trace measurements. We further show that recovery of key can help to reconstruct the sector-specific XTS tweak, eliminating the need to recover the second XTS key. The proposed methodology is evaluated on the hardware XTS-AES of a commercial ESP32-C3 microcontroller. Experimental results demonstrate successful recovery of the encryption key, reconstruction of the sector-specific tweak, and demonstrates how this can be used to recover the flash contents. The results highlight the practical feasibility of blind whole-trace side-channel analysis against the security of hardware-accelerated XTS-AES designs.
papers.authors: Keerthi Kamalakshan, Dirmanto Jap, Trevor Yap, Shivam Bhasin

papers.title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
papers.abstract: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.
papers.authors: Yihan Wang, Haochen Sun, Xi He, Yaoliang Yu, N. Asokan

papers.title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Migration
papers.abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.
papers.authors: Xin Jin, Maximillian Liao, Handong Chen, Yi Nancy Li, Junyu Liu

papers.title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.
papers.authors: Sikha Pentyala, Steven Golob, Daniil Filienko, Ming-Chun Kao, Martine De Cock

papers.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
papers.abstract: Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).
papers.authors: Alper Cakan

papers.title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.
papers.authors: Jungmin Park, Eunha Kim, Wooseop Kim, Seongjoon Cho, Byungho Cha

papers.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.
papers.authors: Meghana Aparna Sistla, Alaia Solko-Breslin, Somesh Jha, Aditya Kanade, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham

papers.title: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Authority Closure at the Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols and Crypto Wallets
papers.abstract: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.
papers.authors: Shengwei You, Aditya Joshi, Andrey Kuehlkamp, Jarek Nabrzyski

papers.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
papers.abstract: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.
papers.authors: John Paul Steinberger, Zhe Zhang

papers.title: Detecting Formation-Preserving GNSS Spoofing of UAV Swarms through Transmitter Parallax in Pseudorange and Doppler
papers.abstract: Swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) detect Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing by checking the drones' reported positions against their known formation. Formation-preserving spoofing evades this check: in GNSS-WASP, one transmitter per satellite, a few kilometres away, shifts the whole swarm while keeping its formation. We show that such an attack still leaves a trace below the position level. Because the transmitters are close, each drone sees them under a slightly different angle, and this parallax bends the signal arrival times across a 90 m swarm by 20-40 cm for a transmitter at 5 km, whatever delays the attacker applies.
